items.title: [Bug][Frontend]: Anthropic system-turn handling (merge or in-place) breaks prefix caching for clients that append a system turn every turn; in-place re-role to user satisfies all constraints
items.author: odeda1
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM serving DeepSeek V4 Flash behind the Anthropic `/v1/messages` frontend; client is Claude Code 2.1.x. Reproduces on any model whose template sends the frontend down the merge path, and (per #52978) will reproduce everywhere once trailing-hoist lands.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Claude Code appends a `role:"system"` turn to the conversation on **every request** (a per-turn budget reminder, e.g. `<total_tokens>N tokens left</total_tokens>`). All three existing/proposed strategies in `entrypoints/anthropic/serving.py` for conversation-level system turns break prefix caching or the model for this traffic pattern:

| strategy | template-reject models (Qwen `loop.first`) | DeepSeek V4 Flash | prefix caching for per-turn system appenders |
|---|---|---|---|
| merge to leading block (#46025 fallback) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ every turn's new reminder mutates the rendered **head**, shifting everything after it — the entire conversation re-prefills every turn |
| preserve in place as `system` (#46025 preferred) | ❌ 400 | ❌ garbled output (#46710) | ✅ |
| hoist only the **trailing** suffix (#52978, open) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ the same message is *trailing* at turn N (hoisted) and *mid-conversation* at turn N+1 (in place) — it flips position between consecutive requests, mutating head **and** middle every turn |

#52978 states "Mid-conversation system turns stay in place so prefix caching … is not undone" — that holds for a one-off mid-conversation system turn, but not for the dominant real client of this API: with a per-turn trailing system message, every consecutive request pair diverges at the previous turn's reminder position, and the cache degenerates to the static system+tools prefix.

**Measured** (real captured Claude Code session, 11 consecutive requests, replayed against a single pinned replica, reading `usage.cache_read_input_tokens`):

- merge-path rendering: per-turn cache reads frozen at the static prefix; **~85% of every prompt re-prefilled every turn**; aggregate hit rate ~48% against a ~95% structural ceiling for the session shape.
- bisection: appending user/assistant turns preserves the prefix; appending one trailing `system` turn collapses the match to the static prefix.
- identical bodies with the transform below applied: **99–100% of the previous prompt re-read on every turn**, aggregate ~97%.

### Proposed fix

When a conversation-level system turn cannot be preserved verbatim, **re-role it to `user` in place** (content unchanged, block form), merging runs of consecutive user turns to keep alternation — instead of merging it into the leading block:

```python
# instead of: system_parts.append(text)  (head merge)
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": text}]})
# then merge adjacent user turns
```

This satisfies every constraint simultaneously:
- template-reject models: no system role remains mid-conversation → no `TemplateError`;
- DeepSeek V4 Flash: user turns are in-distribution → avoids the #46710 garbling attributed to in-place system rendering;
- #48874's trailing-system tool derail: the prompt no longer ends on a system block — the reminder folds into the adjacent user turn;
- prefix caching: renders become strictly append-only across turns (measured above).

The reminder text itself is preserved verbatim (Claude Code already self-labels it `<system-reminder>`), so the model-visible change is role framing only.

Related: #46025 (introduced the three paths), #46710 (in-place garbling on DeepSeek V4 Flash), #48874 / #52978 (trailing hoist). Happy to contribute the patch with the test matrix above if maintainers agree with the direction.

### Addendum: also allow *dropping* mid-conversation system turns, by config

Re-roling to `user` is the right **default** because it is lossless — but operators should also be able to opt into dropping these turns entirely, e.g. a per-endpoint flag on the Anthropic frontend:

```
--anthropic-inline-system-policy {reroll-to-user (default) | drop}
```

Rationale: mid-session system turns from agent harnesses are client bookkeeping (budget countdowns, environment notices), and open models were generally never trained on system content injected mid-conversation. For some of them this is out-of-distribution information however it is framed — we have seen models fixate on the countdown or echo it back. An operator who knows their model handles it badly today has no remedy short of a proxy that rewrites bodies; a `drop` policy gives the same append-only, cache-stable rendering with none of the injected content.

`drop` must stay opt-in and never become a default: it silently changes what the model sees, and a harness that sends *load-bearing* mid-session system content (tool-permission changes, file-change notices) would misbehave with no visible error.

items.title: [Bug]: Responses API streaming aborts mid-stream (nameless ResponseFunctionToolCallItem) with Qwen3.8 + qwen3_coder + DFlash speculative decoding
items.author: ruiwarn
items.body_excerpt:
### Current environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev1104` (main branch, 2026-08-22 dev build). Also verified that no released version up to and including v0.28.0 (2026-08-26) contains a fix for this bug.
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (FP8)
- Speculative decoding: DFlash drafter enabled
- `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
- `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
- Client: `/v1/responses` with `stream: true` (via LiteLLM)

### 🐞 Describe the bug

In agentic (tool-heavy) workloads, the Responses API SSE stream aborts mid-stream with no terminal `response.*` event, leaving the client with an unclassifiable truncated stream. The failure is intermittent but recurrent.

### Error message

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponseFunctionToolCallItem
name
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
...
RuntimeError: Caught handled exception, but response already started.
```

### Root cause analysis

The crash occurs when a single engine step spans the end of a tool call and the start of the following reasoning/content segment — speculative decoding makes such multi-boundary steps common.

`split_delta()` decomposes a compound `DeltaMessage` in the fixed order reasoning → content → tool_calls. When the tool-call part of the compound delta is the *argument tail* of an already-open tool call (its first `DeltaToolCall` carries no function name — e.g. the flush emitted by the parser engine at `</tool_call>`), replaying it *after* reasoning/content means the state machine has already transitioned away and closed the call. The tail then forces `SimpleStreamingEventProcessor.open()` to construct `ResponseFunctionToolCallItem(name=None)`, which fails pydantic validation. Because the SSE response has already started, the exception aborts the stream without any terminal event.

### Reproducing the problem

Serve the model with the configuration above, then send an agentic, tool-heavy prompt to `/v1/responses` with `stream: true`. The crash is intermittent (depends on where step boundaries fall relative to tool-call boundaries) but recurs reliably in tool-heavy workloads with speculative decoding enabled.

### Impact and workaround

We cannot use the `/v1/responses` streaming path for this deployment. As a workaround we set `use_chat_completions: true` in LiteLLM to route traffic through `/v1/chat/completions`, which loses the Responses API path for this deployment. There is no release containing a fix, so we are stuck on a dev build with no supported upgrade path.

items.title: [Bug]: DecodeBenchConnector repeats KV cache fills for shared state tensors at large batch sizes
items.author: Pipiho
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
- Python: 3.12.3
- vLLM: 0.25.1
- PyTorch: 2.12.1
- Engine: vLLM V1
- KV connector: DecodeBenchConnector
- Execution backend: Multiprocessing
- Workload: Long-context decode benchmark with a large batch size (256 requests)
- KV cache layout: Hybrid KV cache with shared state tensors


</details>


### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Bug Description

`DecodeBenchConnectorWorker.start_fill_kv()` currently processes requests one by one and fills the KV cache separately for each request.

For hybrid KV cache layouts, multiple requests may reference the same state tensor. The current implementation fills the same state tensor repeatedly for every request.

Block-indexed KV cache entries are also filled per request, even when block IDs overlap across requests.

As the batch size increases, the repeated fill operations introduce significant overhead before the first decode step.

In our vLLM-MLU testing environment, this behavior was observed during large-batch, long-context decode benchmarks and was associated with worker RPC timeouts.

The repeated-fill behavior can be identified in the upstream `DecodeBenchConnector` implementation. However, the runtime timeout has so far been reproduced on the MLU backend.

## Reproduction

The issue was observed with the following configuration:

- Engine: vLLM V1
- KV connector: `DecodeBenchConnector`
- KV cache layout: Hybrid KV cache containing shared state tensors
- Batch size: 256
- Execution backend: Multiprocessing
- Workload: Long-context decode benchmark

The issue occurs during the initial KV cache fill before the first decode step.

Instrumentation of `start_fill_kv()` shows that shared state tensors are filled repeatedly across requests within a single invocation.

As the number of requests increases, the repeated fill operations can significantly increase the initialization time.

## Actual Behavior

The initial KV cache fill becomes increasingly expensive at large batch sizes.

In our testing environment, the excessive delay was associated with the following errors:

```text
TimeoutError: RPC call to sample_tokens timed out No available shared memory broadcast block found
```

A subsequent error while querying worker memory usage may occur after the worker RPC has already timed out.

The repeated state-tensor fills occur before the first decode step.

## Expected Behavior

`start_fill_kv()` should avoid filling the same shared state tensor more than once within a single invocation.

Block IDs should be merged and deduplicated per KV cache group before the fill operation.

The implementation should also avoid creating a full-batch temporary value tensor when filling a large number of blocks.

These changes should reduce redundant KV cache initialization work without changing the intended cache contents.

## Related Pull Request

This issue is related to PR #56473:

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56473

That PR discusses reducing temporary tensor allocation and fill overhead in `DecodeBenchConnector`.

## Temporary Workaround

A backend-specific workaround currently:

- Merges block IDs by KV cache group.
- Deduplicates block IDs.
- Deduplicates shared state tensors by object identity.
- Fills contiguous block ranges in place.
- Uses indexed writes for sparse blocks.

The workaround reduces redundant operations during the initial KV cache fill.

It can be removed once an equivalent upstream fix is merged and included in the dependency version.

items.title: [Feature]: Logprobs on parsed path streaming `/derender`
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Streaming `/derender` with a reasoning or tool parser (#50550) doesn't return logprobs. #55029 added streaming logprobs but only on the unparsed path. The parsed path builds its stream choices without them. A client that streams with `logprobs: true` through a parser gets nothing back.

Agreed on #47161 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161#issuecomment-5893681568): the engine is the reference for logprob token strings. Standalone `/derender`, including the parsed path should use one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` and `_correct_decoded_token` with parity tests against the engine.

Scope:

- Resolve each chunk's logprobs and attach them to whatever delta the parser emits. `/v1/chat/completions` does the same, with one `logprobs.content` list no matter which field the tokens land in.
- Update `logprob_context_token_ids` on the parsed path, like the plain path does. Keep it starting empty, like the engine.
- Drop logprobs on every chunk when `include_reasoning=false` with a parser, like the engine does.
- Fix batch derender too. `_derender_chat` clears `reasoning` but still returns the logprobs.
- Add parity tests against `/v1/chat/completions` with `include_reasoning` on and off, a chunk the parser swallows (tool-call markup) and a multi-byte char split across chunks.

`DerenderStreamState` stays as is. Chunk logprobs already cover only that chunk's tokens and replay never touches them, so no cursor is needed. #59510 handles streaming stop with a 400, so no pending text field either.

~Blocked on #58181 (still open).~ The shared helper (`decode_token_ids`) and the parity tests depend on it.

@shimib has offered to take this. @hyeongyun0916 will review and help with repros.

### Alternatives

Re-resolving token strings separately in the parsed path. We ruled this out on #47161 because the paths already disagree (see #59241).

### Additional context

- #47161: RFC thread where this was agreed
- #55029: streaming logprobs for the unparsed path
- #50550: parser aware streaming derender
- #58181 / #57574: `GenerateLogProbs` with integer token IDs
- #59241 / #59252: SentencePiece leading space dropped in derender logprob strings
- #57052 / #59510: stop handling on derender. #59510 makes streaming `/derender` return 400 on `stop` and notes that logprobs aren't trimmed to the cut text.

items.title: [Bug]: xLAM tool parser (streaming) drops arguments nested deeper than two levels and truncates at a `}` inside a string
items.author: the-Shallow
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.30.0 (the latest release) and 0.28.0, CPU, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug `xLAMToolParser.extract_tool_calls_streaming` extracts each call's `arguments` object with a regular expression that allows only one inner level of braces and ignores string literals. items.title: [Bug] pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True) raises when a streaming-input session is parked between turns
items.author: shivasathishs-rp
items.body_excerpt:
## What breaks

`pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)` raises `RuntimeError` and leaves the engine in `PauseState.PAUSED_ALL` whenever a resumable streaming-input session is parked between turns.

That call is verbatim the recipe in `docs/training/async_rl.md:18`:

```python
await engine.pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
```

It is also the only one of the four mode/clear_cache combinations that is both cache-sound and trajectory-preserving, and it is the only one that fails.

| mode | clear_cache | result |
|---|---|---|
| keep | True | **RuntimeError** |
| keep | False | ok, KV computed under the old weights survives the update |
| abort | True | ok, trajectory destroyed |
| abort | False | ok, trajectory destroyed |

Over HTTP this is `POST /pause?mode=keep`, where `clear_cache` defaults to `True`. The exception is caught by the generic handler at `vllm/entrypoints/rl/online/api_router.py:70` and returned as HTTP 500 at `api_router.py:74`.

## Reproducer

Pure CPU. No GPU, no weights, no model. Drop next to `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_scheduler_reset_prefix_cache`.

The parking helper is lifted from the suite's existing `test_pause_new_ignores_streaming_session_waiting_for_input` (`tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py:2710`), so this is the suite's own notion of a parked session rather than a hand-built state.

```python
def _park_streaming_session(scheduler):
    """Stop a resumable streaming request so it parks between turns."""
    stop_token = 7
    (session,) = create_requests(
        num_requests=1, num_tokens=4, stop_token_ids=[stop_token], req_ids=["s"]
    )
    session.resumable = True
    scheduler.add_request(session)
    output = scheduler.schedule()
    scheduler.update_from_output(
        output,
        ModelRunnerOutput(
            req_ids=["s"], req_id_to_index={"s": 0}, sampled_token_ids=[[stop_token]]
        ),
    )
    return session


def test_reset_prefix_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    session = _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    assert session.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ
    assert session in scheduler.kv_holding_waiting
    assert not scheduler.running
    # The parked session still holds its KV blocks.
    assert scheduler.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids("s")[0]

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)
```

That is the smallest failing call. One parked session is enough; one block held is enough.

Going through `EngineCore` reproduces the documented call and shows the second half of the problem, which is the state the engine is left in:

```python
def test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    core = object.__new__(EngineCore)
    core.scheduler = scheduler
    core.model_executor = Mock(is_sleeping=False)
    core.mm_receiver_cache = None
    core.batch_queue = None

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)

    # The engine is left paused: the pause state is set before the cache reset.
    assert core.is_scheduler_paused()
    assert scheduler.pause_state == PauseState.PAUSED_ALL
```

### Traceback

Captured before the `pytest.raises` wrapper was added.

```
tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py: in test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session
    core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:932: in pause_scheduler
    self._finish_pause(clear_cache)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:904: in _finish_pause
    self._reset_caches()
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:891: in _reset_caches
    if not self.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:859: in reset_prefix_cache
    return self.scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2869: RuntimeError
E   RuntimeError: Failed to reset KV cache even when all the running requests are
    preempted and moved to the waiting queue. This is likely due to the presence of
    running requests waiting for remote KV transfer, which is not supported yet.

------------------------------ Captured log call -------------------------------
WARNING  vllm.v1.core.block_pool:block_pool.py:839 Failed to reset prefix cache because some blocks (1) are not freed yet
```

## Code path

Six links, each read at the commit below.

**1. A resumable request is not finished, so it is never freed.** `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2464`, `_handle_stopped_request` returns `False` for a resumable request after setting `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ` and calling `_enqueue_waiting_request`. The caller at `scheduler.py:2227` calls `_free_request` only on `True`.

**2. The request leaves `self.running` and lands in `kv_holding_waiting`.** Removal at `scheduler.py:2294`. `_enqueue_waiting_request` at `scheduler.py:2456` routes to `kv_holding_waiting` when `_holds_kv_blocks(request)` is true.

**3. `_holds_kv_blocks` is true for this request.** `scheduler.py:2444`. A session with trajectory tokens has `num_computed_tokens > 0`. Its own comment names the case: "While always the case when status is `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` or `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`".

**4. `reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)` drains only `self.running`.** `scheduler.py:2839`, drain loop at `scheduler.py:2857-2859`. The string `kv_holding_waiting` does not appear anywhere in that function, so a parked session is never drained and its blocks are never released.

**5. `block_pool.reset_prefix_cache()` returns `False` because a block is still in use.** `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:827`, the used-block check at `block_pool.py:838`, the warning at `block_pool.py:839`. The repro log shows `blocks (1) are not freed yet`.

**6. The scheduler raises.** `if` at `scheduler.py:2868`, `raise` at `scheduler.py:2869

items.title: [Feature]: TTL-based Eviction for KV Cache Blocks
items.author: mrghofrani
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

As you may know, major LLM providers apply a retention period to stored KV cache. For example, OpenAI retains the KV cache for GPT-5.6 and later models for 30 minutes after its most recent read or write ([source](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching#cache-lifetime-gpt-5-6-and-later)). vLLM has only limited support for this. The only relevant option I could find is `decoder_kv_blocks_ttl` ([source](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/nixl_kv_cache_lease/#bidirectional-kv-transfer)), which sets time-based eviction for KV cache stored on the GPUs of the decode stage in PD disaggregation. Beyond that, based on [this discussion](https://discuss.vllm.ai/t/how-to-adjust-prefix-caching-timeout/1663) and [this GitHub issue](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/8333), vLLM doesn’t support TTL-based prefix cache eviction.

Note that what I have in mind is simpler than memory pinning, as discussed in GitHub issues #51428 and #37003. vLLM would keep its existing LRU eviction as is, but [`KVCacheBlock`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/624a5ddafd96df23fe2b9f6d4b8f52a08b9fe9ea/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py#L154) would gain an `expires_at` field, and a block would be lazily evicted after expiration time is passed.

So my question is: would this feature be useful for vLLM? I’ve already implemented the eviction method described above and would like to open a PR. Since a PR involves more than just sharing code, I wanted to check first whether there’s interest. If so, I’d be glad to clean up the code, add documentation, and submit it.

### Alternatives

items.title: [Feature] Parallelize module loading to speed up server launch and refit for Diffusion models
items.author: zhaochenyang20
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Based on the detailed breakdown in issue #19087, the current launch process for SGLang Diffusion (using Qwen-Image as an example) is heavily bottlenecked by module loading, which currently happens sequentially.

As shown in the profiling results, `load_modules` takes approximately 63.20s out of the total 77.09s launch time (~82%).

- `text_encoder`: 32.96s (52% of loading time)
- `transformer`: 29.76s (47% of loading time)
- `vae/tokenizer/scheduler`: < 1s combined.

Since these modules (Text Encoder, Transformer, VAE) are independent during the instantiation and weight-loading phase, the current sequential execution is suboptimal. We should implement a parallel loading strategy for `load_modules`. By using multi-threading (e.g., `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` or other parallel weights load strategies in SGLang LLM already) to trigger the initialization and weight transfer of the text encoder and transformer simultaneously, we may theoretically reduce the module loading time from ~63s to ~33s (the max of the two major components).

Benefits:

1. Faster Cold Start: Significantly reduces the time for `launch_server`.
2. Optimized Refit/Wake-up: As discussed in #19090, if we support offloading and waking up, parallelizing the weight reload from CPU/Disk to GPU will make the "wake-up" latency much lower.

Implementation Consideration:

1. Ensure thread safety for CUDA context operations during `model.to(device)`.
2. Monitor Peak CPU memory usage when loading multiple state dicts into RAM simultaneously before moving them to GPU.


---------


Apart from this, it should also be helpful to validate whether we are loading the weights with Pageable memory.


https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/19087#issuecomment-3937649804

Spend 32s in loading `text_encoder` looks strange, since if we are using Pinned memory, the load speed could be much higher.

items.title: [Bug] Decoded audio duration and sample count are unbounded during multimodal preprocessing
items.author: JPengLi
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`load_audio` decodes the entire audio stream into memory with no duration, sample-count, channel-count, or decoded-byte ceiling:

- `python/sglang/srt/utils/common.py:1872-1963` normalizes caller input and invokes the decoder.
- TorchCodec path calls `decoder.get_all_samples()` at lines 1917-1925.
- SoundFile fallback calls `sf.read(source)` at lines 1938-1942.
- PyAV path in `multimodal/audio_from_video.py:89-128` appends every resampled frame and then `np.concatenate(chunks)`.
- `multimodal/processors/base_processor.py:993-997` passes attacker-controlled audio data directly to this function.

A compressed audio container can therefore be small on the wire but expand to hours of PCM in memory. If resampling is needed, the fallback also creates an additional floating-point tensor before returning a NumPy waveform.


### Reproduction

This source-audit reproduction needs an audio-capable model. In an isolated environment, create a long mono FLAC file:

```bash
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anullsrc=r=16000:cl=mono" \
  -t 21600 -c:a flac long-silence.flac
```

Submit it to an audio-capable chat endpoint as an `audio_url` data URL or through the engine's `audio_data` input. Set generation length to the minimum and monitor worker RSS/cgroup memory.

At 16 kHz mono, 21,600 seconds decodes to 345.6 million samples. Depending on the decoder and resampler, this becomes hundreds of MB to multiple GB before feature extraction. Multiple concurrent requests multiply the peak.

A negative control should use the same container format with a short clip (for example, one second) to show that the issue is specifically the absent duration/sample cap rather than container support.

### Evidence

Source on `51686cf8e7fee0ae773c5c9b8ede356507abef7b`:

```python
samples = decoder.get_all_samples()
```

```python
audio, original_sr = sf.read(source)
```

```python
chunks: list[np.ndarray] = []
for packet in container.demux(audio_stream):
    for frame in packet.decode():
        _append_resampled_frames(chunks, resampler.resample(frame), mono=mono)
...
waveform = np.concatenate(chunks, axis=0)
```

No argument in these paths represents a maximum duration or maximum decoded samples. The `asr_max_buffer_seconds` server option is used by the realtime/audio-session path; it is not a cap applied to this generic `load_audio` path.

### Impact

**Availability:High**

A request with a modest compressed payload can cause unbounded PCM expansion, CPU-heavy decoding/resampling, large transient allocations, queue starvation, or worker OOM. 

Prerequisites:
- A model or endpoint that passes user audio through `load_audio`.
- Attacker-controlled audio bytes or URL.
- No outer proxy enforcing both encoded size and decoded duration.``

items.title: [RFC]: Porting compiler fusions to manual fusion
items.author: mgoin
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation.

#42770 lays out the move from full-graph `torch.compile` to manual fusion expressed directly in model code. This issue tracks the concrete porting work for **section 1-1** of that RFC: enumerating the fusions currently performed by `vllm/compilation/passes/` and mapping each one to a work item to port to a manual call site in model code. To be clear this workstream is meant to touch all existing portable model definitions where compiler fusion pass would apply previously.

The goal is **no performance regression** as we delete each compiler pass. Each fusion below is either:
- ported to a "big fused op" callable from model code,
- collapsed into another fused op,
- or explicitly dropped (with rationale).

## Proposed Change.

### Changes to QuantMethod

This is clearly needed for fusions where we are fusing the input quant op from a downstream Linear layer. When a linear layer ops in, by registering a `self.input_quant_key = QuantKey.XX`, the fused operation will return a new `QuantizedActivation` instead of a `torch.Tensor`. When the linear's kernel sees that the input is not a simple unquantized tensor, it will pass it through directly to the matmul without requantizing.

For an illustrative example for `RMSNorm + Quant` see https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42469

### Changes to Attention

TBD

### Changes to model definitions

We will initially implement these fusions for the simplest models that we can start with, and produce several subsequent PRs where we migrate groups of models to use these manual fusions, carefully testing performance and accuracy for at least one model within an architecture.

### Inventory of fusion passes

In rough priority order. Sub-issues will be filed per fused op to track ownership, kernel coverage, and the model PRs that switch over to it.

#### CUDA

- [ ] `allreduce + rms_norm[+quant]` (`AllReduceFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43499
  -  [ ] No quant
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor/per-token
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `rms_norm[+add] + quant` (`RMSNormQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43500
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor/per-token
  -  [ ] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
- [ ] `silu_mul + quant` (`ActivationQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43501
  -  [x] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [x] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
  -  [x] NVFP4
- [ ] `attn + output_quant` (`AttnQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43502
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `mla_attn + output_quant` (`MLAAttnQuantFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43498
  -  [ ] FP8 per-tensor
  -  [ ] FP8 per-token-block (1×128)
  -  [ ] NVFP4
- [ ] `q_norm + k_norm + rope` (`QKNormRoPEFusionPass`) - GLM4/Qwen3 / Gemma path. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43497
- [ ] `rope + kv_cache_write` (`RopeKVCacheFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43503
- [ ] `mla_rope + kv_cache_concat` (`MLARoPEKVCacheCatFusionPass`) https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/43504
- [ ] `minimax_qk_allreduce + norm` (`MiniMaxQKNormPass`)   https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43410

#### ROCm / aiter

- [ ] `allreduce + rms_norm[+add]` (`RocmAiterAllReduceFusionPass`)
- [ ] `rms_norm[+add] + (group/dynamic) fp8 quant` (`RocmAiterRMSNormQuantFusionPass`)
- [ ] `silu_mul + group fp8 quant` (`RocmAiterSiluMulFp8GroupQuantFusionPass`)
- [ ] `add + rms_norm + router_pad` (`RocmAiterTritonAddRMSNormPadFusionPass`)
- [ ] `mla_dual_rms_norm` (`MLADualRMSNormFusionPass`)

#### Compiler housekeeping (to drop, not port)

These exist only to clean up the IR and keep the compiler-fusion world consistent. With manual fusion they have no role:
- `NoOpEliminationPass`
- `VllmIRLoweringPass`
- `UnsafeCloneEliminationPass`
- `ScatterSplitReplacementPass` + `SplitCoalescingPass`
- `FixFunctionalizationPass`
- `PostCleanupPass`

These will be removed alongside the `torch.compile` integration removal (roughly the end-of-June milestone in #42770).

### Open questions.

1. **Sequence parallelism** SP today is opt-in (`pass_config.enable_sp`) and matters most for long-context + high TP. Basically it is a special case of all-reduce + rms_norm, where it turns `AR + RMSNorm[+Quant]` into `ReduceScatter + RMSNorm[+Quant] + AllGather`. We should decide whether to keep an SP path at all in the manual-fusion world.
2. **Async-TP** Not sure if this is possible to port to manual fusion.

### In-Progress.

- @mgoin tracks per-pass porting and files sub-issues from this list.
- @WoosukKwon's DSv4 NVIDIA implementation will be the reference port for P0 CUDA ops.
- @tjtanaa will handle the P0 ROCm ops.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: vLLM Simulator: CPU-Based CI and Hardware-Aware Performance Simulation
items.author: zhuzi-z
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation. Inference performance depends on the model, target hardware, engine version, parallelism, cache policy, and serving configuration. Exploring this space on GPU clusters is expensive, slow, and difficult to reproduce. Existing CPU-only tests cover isolated components, leaving no low-cost way to reproduce the production engine's end-to-end initialization, scheduling, cache management, and request lifecycle. The same limitation also constrains CI coverage. vLLM exposes a large and growing set of serving arguments, but testing their combinations on accelerators is slow and resource-intensive. A CPU execution path that preserves the production control flow would provide the foundation for simulation while also enabling rapid configuration and integration testing. This RFC proposes **vLLM Simulator**, with two complementary capabilities: 1. **CPU-based CI with meta tensors.** Build the model and KV cache with meta tensors and run the v1 engine end to end on a CPU host without materializing model-sized storage. This provides the initialization foundation for simulation and lets CI execute the actual model-forward path for structural validation. 2. **Simulation clock management.** Simulation requests bypass model forward and obtain a hardware-aware step duration from the clock manager. `BLOCKING` waits on wall-clock time for real-time simulation deployment, while `NON_BLOCKING` advances a virtual clock to produce performance metrics without real-time waiting. The design follows a clear ownership boundary: reusable CPU-based CI support remains in vLLM, while simulator-specific scheduling, clock management, and workload replay remain external and are integrated through hooks. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. A reusable CPU-based CI foundation in vLLM The CPU-based CI foundation belongs inside vLLM because its meta-tensor execution depends directly on model, operator, and engine shape contracts. Keeping it in-tree allows component owners to update meta support and CI coverage together with production-path changes. The proposed `load_format="meta"` path runs the complete eager v1 initialization and request-processing path without real weights or KV storage. The real vLLM configuration, model construction, quantization post-processing, backend selection, KV-cache specification, scheduler, and engine state transitions remain active. Value-dependent outputs such as sampled token IDs are synthetic; numerical and kernel correctness remain the responsibility of hardware tests. Meta mode skips device-memory profiling and derives its zero-storage KV budget from the model's native KV-cache specifications, sized for the configured sequence and context limits. The standard cache grouping, block calculation, block tables, and scheduler integration therefore remain active without requiring a parallel model-memory estimator. CPU CI executes the actual model-forward path on meta tensors. Most operators require no meta-specific work: opaque vLLM custom ops use their registered fake implementations, compiled operators whose schemas return nothing or alias an input receive schema-derived meta kernels, and accelerator-only launches are skipped at the launcher when outputs are preallocated. Value-carrying control metadata remains on CPU through request classification, while attention builders project compute-only views to the meta forward device. Explicit handling is limited to independent-output shape rules and host-side logic that reads tensor values, such as weight repacking or metadata construction. Simulation modes bypass model forward at the worker boundary, so they do not intercept or execute lower-level kernels. #### 2. A non-invasive simulator package Simulation changes runtime behavior, including request arrival, model-execution timing, and clock progression, so the simulator would be maintained independently under `tools/vllm-simulator`. Import-time hooks around a narrow set of engine, scheduler, executor, and worker seams keep simulation policy outside the vLLM serving path and limit the version-aligned maintenance surface. The hooks would be installed before importing vLLM and perform the following functions: - inject trace or synthetic request arrival times; - observe the native scheduler output for each step; - convert scheduled requests into predictor inputs such as scheduled-token count and past-KV length; - return shape-correct synthetic model outputs; and - record per-request and per-iteration metrics. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph META[In-tree CPU-based CI] A[Initialize model with meta tensors] B[Build native KV-cache specifications
from the model configuration] C[Derive the KV budget from per-sequence
requirements and configured limits] D[Allocate native block tables and
the zero-storage meta KV pool] A --> B --> C --> D D --> CI[CPU CI executes the actual
model-forward path on meta] CI --> MK[Registered fakes, schema-derived meta kernels,
metadata projection, and launch-layer skips] MK --> V[Structural validation] end subgraph HOOKS[External simulator hook points] H1[EngineCore add-request and step hooks
replay logical request arrivals] H2[Scheduler hooks
keep deferred requests visible] H3[Executor hook
extract the scheduled batch] H4[Worker hook
bypass model forward and return synthetic results] H5[Clock manager
predict and account step latency] H1 --> H2 --> H3 --> H4 --> H5 end R[Simulation requests] --> H1 D --> H2 H5 --> O[Native post-step processing and metrics] ``` #### 3. Simulation clock management For every native scheduler step, the external clock manager would build timing input from each request's scheduled-token count and past-KV length. items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to join lmcache slack channel. https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-4d1c2uk6t-55YZVvOQnJFNeAJK32U~Gg 

👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)

items.title: [RFC][MP][L2] End-to-end integrity check for the fs L2 adapter (CRC32 trailer, verify on load)
items.author: malikoyv
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The MP `fs` L2 adapter checks only a file's **length** when it loads a KV chunk. A file of the right size but with wrong bytes is served to the engine as a cache hit. The model then produces fluent garbage, and users debug the model rather than the cache.

This RFC proposes an **opt-in** integrity check:
- On store, write a small trailer (magic + CRC32) after the payload.
- On load, verify it; a mismatch becomes a cache miss and the file is deleted.

A draft implementation with tests is ready. I'd like agreement on the on-disk format and the failure semantics before opening the PR.

## Motivation

Silent-corruption reports keep reaching the tracker, and each was found by a person reading bad output rather than by LMCache:

- **#4991:** `fs_native` failed stores stay visible and cache hits produce gibberish. The analysis there found two concurrent writers of one key sharing a staging file, which leaves a torn file in place.
- **#5263:** a buffer is reclaimed while an L2 load is still writing into it.

A checksum does not fix any of these root causes. It turns an L2 content error into a detected miss, so the engine recomputes instead of silently serving wrong KV. Some related reports are not L2 content errors and a checksum would **not** catch them: #5344 (a tensor-parallel shard never written to L1) and #4247 (layout/view mismatch). This RFC is scoped to the L2 bytes.

Ways the same-size wrong bytes can reach `fs` today:
1. **Torn concurrent writes.** Writers of the same key share one temp path. The Python `fs` adapter uses the same `<name>.tmp` pattern as `fs_native`.
2. **Files from another writer or version** in a shared or reused directory.
3. **Media or firmware errors** (silent data corruption): rare per drive, but non-zero at fleet scale.
4. **Power loss or crash.** There is no `fsync` before rename, so after a crash a renamed file can contain stale or zeroed blocks.

What exists today:

| Mechanism | Covers |
|---|---|
| `fs` load length check | Truncated files only |
| AES-GCM serde | Tampering, but only when encryption with key management is enabled |
| `POST /cache/checksums` | Manual GPU-block debugging, not the load path |

## Proposal

**Config.** A new `fs` adapter field, a string rather than a boolean so it can gain algorithms later:

```json
{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/data/lmcache/l2", "checksum": "crc32"}
```

`"none"` is the default and keeps today's on-disk format byte for byte.

**On-disk format** (with `crc32`):

```
<payload bytes> | trailer: magic "LMC1" (4 B) | zlib.crc32(payload) (4 B, little-endian)
```

- Under `use_odirect`, the trailer is padded to one filesystem block so all writes stay aligned. Readers only look at the first 8 bytes after the payload, so buffered and O_DIRECT files are readable by either mode.
- The magic carries a format version (`LMC1`), so the layout can change later without misreading old files.

**Load semantics.**
- The payload is re-hashed off the adapter's event loop (`run_in_executor`; `zlib.crc32` releases the GIL on large buffers).
- A mismatch, missing trailer or unknown magic becomes a **miss** for that key. The prefetch controller already treats it as a gap, and the engine recomputes.
- The file is **deleted**, and listeners get `on_l2_keys_deleted`. Otherwise the key would miss forever: `_execute_store` skips existing files, and `fs` never evicts.

**Accounting.** Store reports the full file length, so usage stays consistent with `delete()`, which subtracts `st_size`.

**Related fix.** On the O_DIRECT path, check the byte count `os.write` returns. Today a short write is renamed into place as if complete.

## Cost

A typical chunk: Llama-3-8B, bf16, 256 tokens, about 32 MiB.

| | Overhead |
|---|---|
| Space | 8 B per file (one extra 4 KiB block allocated; 4 KiB under O_DIRECT), about 0.01% |
| Extra read bandwidth | 8 B per load (at most one extra 4 KiB page) |
| CPU per store and per load | One CRC32 pass. Measured on one host with zlib-ng 1.3.1: about 48 GB/s per core, about 0.7 ms per 32 MiB. Classic zlib is several times slower. |

Space and bandwidth are negligible; the real cost is **latency**. `_execute_load` handles keys sequentially, so each CRC adds directly to that chunk's load time. That's why this is opt-in. Hashing chunk N while reading chunk N+1 is the obvious follow-up. I'll post a `none` vs `crc32` load-throughput table on NVMe with the PR.

## Compatibility

- **Default `"none"`:** no behaviour or format change.
- **Enabling `"crc32"` on an existing directory:** old files have no trailer, so each is discarded on first access, a one-time miss.
- **A `"none"` reader on files written with `"crc32"`:** reads the payload length and ignores the trailer, so it works.
- **Shared directories:** all writers sharing a directory should use the same setting. It's documented.
- **Shared directories with `fs_native`:** it uses the same filenames, so the same rule applies. This RFC changes only the Python `fs` adapter.

## Alternatives considered

| Option | Why not (for now) |
|---|---|
| A checksum serde type (runs through the existing `SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`) | Covers every backend, but an adapter takes only one serde today, so it can't combine with fp8/turboquant; it also adds a temp-buffer copy. It's a good follow-up once serdes can chain. |
| xattr for the CRC | Not available on every filesystem (some NFS/FUSE setups); lost when files are copied. |
| A separate checksum file per object | Two files per object, and no atomic publish of both. |
| XOR / parity | No faster in practice (numpy XOR fold about 42 GB/s vs zlib-ng CRC32 about 48 GB/s on the same host), and it misses word reordering and paired bit flips. |
| crc32c (`google-crc32c`) / xxh3 | Faster on some CPUs but adds a dependency. The `checksum` string leaves room to add them. |
| Verifying at lookup | Would need a full read per lookup; load time is the natural point. |

items.title: [Bug] Client disconnect during active request crashes entire engine (uncaught asyncio.CancelledError bypasses except Exception)
items.author: MarkSight
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

- **System**: 4x NVIDIA RTX 6000D (SM120 / Blackwell, no NVLink, PCIe only)
- **Docker Image**: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv41`
- **Image Digest**: `sha256:4a5d132a06a77c8331e15845f2e925adc788b00105097ad55409afa3f4fa4860`
- **sglang Version**: 0.0.0.dev1+gda64c5cbb
- **Model**: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
- **Python Version**: 3.12
- **Server Runtime**: uvicorn (as deployed in dev-dsv41 image)

## Description

A long-context chat completion request (~200,000 input tokens) was sent to sglang via `POST /v1/chat/completions` with a client-side timeout of 120 seconds. The prefill phase exceeded this timeout, so curl aborted the TCP connection mid-request.

**Instead of failing gracefully for that single request, the entire sglang engine process crashed**, causing a complete outage of all in-flight and future requests. This is a critical production robustness issue.

## Root Cause Analysis

The sglang engine has a request-state monitoring loop (in `tokenizer_manager.py`'s `_stream_one_response` / `_wait_one_response`) that periodically polls whether the client is still connected. This poll runs every `SGLANG_REQUEST_STATE_WAIT_TIMEOUT` seconds (default: 4 seconds from `environ.py`).

The poll calls `await request.is_disconnected()` (from Starlette), which internally calls `await self._receive()` on the underlying ASGI channel. When the TCP connection is forcibly closed by the client, uvicorn cancels the pending receive operation, raising `asyncio.exceptions.CancelledError` from *inside* that call.

**Key issue:** Since Python 3.8, `asyncio.CancelledError` is a subclass of `BaseException`, **not** `Exception`. This is deliberate Python design to prevent generic `except Exception` handlers from swallowing task cancellation. However, sglang's request-handling code has numerous `except Exception as e:` blocks throughout `http_server.py` and related modules. None of these catch `CancelledError`.

The uncaught `CancelledError` propagates all the way up the stack, and something at a higher level in the process interprets any uncaught exception as fatal, calling `kill_process_tree` and terminating the entire engine.

Because the disconnect check runs every ~4 seconds for every actively-processing request, this is not an edge case — it's a broadly reproducible failure mode affecting any request where the client disconnects (timeout, user cancellation, network blip, load balancer health-check churn) while the server is mid-generation.

## Traceback

```
Traceback (most recent call last):

    raw_response = await run_endpoint_function(
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/opt/sglang/lib/python3.12/site-packages/fastapi/routing.py", line 352, in run_endpoint_function
    return await dependant.call(**values)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/sgl-workspace/sglang/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py", line 1742, in openai_v1_chat_completions
    return await raw_request.app.state.openai_serving_chat.handle_request(
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/sgl-workspace/sglang/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_base.py", line 107, in handle_request
    return await self._handle_non_streaming_request(
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/sgl-workspace/sglang/python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_chat.py", line 1987, in _handle_non_streaming_request
    ret = await self.tokenizer_manager.generate_request(

items.title: [Bug] HiCache write_through does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction
items.author: donghyq
items.body_excerpt:
# [SGLang] HiCache `write_through` does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction

## Summary

When `--hicache-write-policy write_through` is used with Mooncake Store, a first-seen prefix can be evicted from L1/L2 before all of its KV is backed up to storage. Replaying that prefix after eviction restores only part of it from L3; the rest is recomputed.

Using `--hicache-write-policy write_back --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` on the same workload restores the full prefix from Mooncake Store, so the storage backend and restore path are functional.

## Environment

- SGLang commit: `bdf8886ad3`
- Branch: `main`
- Model: Qwen3-4B
- GPU: 1 × NVIDIA H20-3e
- Attention backend: Triton
- HiCache:
  - `--enable-hierarchical-cache`
  - `--hicache-size 4`
  - `--hicache-write-policy write_through`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend mooncake`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"standalone_storage": true, "client_server_address": "127.0.0.1:50300", "enable_group_semantics": false}'`
- Mooncake Store:
  - master/client started independently
  - `root_fs_dir` and `cluster_id` configured
  - global segment size: 16 GiB
- Prompt: 5 distinct 16,011-token prefixes, `max_new_tokens=1`
- L1 capacity: 42,763 tokens
- L2 capacity: 27,127 tokens

## Reproduction

1. Start SGLang with the `write_through` configuration above.
2. Flush the cache.
3. Send five distinct 16,011-token prefixes sequentially.
4. Replay prefix A after prefixes B–E have displaced it from L1/L2.

## Expected

Prefix A should be restored from Mooncake Store with roughly:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Actual

Prefix A restores only part of the KV from storage:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 2551,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 2551,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

A second replay then reports a full device hit:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16009,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 16009,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 0,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Control experiment

The same workload with:

```text
--hicache-write-policy write_back
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete
```

returns:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

This indicates that Mooncake Store can persist and restore the full prefix when the write path is forced.

## Possible cause

In `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hiradix_cache.py`:

- `_inc_hit_count()` at line 926 skips chunked requests.
- `write_backup()` at line 856 is only called after `hit_count` reaches `write_through_threshold`.
- For a first-seen prefix, the leaf node may therefore not be backed up before eviction.
- `write_backup()` also requires the parent node to already be backed up, so a long first-seen prefix may only be partially persisted.
- `_evict_write_back()` at line 1105 shows the working control path: it stages the node to host, waits for the backup, and then writes storage.

## Suggested fix

One of the following would make the behavior clearer:

1. Add a true “write-through on insert” mode that persists the full prefix chain when a request finishes.
2. Document that `write_through` means “second-hit persistence” rather than “insert-time persistence”.
3. Keep the current optimization, but add a warning when a first-seen prefix is evicted before its backup completes.

## Impact

This affects long first-seen prompts that are evicted before a second request arrives. It can silently reduce L3 hit rate and make shared-cache routing less effective.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache + hybrid (SSM/Mamba): failed cudaHostRegister on a secondary host pool aborts the whole instance, and the error path throws TypeError thereby hiding the real rc
items.author: flymysql

### Summary

On sglang `0.5.19` (torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0, H20), starting a **hybrid SSM/Mamba** model
with `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend dynamic` fails during
`attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache` and **kills the entire instance**.

Two coupled defects:

1. **`cudaHostRegister` failure is treated as fatal.** `alloc_with_host_register` raises, which
   aborts scheduler init for all TP ranks. But the failure only means "this host pool is not
   zero-copy registered" — and sglang's own non-zero-copy path (`_generic_page_get/_set`) is
   fully functional without registration. A missing acceleration is escalated into a full outage.
2. **The error path destroys its own diagnostic.** Inside the `raise`, `cudart.cudaGetErrorString(rc)`
   is called with a **plain `int`**, which raises `TypeError` on this torch build — so the real
   `rc`/`offset`/`size` are swallowed. Operators only see a bare `TypeError`.

Additionally, the failure **leaves a sticky CUDA error**, which then surfaces later at an unrelated
call site (`_create_sync_groups` → `all_gather_object` → `torch.zeros`), which made this
considerably harder to root-cause.

### Environment

- sglang `0.5.19`
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0
- 8 × H20 (96 GiB) / 8 × H20-3e (141 GiB), driver `535.161.08`
- Model: `Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8` (`Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration`, pool stack **KV + MAMBA**)
- Backend: `--hicache-storage-backend dynamic` with `interface_v1: 1` in the extra config
  (this selects the zero-copy page functions; the crash itself is in host-pool allocation and is
  not specific to any particular dynamic backend)
- Relevant flags: `--mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct
  --hicache-io-backend direct --tp 8`

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path <hybrid SSM/Mamba model, e.g. Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8> \
  --tp-size 8 --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.80 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-ratio 1.0 \
  --hicache-storage-backend dynamic \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct \
  --hicache-io-backend direct \
  --mamba-full-memory-ratio 0.37 \
  --mamba-radix-cache-strategy extra_buffer_lazy \
  --mamba-ssm-dtype bfloat16 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 \
  --hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"backend_name":"...","module_path":"...","class_name":"...","interface_v1":1,...}'
```

Failures are **not deterministic per machine** — we observed the same config **succeed on a 96 GiB
box and fail on a 141 GiB box**, consistent with a pool-geometry / allocation-order dependence.

### Observed failure trace (verbatim)

```
[TP5] attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache failed
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../mem_cache/hybrid_cache/hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1759, in attach_hybrid_pool_to_unified_cache
    result = strategy.build(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 1329, in build
    host_pool_group, cache_controller = build_hybrid_mamba_stack(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 735, in build_hybrid_mamba_stack
    kv_host_pool = build_kv_host_pool(
  File ".../hybrid_pool_assembler.py", line 160, in build_kv_host_pool
    return kv_host_pool_cls(

    self.kv_buffer = self.init_kv_buffer()

    buffer = alloc_func(
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 235, in alloc_with_host_register
    _cuda_host_register(buffer, registration_granularity_bytes)
  File ".../mem_cache/pool_host/common.py", line 163, in _cuda_host_register

TypeError: cudaGetErrorString(): incompatible function arguments. The following argument types are supported:
    1. (arg0: torch._C._cudart.cudaError) -> str
Invoked with: 1                      <-- the real rc is only visible here, by accident
```

first pool *does* register successfully:

```

items.title: [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via /dev/shm
items.author: VNG-VMONITOR
items.body_excerpt:
# [RFC / HiCache] Same-node peer L2 sharing across DP ranks via `/dev/shm`

## Motivation

In deployments running multiple DP ranks on a **single node** (e.g. one host with 8 GPUs and `--dp-size 8`), each rank maintains a fully private L2 host KV cache. When two ranks receive requests with the same prefix — a common pattern for system prompts, few-shot examples, or shared document context — Rank B cannot see the KV pages that Rank A already produced, and must recompute the prefix from scratch.

Existing HiCache L3 backends (Mooncake, NIXL, AIBrix, 3FS, LMCache) do solve cross-instance sharing, but they all go through a networked / service-mediated data path. For **same-node** sharing that is common in single-box multi-DP deployments, the network round-trip is pure overhead — the ranks are all local processes with access to the same physical DRAM.

## Proposed design: `shm_peer_l2` HiCache storage backend

Two DP ranks on the same node map the same L2 host pool via named shared memory (`/dev/shm` tmpfs). Metadata (key → owner rank + slot address) is exchanged through a small direct-mapped index (also in `/dev/shm`). When Rank B misses in its own L1/L2, it looks up the index; on a hit, it performs one `memcpy` within the shared SHM to bring the peer's page into its own slot, then DMAs to GPU — no recompute.

Compared to a hypothetical "share via existing L3 file" approach (see `shm_cross_dp` below), the peer variant eliminates the L3 data copy: only a 288-byte pointer per page is written, giving:

- **Storage overhead**: ~55 MB total for a 475 GB L2 (vs. ~L2_size for a full mirror)
- **Read path**: 1 index lookup + 1 SHM memcpy + 1 DMA (vs. L3→CPU_buf→L2 + memcpy + DMA)
- **Write path**: 1 GPU→shared_L2 DMA + 1 index write (vs. + 1 memcpy to L3 file)

### Correctness

A per-page **generation counter** in shared memory prevents stale reads: when Rank A evicts and reallocates a slot, its generation counter increments. Rank B compares the stored generation against the current one; a mismatch is treated as a miss instead of copying whatever bytes now occupy the slot. The check is best-effort (no full memory barrier) — the tiny TOCTOU window between the generation read and the memcpy is accepted as per the "stale reads may be silently accepted" contract already present in HiCache read paths.

### Operational envelope

- `--dp-size >= 2`
- All DP ranks on the **same node** (`/dev/shm` is node-local tmpfs)
- `--hicache-write-policy write_through` required (`write_back` only flushes on eviction, so Rank B would not see data timely)
- Optionally with `--hicache-io-backend kernel` and `page_first`/`page_first_direct` layouts

Auto-computed capacity (`page_num × 4`, 25% load factor) at startup; explicit override via `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"peer_l2_capacity": N}'`.

Collision rate emitted every 10,000 writes; WARNING once it exceeds 10% (actionable — increase capacity).

## Existing prototype

A working implementation exists in a downstream fork. It shipped as two related backends registered through `backend_factory.py`:

- `shm_cross_dp` — shared L2 pool + full SHM L3 data file (simpler, more memory, extra copy)
- `shm_peer_l2` — shared L2 pool + tiny SHM index only (optimized; strict improvement)

Both reuse a common `ShmHostTensorAllocator` and named-SHM helpers added to `pool_host/common.py` and `storage/mmap/mmap_allocator.py`. Tests included: `test/registered/mem_cache/test_shared_l2_hicache.py` (CPU-only, `register_cpu_ci`), covering allocator wiring, slot partitioning, index CRUD, generation-counter stale-slot behavior, collision detection, auto-capacity, and a cross-process shared-L2 round-trip via subprocess.

The prototype hooks into:
- `HiRadixCache` — for `shm_name` derivation, `dp_rank/dp_size` forwarding to `MHATokenToKVPoolHost`
- `HostKVCache` (`pool_host/base.py`) — `clear()` partitions `free_slots` to `[slot_start, slot_start+local_size)`; `alloc()` fires registered callbacks; `slot_used` spans the full pool for cross-DP double-free detection
- `cache_controller` — `shm_peer_l2` added to the V1 interface allow-list

## The upstreaming question

We noticed [#40787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40787) (merged 2026-09-22) removed `HiRadixCache` since [#35081](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35081) migrated HiCache to `UnifiedRadixCache`. The prototype above was written against `HiRadixCache` and does **not** apply cleanly to current `main`.

Before we invest in porting to `UnifiedRadixCache`, we would like guidance from HiCache maintainers on a few design points:

1. **Integration point in UnifiedRadixCache** — where is the equivalent of `HiRadixCache.write_backup`, `_inc_hit_count`, and `prefetch_from_storage` in the unified architecture? Is there a documented extension surface for backends that need per-page alloc callbacks and slot-partitioned allocators?

2. **Shared L2 pool ownership** — is there interest in a first-class "shared host pool" concept inside `MHATokenToKVPoolHost` (dp_rank / dp_size / shm_name parameters)? The prototype adds them minimally, but a maintainer-blessed shape would be preferable.

3. **Scope split** — would you prefer:
   - (a) A single PR introducing the shared L2 pool infrastructure + one backend using it (either `shm_cross_dp` or `shm_peer_l2`), then a follow-up for the other, or
   - (b) The infrastructure alone first (no backend), then backends as separate PRs?

4. **Naming / positioning** — `shm_peer_l2` vs `shm_cross_dp` overlap significantly; would maintainers prefer we upstream only `shm_peer_l2` (the optimized variant) and drop `shm_cross_dp`, or keep both as complementary options?

5. **Alternative direction** — is there an existing or planned effort (Mooncake local mode, an internal HiCache broadcast, etc.) that already covers the same-node peer sharing use case and would make this redundant? We searched issues/PRs and did not find one but want to double-check.

Happy to open a draft PR against `main

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid attention models can fail to start with speculative decoding and --disable-radix-cache
items.author: rystewart-nvidia
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Adding `--disable-radix-cache` can make a hybrid model that works with speculative
decoding fail while setting up its caches. This happens when the target and draft
weights fit, but the default state-cache size exceeds the memory left for caches.
Hybrid models mix standard attention with layers such as Mamba or gated delta
networks, which also need memory to store their state.

I reproduced this on SGLang v0.5.21 with
`Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8` on a DGX Spark with one GB10.
It should also reproduce on any supported hardware with hybrid models that use
the same state-cache sizing code, if the target and draft weights fit but leave
too little memory for the saved state and temporary draft state of the default
48 requests.

The runs below show the failure when radix caching is disabled and the workaround
of setting a smaller request limit. Only the last run sets `--max-running-requests`:

| Mode | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Target model only, radix caching enabled | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and a test chat returns the correct answer. |
| Target model only, radix caching disabled | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and all eight test chats return the correct answers. |
| NEXTN, five steps, radix caching enabled | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and a test chat returns the correct answer. |
| Same NEXTN command, with only `--disable-radix-cache` added | Startup fails after both target and draft weights load. |
| Failing command plus `--max-running-requests 10` | Server starts, health and model-list checks pass, and all eight test chats return the correct answers. |

The target-only runs work with either radix setting. With speculative decoding
enabled and radix caching disabled, the server loads both the target and draft
weights successfully, then fails during cache sizing with the following error:

```text
ValueError: Loaded weights leave no GPU memory for the KV cache under --mem-fraction-static=0.82. Raise --mem-fraction-static above 0.686 (minimum viable = 1 - available/pre = 0.6853). If using speculative decoding, draft weights are now counted.
```

The suggested fix is confusing because the command already uses
`--mem-fraction-static 0.82`, above the suggested minimum of `0.686`. Both sets
of weights fit. The failure happens when SGLang then reserves too much memory
for the state cache, leaving none for the KV cache used by attention layers.

I would expect SGLang to choose a default state-cache size that fits the available
memory and leaves room for the KV cache, without needing an explicit request limit.

The cause appears to be in `KVCacheConfigurator._handle_max_mamba_cache`.
For these speculative runs, SGLang sets `--max-running-requests` to 48 when it
is omitted. With radix caching disabled, the cache planner treats that default
as a limit chosen by the user and sizes the state pool around it. For Qwen's
default FP32 state and six draft tokens, the saved state and temporary draft
state together need about 24.68 GiB.

Without speculative decoding, `--max-running-requests` stays unset, so the
planner fits the state cache to the available memory even with radix caching
disabled. There are also no draft weights or temporary draft states to reserve.
The target-only, radix-disabled run gets an effective limit of 114 requests;
that is calculated from the available memory, not a fixed default.

With speculative decoding and radix caching enabled, the planner fits the
state pool to the available memory. That Qwen run gets 41 state slots,
allows eight active requests, and serves successfully.

This has also been reproduced with other models that use the same state-cache
sizing code.

The GPU tests described here were run on a GB10.

Related reports:

- [#38846](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/38846) discusses showing
  the actual request limit after it is reduced to fit the state cache.
- [#24364](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/24364) reports running out
  of memory while allocating hybrid state on WSL2, including runs with explicit
  request limits. In this report, the failure occurs with the automatic limit.

### Reproduction

This reproduces on both v0.5.21 and main. I tested main at commit
`3a9cae27edec392ff8cc9f09d1164f557c653f42` with the dependencies required by that commit.

The following command reproduces the failure. I tested it on one GB10 using
the unmodified `lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.21` image:

```bash
sglang serve \
  --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 \
  --revision c5f5f263bdd5cc134092897864e8905d8fe7b928 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.82 \
  --context-length 262144 \
  --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \
  --speculative-num-steps 5 \
  --speculative-eagle-topk 1 \
  --disable-radix-cache
```

Removing only `--disable-radix-cache` makes the command
work. Leave `--max-running-requests` unset in both cases. To try the workaround, keep
`--disable-radix-cache` and add `--max-running-requests 10`.

Removing the three `--speculative-*` options also makes the command work,
with radix caching still disabled and `--max-running-requests` still unset.

### Environment

The environment below is from the v0.5.21 image used for these tests.
I also reproduced the failure on main at the commit listed under Reproduction,
using PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, sglang-kernel 0.4.9, Transformers 5.19.0, and
FlashInfer 0.7.1.

Recorded `check_env` output from v0.5.21:

```text
Python: 3.12.3 (main, Aug 31 2026

items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### MOTIVATION.

[PR #26468](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/26468) moved vLLM config hashing toward an opt-out model so new compilation-relevant config fields are less likely to be accidentally omitted from torch.compile cache keys. 

This issue tracks the follow-ups and to-dos.

## TODOs
1. Refactor all locations of `compute_hash` to `compile_factors`.  `compute_hash` isn’t the right name because real computation of the hash is actually done by `utils.hash_factors`.
2. before calling `normalize value` in `get_compile_factors`, it needs to check if .compile_factors exists on the subobject. This allows us to avoid handling `PassConfig` specially as in the case for compilation.py 
4. Uniform use of `normalize_value` & `hash_factors` across configs with a compute_hash function.
5. address this comment: [comment here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/26468#discussion_r2545031784)
6. Create a shared helper instead of inlining both `_compute_code_hash` and `compilation_config_hash_factors`
7. Refactor all locations of `compute_hash` to `compile_factors`
8. Follow up on docstrings not being up-to date in the opt-out configs
9. typing cleanups (e.g., return {} where configs don’t affect graphs; use Path for traced files; consistent DP hash validation.

always print hashed configs into cache_key_factors.json

items.title: [Bug][MP] "full" prefetch drops columns that are partly in L1 when an L1 reservation fails
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `fetching_policy="full"`, if any L1 staging reservation fails, the prefetch controller trims the request to whole columns (Step 3.5 in `_transition_to_load_phase`, added in #5434). The trim only looks at `l1_reserved_keys`, so rows of a column that are already in L1 (`l1_locked_keys`) don't count. A column that is partly in L1 and partly loaded from L2 is never seen as whole, gets released, and turns into a miss.

`_finish_request` does count L1 rows when it picks the whole columns, so the same column is a hit when every reservation succeeds and a miss when some other column's reservation fails.

This affects the "full" callers: the blend sparse leg, warm prefetch and P2P. It shows up under L1 pressure, which is also when some rows of a chunk tend to get evicted.

**To Reproduce**

Three rows, two columns. Column 0 is in L1 for rows 0 and 2 and only in L2 for row 1. Column 1 is only in L2. L1 has room for three staging buffers, so the last row's reservation fails.

```python
rows = [make_group([make_object_key(i, gid=g) for i in range(2)], gid=g) for g in range(3)]
write_keys_to_l1(l1_manager, [rows[0].keys[0], rows[2].keys[0]], layout)
store_keys_in_l2(adapter, [rows[1].keys[0]] + [r.keys[1] for r in rows], layout)
# L1Manager sized for 5 objects
```

(helpers from `tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_controller.py`)

| case | hits |
| --- | --- |
| `full`, L1 big enough | `[[0, 1], [0, 1], [0, 1]]` |
| `full`, one reservation fails | `[[], [], []]` |
| `prefix`, one reservation fails | `[[0], [0], [0]]` |

**Expected behavior**

Column 0 is complete (two rows in L1, one loaded from L2), so the second case should return `[[0], [0], [0]]`.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at 6448b447. Adding `l1_locked_keys` to the cells the trim checks fixes it.

items.title: [Bug][MP] A DAX L2 adapter can map a device L1 already uses when set at startup
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`StorageManager` doesn't check DAX device ownership when it builds the L2 adapters at startup. `add_l2_adapter` does, and `storage_manager.md` says duplicate device ownership is rejected, so this looks like a gap in the constructor.

The easiest way to hit it is a DEVDAX `--l1-manager` plus a DAX L2 adapter on the same device. With the old `--l1-devdax-path` flag that config was fine, because the matching device got moved out of L2 and used as L1 overflow. Since #5461 that only happens for the legacy single-L1 config. With the new JSON config both sides keep the device and both map it from offset 0, so L1 and L2 quietly overwrite each other's KV.

Two DAX L2 adapters on the same device get through too, and so does the same device under a different path (a hard link or symlink).

**To Reproduce**

```bash
--l1-manager '{"type":"DRAM","tag":"_default","size_gb":1}' \
--l1-manager '{"type":"DEVDAX","tag":"dax","size_gb":1,"path":"/dev/dax0.0"}' \
--l2-adapter '{"type":"dax","slot_bytes":4096,"devices":[{"device_path":"/dev/dax0.0","max_dax_size_gb":1}]}'
```

It starts without complaint. `_device_owner_names("/dev/dax0.0")` returns `['L1[dax]', 'dax']`, and bytes written through the L2 mapping show up in the L1 arena. Adding the same adapter with `add_l2_adapter` after startup fails with "already mapped", as it should.

**Expected behavior**

Startup should reject a DAX device that L1 or an earlier L2 adapter already maps, the same way `add_l2_adapter` does.

**Additional context**

Seen on `dev` at b9a5ce02. I reproduced it with regular files standing in for the device.
