items.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
items.author: mrBenBern
items.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

items.title: RadixView: a live radix-tree view of SGLang KV-cache events
items.author: ClaudeLiang
items.body_excerpt:
Hey everyone,

We are working on an agent that already has active users. While reviewing its cache behavior, aggregate metrics such as hit rate were not enough—we wanted to see which prompts and tool definitions were actually shared, and where sessions started to branch.

That led us to build RadixView. It subscribes to SGLang's ZMQ KV-event stream and reconstructs a continuously updated radix-tree view of prefix sharing and eviction.

![RadixView showing shared prompts and session branches](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ClaudeLiang/RadixView/main/docs/images/page.png)

On our own traffic, the tree exposed branches much earlier than we expected. Following those branches back to their text helped us find several problems in the agent and tool design that were reducing prefix reuse.

Shared prefixes stay on the same path, sessions branch where their text differs, and the view updates as store and eviction events arrive. You can open any node to inspect its decoded text or search across the observed cache blocks.

RadixView is only a viewer. It does not proxy requests or read the cache in-process, and it can run on a different machine from the GPU server.

Install:

`pip install radixview`

<sub>Note: The synthetic demo is not included in the pip package. Clone the repository and run `python -m examples.demo` to try it without a GPU or model.</sub>

Source and setup instructions:

https://github.com/ClaudeLiang/RadixView

Feedback is welcome, especially from people working on agent or other prefix-heavy workloads.

items.title: Resident CPU-tier prefix cache entry spuriously measures as a full miss under concurrent write load (not explained by capacity or same-key contention)
items.author: osteele
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With `LMCacheConnectorV1` (local CPU backend) serving concurrent requests, a prefix that is confirmed resident (freshly warmed immediately before measurement) still frequently returns full-recompute-level TTFT if any other request is concurrently writing a different prefix to the CPU tier, even with generous capacity headroom and no contention on the same key.

## Environment

- lmcache==0.3.12, vllm==0.13.0
- `vllm serve <model> --enable-prefix-caching --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector": "LMCacheConnectorV1", "kv_role": "kv_both"}'`
- `LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True`, `LMCACHE_MAX_LOCAL_CPU_SIZE=20` (GiB), `LMCACHE_CHUNK_SIZE=256`
- Single RTX 4090, single vLLM server process, `ThreadPoolExecutor`-dispatched HTTP client (4 workers)
- Prefix length: 28,000 real tokens (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct)

## Reproduction

1. Maintain a small pool of 2 "resident" prefixes, each re-warmed with a `max_tokens=2` request immediately before I measure it.
2. Interleave concurrent "miss" requests: brand-new, globally-unique 28K-token prefixes, never reused.
3. Dispatch both kinds concurrently (Poisson arrivals, 4 worker threads, hit_ratio≈0.5) against the same server.
4. Measure TTFT for each "hit"-kind request (the one just re-warmed) and compare against the known hit/miss TTFT distributions from isolated, sequential measurement on the same hardware/model (clean, non-overlapping: hit max 95.9ms, miss min 395.7ms).

## Result

At n=150 (66 realized "hit" draws), 80.3% of hit-kind requests measured miss-level TTFT (>150ms; observed range 850-2400ms). I tested and ruled out three candidate causes:

- **Capacity**: raising `LMCACHE_MAX_LOCAL_CPU_SIZE` from 6 to 20 GiB didn't reduce the failure rate. Each request's KV footprint at this prefix length is ~343MB (12,288 bytes/token × ~27,890 real tokens); even 4 concurrent workers plus both resident identities live at once, doubled for margin, is only ~4.1GB, well under the 20GiB cap.
- **Same-key contention**: I instrumented whether another request was concurrently warming/measuring the same resident identity (`same_identity_concurrent`). No significant relationship with failure (Mann-Whitney U, p=0.072), and the trend runs the wrong direction for a same-key-race explanation (failed rows: mean 0.34 concurrent same-key accessors; ok rows: mean 0.62).
- **Sequential timing race**: repeating the exact warm-then-measure pattern 30 times fully sequentially (zero concurrency, zero other traffic) produced 0/30 failures, ruling out an intrinsic async-write-vs-read race independent of concurrency.

What does predict failure: whether any miss request (to an unrelated key) is concurrently in flight during the hit's own measurement window (`concurrent_miss_count`):

| | ok | failed | failure rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `concurrent_miss_count == 0` | 12 | 8 | 40.0% |
| `concurrent_miss_count >= 1` | 1 | 45 | 97.8% |

Fisher's exact test: odds ratio 67.5, p = 2.9e-7.

The residual 40% failure rate at `concurrent_miss_count == 0` is plausibly a measurement-granularity artifact: the counter is sampled once, immediately before the hit's final request is issued, so a miss that begins microseconds later isn't captured. I haven't confirmed this.

## Root cause

I believe this is a request-scoping bug, not a dict-corruption or capacity issue. In `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/local_cpu_backend.py` (v0.3.12), `LocalCPUBackend` keeps a single, instance-level list of looked-up keys, and its own comment documents an assumption this violates under concurrency:

```python
# to help maintain suffix -> prefix order in the dict
# assumption: only one request is looked up at a time
# (only one worker per cache engine)
self.keys_in_request: List[CacheEngineKey] = []

def contains(self, key, pin=False):
    with self.cpu_lock:
        if key not in self.hot_cache:
            return False
        if pin:
            self.hot_cache[key].pin()
            self.keys_in_request.append(key)   # shared across ALL requests
        return True

def touch_cache(self):
    with self.cpu_lock:
        for key in reversed(self.keys_in_request):
            self.cache_policy.update_on_hit(key, self.hot_cache)
        self.keys_in_request = []              # clears the WHOLE shared list
```

The same pattern recurs in `batched_async_contains` (same file, ~line 211-228), which is on the actual request-serving hot path.

`self.cpu_lock` correctly serializes raw `hot_cache` dict access, so `contains()`/`get_blocking()` should still find a resident key's entry. The corruption is in the eviction bookkeeping: one request's `touch_cache()` can clear another request's just-appended keys before that second request records its own `cache_policy.update_on_hit()` call, silently dropping the "this key was just touched" signal for an unrelated, already-resident key. That makes the key look stale to the eviction policy regardless of how much raw capacity is available, which matches what I saw in the Capacity test above: the failure rate didn't move because the cause was never capacity.

Tracing the caller in `storage_manager.py`: `StorageManager` runs a single dedicated background thread with its own asyncio event loop, and `async_lookup_and_prefetch()` (which awaits `batched_async_contains()`) runs on that loop. So all concurrent requests' lookups execute as interleaved coroutines on a single OS thread, not on separate threads. A `threading.local()` fix wouldn't be enough here since every request shares one thread; a correct fix likely needs per-task scoping (`contextvars.ContextVar`) or explicit per-request key-list threading through the call chain, spanning at least `local_cpu_backend.py` and `storage_manager.py`. `touch_cache()` is also called from `cache_engine.py`, which I haven't inspected yet.

This file has no async device-copy code (no `.to(device, non_blocking=True)`, no CUDA streams/events), so as far as I can tell this is a pure Python scoping bug in LMCache's own request handling, not an upstream PyTorch/

items.title: [Bug] Cross-request KV contamination with local disk backend: returning sessions answer with OTHER requests' content (v0.5.2, vLLM 0.26.0)
items.author: KPST-LAB
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team,

First off, thanks for maintaining LMCache! 

I ran into a critical silent KV cache corruption issue where long-context sessions served from the disk tier end up getting KV cache belonging to *other* requests. 

Below are the details and reproduction steps.

---

### Bug Description

When using `local_cpu` + `local_disk` backends, long-context sessions returning after their KV cache has been paged to the disk tier receive KV data belonging to **other requests**. 

As a result, the model answers questions using facts from a completely different conversation (and sometimes includes fragments from unrelated concurrent short requests). No errors/warnings are logged—the corruption is entirely silent.

### Environment

- **LMCache Version:** 0.5.2 (latest)
- **vLLM Version:** 0.26.0 (matched per v0.5.2 release notes)
- **GPU:** Single GPU (24 GB)
- **OS:** Linux
- **Model:** `hugging-quants/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ-INT4` (FP16 KV)
- **Config:** 
  - `chunk_size`: 256
  - `local_cpu`: true, `max_local_cpu_size`: 8
  - `local_disk`: `file://...`, `max_local_disk_size`: 28 (sized large enough so eviction is never triggered, keeping issue #1981 out of scope)
- **Connector:** `{"kv_connector": "LMCacheConnectorV1", "kv_role": "kv_both"}`

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Created 6 distinct sessions of ~32K tokens each. Each session contains a unique needle (`"the vault code is ZK-600<i>"`) inserted at 10% depth (Needle-In-A-Haystack setup).
   - Total working set ≈ 24 GB KV, forcing most chunks onto the disk tier (`local_cpu` is limited to 8 GB).
2. Ran a 150-second mixed load:
   - The 6 long-context sessions periodically return (full prompt resent, prefix served via LMCache).
   - Concurrently, 3 background workers send short unrelated requests (`"the ticket number is TK-<k>..."`).
3. Verified the generated answers against each session's ground-truth needle.

### Observed Behavior

Returning sessions consistently answered with the **WRONG** session's needle. 

A single-return probe after the load test yielded:
- **Session 0:** Expected `ZK-6000` $\rightarrow$ Got `"ZK-6001. The ticket number is TK-"`
- **Session 2:** Expected `ZK-6002` $\rightarrow$ Got `"ZK-6000. ..."`
- **Sessions 3, 4, 5:** Expected `ZK-6003/4/5` $\rightarrow$ All got `"ZK-6001 ..."`

Notice that responses also contain text fragments from concurrent short requests (`"The ticket number is TK-"`), confirming KV cross-talk across completely independent requests.

Across the entire 150s window (138 total session returns), **only 14 answered with their own needle (~10% accuracy)**.

#### Sanity Checks / Controls
- **Clean Environment:** Successfully reproduced twice on a completely reset environment (fresh server processes, wiped store directories, 40GB free RAM, empty GPU memory).
- **Control Test:** Running the exact same benchmark harness on stock vLLM (no connector) and another KVConnector implementation yields **100% accuracy**, confirming the harness itself is clean.
- **Cold Run:** Cold runs (initial store population, few returns) do NOT show this bug—it only emerges once requests start being served back from the disk tier at scale.

### Expected Behavior

A returning request should only ever be served KV chunks derived from its own exact token prefix. If a key mismatch occurs, it should trigger a cache miss (recompute), never silently inject cross-talk/corrupted KV content.

---

### Additional Context

* Note: While isolating this, we also hit the eviction crash already tracked in #1981 (`FileNotFoundError` in `local_disk_backend.remove` during `batched_remove`) on a single-GPU setup, and left a comment there.
* I have the full benchmark script and logs ready if needed. Happy to share them to help debug!

Thanks again for looking into this!

items.title: [Bug][GPU Connector] SGLang layerwise connector ignores the partial slot-mapping offset, writing retrieved KV to the wrong paged slots
items.author: elbourne12345
items.body_excerpt:
**Labels:** `bug`

## Describe the bug

`SGLangLayerwiseGPUConnector.batched_to_gpu` never reads the `offset` kwarg it is
given, and slices the slot mapping with *absolute* token indices. On the SGLang
load path the slot mapping is **partial** — its element 0 is the slot of token
`offset`, not token 0 — so every retrieved token is written to the slot
belonging to a token `offset` positions later.

There is no error and no log line. The KV cache for the request is populated
from the wrong slots, so the model generates from corrupted state.

`SGLangLayerwiseXPUConnector` has the same defect. The non-layerwise connectors
and the MUSA layerwise connector are correct.

## The contract

Both SGLang paths go through `LMCacheConnector`, and the two mapping contracts
are different — each is enforced in the adapter:

| Path | Enforced in | Mapping | Correct indexing |
|---|---|---|---|
| load  | `load_kv`, `sglang_adapter.py:195-198` — `len(token_ids) - offset == len(slot_mapping)` | **partial**, element 0 = token `offset` | `slot_mapping[start - offset : end - offset]` |
| store | `store_kv`, `sglang_adapter.py:219-220` — `len(token_ids) == len(slot_mapping)` | full length | `slot_mapping[start:end]` |

`start_load_kv` (the layerwise entry point) consumes the same `LoadMetadata`
dataclass as `load_kv` and forwards `offset` into `retrieve_layer`
(`sglang_adapter.py:333-340`), so the load contract applies — but the connector
drops it.

## Where

`lmcache/v1/gpu_connector/gpu_connectors.py`, `SGLangLayerwiseGPUConnector.batched_to_gpu`:

```python
slot_mapping: torch.Tensor = kwargs["slot_mapping"]   # `offset` is never read

slot_mapping_chunks = []
for start, end in zip(starts, ends, strict=False):
    slot_mapping_chunks.append(slot_mapping[start:end])       # absolute
slot_mapping_full = torch.cat(slot_mapping_chunks, dim=0)
...
        device_ops.single_layer_kv_transfer_sgl(
            memory_obj.tensor,
            self.kvcaches[0][layer_id],
            self.kvcaches[1][layer_id],
            slot_mapping[start:end],                           # absolute
            lmcache_native.TransferDirection.H2D,
            token_major=True,
        )
```

Both the `use_gpu=True` branch (via `slot_mapping_full`) and the direct branch
are affected.

Compare `SGLangGPUConnector.to_gpu` in the same file, which rebases correctly:

```python
offset = kwargs.get("offset", 0)
...
    slot_mapping[start - offset : end - offset],
```

A likely reason this was missed: `batched_to_gpu` already binds a *local*
`offset = starts[0]` for indexing the staging buffer. The name collides with
the kwarg, so the function reads as though `offset` were already handled.

## To Reproduce

**Confirmed on hardware.** Verified against `dev` @ `913016b` on an NVIDIA L4
(driver 580.173.02, CUDA 12.9, torch 2.9.1+cu129, Ubuntu 22.04), source build.

The test added in the accompanying PR round-trips one request with `offset=300`,
`num_tokens=512`, `chunk_size=256` — gathering with the full-length mapping the
store path requires, then scattering with that mapping's tail plus `offset`, as
the load path delivers it.

- **Unpatched `dev`:** FAILS
  ```
  RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (212) must match the size of tensor b (256)
    at non-singleton dimension 0
  lmcache/v1/gpu_connector/gpu_connectors.py:1811
  ```
- **With the rebase applied:** PASSES
- **Full `tests/v1/test_gpu_connector.py` with the fix:** 34 passed, 1 skipped,
  0 failed — no regressions.

The arithmetic in that error is the bug, exactly. The partial mapping holds 512
entries (tokens 300–812). The chunks are `(300, 556)` and `(556, 812)`, and the
connector slices the mapping at those *absolute* indices: `slot_mapping[300:556]`
on a 512-element tensor yields **212** elements, and `slot_mapping[556:812]`
yields **0**. The staging buffer is then sized from that truncated
concatenation (212) while the memory objects still carry 256 tokens per chunk.

### Why production corrupts silently instead of raising

In this test the truncation shrinks the buffer, so it raises. In the real
adapter it does not: `start_load_kv` passes `slot_mapping[:retrieve_token_num]`
(`sglang_adapter.py:337`), which leaves the mapping long enough that the
shifted slices stay in bounds. With `T=1024`, `offset=256`,
`retrieve_token_num=768`, `chunk_size=256`, the connector reads
`slot_mapping[256:512]` and `slot_mapping[512:768]` — the slots belonging to
tokens 512–768 and 768–1024. Every chunk lands exactly `offset` tokens late,
in bounds, with no error: silently corrupted KV.

Same root cause, two manifestations depending on how much slack the mapping has.

## Expected behavior

Token `i` is written to `slot_mapping[i - offset]`, so a warm-prefix retrieve
produces the same output as a cold one.

## Why it survived

No CUDA or XPU test ever passes a nonzero offset:

- `tests/v1/test_gpu_connector.py` — every `offset` is `offset=0` (lines 193,
  206, 324, 336, 774, 784, 878).
- `tests/v1/test_xpu_sglang_connector.py` — no occurrence of `offset` at all.
- `tests/v1/platform/musa/test_sglang_connectors.py` — has
  `test_sglang_musa_connector_respects_partial_slot_offset` and a layerwise
  round trip, both with `offset = 5`.

MUSA is the only platform with nonzero-offset coverage, and the only one that
implements it correctly (`_slot_slice`, whose docstring reads "Return a
device-local slice from a **possibly partial** slot mapping"). The CUDA path was
refactored 13 times in the last four months without this being caught.

## Separate defect found while verifying

`SGLangLayerwiseGPUConnector` with `use_gpu=False` cannot round-trip at all,
independently of this issue. `batched_from_gpu`'s direct branch passes the 3-D
per-layer tensor `self.kvcaches[0][layer_id]` to
`single_layer_kv_transfer_sgl`, which indexes dim 3; the buffered branch passes
`.view(t, 1, h, d)` instead. Reproduced with `offset=0` and a full-length
mapping — the ordinary contract:

```
IndexError: Dimension out of range (expecte

items.title: VLLMPagedMemGPUConnectorV2 crashes at init on DeepSeek-V3.2 / DSA models (indexer caches not counted in num_layers)
items.author: DanielDubinsky
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`VLLMPagedMemGPUConnectorV2` crashes at engine init on any model with DeepSeek-V3.2 sparse attention (DSA): DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5.3, and similar. It sizes its KV pointer array to `num_layers`, but vLLM hands it one KV cache per main attention layer plus one per DSA indexer layer, so the arrays mismatch.

### Error

```
File "lmcache/v1/gpu_connector/gpu_connectors.py", line 256, in _initialize_pointers
    self.kv_cache_pointers.numpy()[:] = [t.data_ptr() for t in kv_caches]
ValueError: could not broadcast input array from shape (99,) into shape (78,)
```

Deterministic, during the init dummy run, before any request.

### Root cause

`num_layers` comes from `metadata.kv_shape[0]` (main attention layers: 78 for GLM-5.3). vLLM's DSA models register an extra `DeepseekV32IndexerCache` per sparse layer (head_size 128 vs the main MLA 576) and pass all of them to `register_kv_caches`. So `kv_caches` holds 99 tensors (78 main + 21 indexer) against a 78-slot `kv_cache_pointers`.

Boot logs the mismatch source right before the crash:
```
num_layer: 78, use mla: True, kv shape: (78, 1, 256, 1, 576)
```

### Repro

- vLLM 0.28.0, LMCache 0.5.4 and 0.5.5rc5 (both affected).
- Any DSA model, e.g. GLM-5.3, TP4 or TP8, `--enable-expert-parallel`, connector `LMCacheConnectorV1Dynamic`.

### Proposed fix (verified correct, needs hardening)

Filter the indexer caches out of `register_kv_caches` so LMCache manages only the main attention caches:

```python
# LMCacheConnectorV1Impl.register_kv_caches
sfc = get_current_vllm_config().compilation_config.static_forward_context
kv_caches = {n: t for n, t in kv_caches.items()
             if type(sfc.get(n)).__name__ != "DeepseekV32IndexerCache"}
```

With this filter, GLM-5.3 on vLLM 0.28.0 boots and passes needle retrieval at 19,335 / 55,061 / 91,743 token depths, so dropping the indexer caches is correct here (vLLM handles the indexer itself).

Two decisions for maintainers before merge:

- Whether dropping the indexer caches is always safe, or whether they should be offloaded too.
- The discriminator is a class-name string match via `static_forward_context`, which is fragile and vLLM-version-specific. Keying off the KV-cache spec or shape, or a proper indexer API, would be more robust.

items.title: [Bug] First-rank MLA retrieval stages the whole cache hit on the device
items.author: orthur2
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With `save_only_first_rank` (the default for MLA models), a non-layerwise retrieve stages the entire cache hit on the device before any of it is written to the KV pages. `_broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs` copies each hit chunk to the device on rank 0, broadcasts it, and keeps every device copy alive until the single `batched_to_gpu` call at the end. A hit of N chunks therefore costs N chunk-sized device allocations on every rank, all live at the same time.

These allocations happen at serving time, after vLLM has planned and allocated its KV pool, so no budget covers them. They come out of whatever headroom `gpu_memory_utilization` leaves, which is a few GB at most, and a hit longer than that kills the engine. We ran into it with a hit of about 500k tokens: staging grew to several GB per rank and every rank died with an OOM raised from `_broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs`.

**To Reproduce**

Run an MLA model with LMCache in-process, keep `save_only_first_rank` at its default, and disable vLLM prefix caching so the hit goes through LMCache. Then make the hit larger than the device memory left after startup, either by raising `gpu_memory_utilization` or by storing a longer prompt. Send the prompt once so it is stored, then send the same prompt again. TP=1 is enough: the first rank stages every chunk on the device whether or not there is anyone to broadcast to.

Expected: the hit is written into the KV pages with bounded temporary device memory.

Actual: device memory grows with the hit, the retrieve fails with an OOM in `_broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs`, and the engine dies.

<details>
<summary>Verified example: DeepSeek-V2-Lite on one 32 GB card</summary>

vLLM 0.28.0, one RTX 5090 (32 GB), DeepSeek-V2-Lite with fp8 online quantization so it fits on the card. Its KV is about 30 KB per token, so a 256-token chunk is about 8 MB on the device and a 160k-token hit stages about 5 GB, well above the headroom that `gpu_memory_utilization` 0.85 leaves.

```bash
LMCACHE_CHUNK_SIZE=256 LMCACHE_LOCAL_CPU=True LMCACHE_MAX_LOCAL_CPU_SIZE=20 \
vllm serve deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --max-model-len 163840 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --quantization fp8 \
  --enforce-eager \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_both"}'
```

Startup reports a KV pool of 10.08 GiB (347,984 tokens). A 160k-token completion request with `max_tokens=1` is stored in 89 s. The same request again is looked up as `LMCache hit tokens: 160000, need to load: 159999`, device memory climbs for about 36 s, and the engine dies with:

```
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 20.00 MiB. GPU 0 has a total
capacity of 31.36 GiB of which 10.00 MiB is free. Including non-PyTorch memory, this process
has 31.30 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated memory 29.74 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, and
932.15 MiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.
  File "lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_v1_adapter.py", line 852, in start_load_kv
  File "lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py", line 859, in retrieve
  File "lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py", line 1863, in _broadcast_or_receive_memory_objs
```

followed by `EngineDeadError`. PyTorch had 29.74 GiB allocated against a 0.85 budget of 26.66 GiB; the difference is the staging that had accumulated before the allocation failed.

</details>

**Expected behavior**

Retrieval should stream the hit through a fixed, configurable device buffer, so that the device memory a retrieve needs depends on that buffer rather than on the hit size. That budget should also be something vLLM can account for, or at least be documented as living outside its KV plan.

**Additional context**

#5292 implements this with a fixed per-engine staging buffer and a windowed broadcast. Layerwise and multiprocess retrieval do not go through this path.

items.title: Misc. bug: mmproj memory margin is added twice on resume from sleep, causing CPU offload
items.author: crmky
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
# llama-cli --version
version: 10217 (ddd4ec142)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux x86_64
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.6-27B-UD-IQ3_XXS.gguf --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf -c 32768

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When running llama-server with a multimodal model, the first cold start fits the model correctly with all offloadable layers on the GPU. However, after the server enters sleeping state and then resumes, the memory-fit logic uses a larger free-memory target, causing some layers to be offloaded to the CPU.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Start llama-server with a multimodal model and sleep enabled.
2. Wait for idle timeout or trigger sleep.
3. Send a new request to wake the server.

Unknown. The bug appears to be in the sleep-resume path of tools/server/server-context.cpp.

items.title: [RFC]: Hot Standby Mode for Master Service Metadata High Availability
items.author: Libotry
items.body_excerpt: ## Introduction To address the issue where all metadata is lost after a master service failure and recovery, this solution proposes a **hot-standby synchronization mechanism** and a **hybrid approach** combining hot standby with snapshots, ensuring rapid data recovery following a master service failure. ## Motivation The current HA (High Availability) mode only supports rapid restart of the master service after a failure but cannot guarantee fast data recovery. The pain points of the current HA mode are as follows: | Issue | Impact | Severity | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | | **Complete loss of metadata after Leader failure** | All KV cache location information is lost and must be rebuilt | 🔴 Critical | | **Follower lacks data pre-warming** | After successful election, the new Leader must start serving from scratch | 🟠 Medium | | **Long recovery time** | Relies on clients to re-register; may take several minutes to tens of minutes | 🟠 Medium | | **Service unavailability window** | Requests cannot be processed during Leader failover | 🟡 Low | ## Goals: 1. **Near-zero RPO**: Minimize the data loss window 2. **Fast failover**: Achieve second-level RTO (Recovery Time Objective) 3. **Data consistency guarantee**: Ensure correct synchronization between primary and standby 4. **Verifiability**: Include mechanisms to validate data integrity 5. **Low performance overhead**: Avoid impacting normal business operations ## Proposal ### 1. Core Design Approach **Use etcd as an intermediate reliability component to implement OpLog primary-standby synchronization**: - **OpLog Mechanism**: Primary Master records all state change operations to OpLog - **etcd Storage**: OpLog is written to etcd, leveraging etcd's strong consistency and persistence capabilities - **Watch Mechanism**: Standby Master receives OpLog in real-time through etcd Watch mechanism - **Ordering Guarantee**: Guarantee operation order through global sequence_id and key-level key_sequence_id ### 2. Architecture Design #### (1) Overall Architecture The overall architecture diagram shows the interaction relationships between Primary Master, etcd Cluster, and Standby Master: **Architecture Description**: - **Primary Master**: Handles client requests, records OpLog and writes to etcd - **etcd Cluster**: Acts as intermediate storage, providing strong consistency and Watch mechanism - **Standby Master**: Receives OpLog in real-time by watching etcd and applies to local metadata store #### (2) Data Flow Diagram The data flow diagram shows the complete flow from Client request to Standby synchronization: **Flow Description**: a. Client sends `PutEnd` request to Primary Master b. Primary Master records operation through `OpLogManager`, generating sequence_id c. `EtcdOpLogStore` writes OpLog to etcd d. etcd notifies Standby Master through Watch mechanism e. `OpLogWatcher` receives events and passes to `OpLogApplier` f. `OpLogApplier` checks order and applies to Standby's metadata store #### (3) Failover Sequence The failover sequence diagram shows the complete process from Primary failure to Standby promotion to Primary: **Flow Description**: a. **Normal Operation**: Primary maintains Lease, Standby continuously synchronizes OpLog through Watch b. **Primary Failure**: Primary's Lease expires, etcd notifies Standby c. **Standby Promotion**: Stop Standby service, initialize Lease, clean expired metadata, start leader election ### 3. Problem & Assumptions #### 1.1 Problem After a `Delete` (or eviction) on the primary master: - The primary frees a replica’s memory (returns buffer to allocator’s free list). - The `Delete` event is **not** replicated to the standby master. - The primary then crashes; the standby is promoted to new master. - The new master still believes that this replica exists, and returns its address to clients. - That buffer may already have been **reused by another object**, or may still contain **logically deleted data**. We must **never** return data that belongs to some other key/object/tenant due to buffer reuse, even if we allow some metadata loss. #### 1.2 Accepted Semantic Constraints We explicitly accept the following semantics: - **Metadata / delete operations may be lost across failover**: - A delete acknowledged by the old master may be “rolled back” after failover. - That is acceptable because the KV cache can be recomputed. - **Hard safety requirement**: - It is strictly forbidden to read data that **belongs to another key/object/tenant** as if it were the requested key. - In other words: buffer reuse must not cause **cross-key contamination**. Under these constraints, it is acceptable that: - A key that was “deleted” on the old master may reappear after failover (logical delete rolled back). - But it is **not** acceptable to read someone else’s data due to buffer reuse. --- ### 2. Idea We upgrade each replica from a “raw pointer” into a **versioned capability**: - In-memory layout of a replica buffer becomes: - The master generates a **64-bit version** for each successful `Put` of a key. - This `version` is stored: - In `ObjectMetadata` on the master. - In the `ReplicaDescriptor` returned to clients. - In the first 8 bytes of the actual buffer in the KV store. - On **Get**, the client always verifies: - Read the first 8 bytes of the buffer. - Compare with the expected version from `ReplicaDescriptor`. - If versions match → buffer still belongs to this key/epoch → safe to read payload. - If versions differ → buffer was reused by someone else → mark this replica invalid, do not use it. Thus, even if the physical address is reused for a different object, the client will detect it and reject the replica. --- ### 3. comments.author: ykwd
comments.body:
Thanks for sharing the proposal. Unfortunately, this approach is not safe and does not actually guarantee the hard safety requirement you described, for two reasons:

First, RDMA reads and writes do not provide ordering and atomicity guarantees, which breaks the version-only validation scheme. In your design, correctness relies on the assumption that the first 8 bytes (the version) and the payload are written and observed atomically and in order. That assumption does not hold.

Second, the allocator does not guarantee alignment between successive allocations, which makes the embedded-version assumption invalid. Your scheme assumes that when a buffer is freed and later reused, the next allocation will reuse the same start address and layout, so that the version stored in the first 8 bytes corresponds exactly to the logical object boundary.

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek V4/V3.2 DSML tool-call parser occasionally wraps arguments in a spurious "arguments"/"input" key
items.author: martinoturrina
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

The DeepSeek V4 / V3.2 DSML tool-call parser (`deepseekv4_detector.py` / `deepseekv32_detector.py`) occasionally emits the arguments of a tool call wrapped in a spurious top-level `"arguments"` (or `"input"`) key instead of the tool's real parameter names, e.g.:

```json
{"arguments": {"path": "/some/file.py"}}
```
instead of
```json
{"path": "/some/file.py"}
```

and, for single-string-argument tools, even a bare-scalar variant:
```json
{"arguments": "some shell command"}
```
instead of
```json
{"command": "some shell command"}
```

This reaches OpenAI-compatible clients verbatim in `message.tool_calls[].function.arguments` / the streaming `delta.tool_calls[].function.arguments` chunks, so any client doing JSON-schema validation against the tool's declared parameters (which is standard practice, e.g. any agent framework) rejects it with an error like:

```
(root): 'command' is a required property
```

We observed both a Direct-JSON invoke-body variant and an XML `<｜DSML｜parameter name="arguments" string="true">...` variant of the same underlying mistake.

This appears closely related to vllm-project/vllm#41240 ("DeepSeek V4 DSML tool parser mishandles wrapped and reserved arguments") and vllm-project/vllm#48931, which notes the analogous DSML mis-parsing becomes more likely at longer context lengths. We see the same context-length correlation here: the bug essentially never appears on a fresh, short conversation, but shows up repeatedly (several times per multi-turn session) once an agent has accumulated tens of thousands of tokens of tool-call history.

## Reproduction

- Image: `lmsysorg/sglang:dev-dsv4-flash-vision`
- Model: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp`
- Launch flags: `--tool-call-parser deepseekv4 --reasoning-parser deepseek-v4`
- Client: an OpenAI-compatible coding agent registering several tools (`bash`, `read`, `ls`, ...) and running a normal multi-turn session that reads/explores a handful of files and runs a few shell commands. The bug shows up intermittently, more reliably once context grows past a few turns / several thousand tokens, especially with multiple parallel tool calls in one turn.

Example malformed streamed argument accumulation for a `bash` tool with schema `{"type": "object", "properties": {"command": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["command"]}`:

```
{"arguments": "cd /some/dir && git log --oneline -10"}
```

instead of

```
{"command": "cd /some/dir && git log --oneline -10"}
```

## Expected behavior

`function.arguments` should always match the tool's declared JSON schema (the real parameter names), regardless of which internal DSML shape the model happened to emit.

## Proposed fix

We wrote and validated a targeted patch to `deepseekv32_detector.py` (inherited by `DeepSeekV4Detector`) that:
- Detects, from the raw invoke content (both Direct-JSON and XML parameter-tag forms), when the first/only key is a known wrapper key (`arguments`/`input`) that isn't itself a real declared property of the tool.
- For streaming, holds back emitting that call's arguments until it's complete (never streams a shape it may have to rewrite; clients only ever act on the argument string once `finish_reason: tool_calls` fires anyway), then emits the corrected, unwrapped JSON in one chunk.
- Unwraps a dict-valued wrapper directly, remaps a scalar-valued wrapper to the tool's sole required/only property, and also handles a double-JSON-encoded string value (the XML `string="true"` sub-case).
- Leaves every non-buggy call completely untouched (verified across parallel calls, mixed tool types, multi-property tools, and the XML parameter-tag format with real parameter names).

Happy to open a PR with this if it's useful; wanted to file the issue with a full writeup first since I couldn't find an existing sglang-side issue for this specific "wrapped arguments" shape (only the related-but-different #14695 about *missing* DSML markers).

# Goal

This roadmap continues #14199, initiated by @ClawSeven, and builds on the community's work toward robust, efficient block-diffusion serving and Jev-style decisions on diffusion LLMs.

Carry forward unfinished serving goals alongside newer work. Fixes for crashes and wrong results on main come before new features. Full-sequence models get baseline compatibility. Checked items record merged work. Unchecked items track remaining work or evaluation. Phases can overlap. Jev-style decisions on causal models are tracked separately, starting with #40826.

# Roadmap

### Phase 1: Shared runtime and request lifecycle

- [ ] Complete shared scheduling support.

  - [x] Dynamic batching. #14883
  - [x] Prefill/decode separation. #17484
  - [x] Algorithm-independent FDFO and early block departure. #27551
  - [ ] Refine scheduling interfaces and isolate model behavior.
  - [ ] FDFO + LowConfidence overlap scheduling. @Betelgeu #40756
  - [ ] Extend overlap to other algorithms after state-lifetime qualification.
  - [ ] Derive the default running-request count and graph capture sizes from available memory instead of serving one request at a time.

- [ ] Fail early on unsupported configurations.

  - [ ] Refuse speculative decoding, two-batch overlap, unsupported deterministic backends, and logprob requests. #43452
  - [ ] Refuse or support attention data parallelism, which crashes today.
  - [ ] Refuse or fix the FA3 attention backend, which crashes on the first request.
  - [ ] Reject sampling and grammar fields that the selected algorithm does not apply.
  - [ ] Reject unknown algorithm configuration keys instead of falling back to defaults.

- [ ] Harden request lifecycle and caching.

  - [x] Block-level radix caching. #18724
  - [x] Retain block KV and request slots. #27877
  - [x] Keep one request row across FDFO blocks. #42846
  - [ ] Qualify aborted FDFO cleanup and retained KV recovery.
  - [ ] Apply the waiting timeout to requests queued for dLLM scheduling. @lsnchow #42453
  - [ ] Bound staging admission by block size and available capacity. #32992
  - [ ] Fix the radix double count that stops an idle scheduler. #35781
  - [ ] Settle how literal mask text and caller input IDs holding the mask id are handled. #35998
  - [ ] Qualify committed streaming, EOS/stops, cancellation, and final assembly. @zxr-creator
  - [ ] Define opt-in provisional output separately from committed streaming.

### Phase 2: Prefill and CUDA graphs

- [ ] Expand attention and prefill support.

  - [ ] Round preparation and staging liveness, split from #31586.
  - [ ] Multi-block pure prefill in eager mode.
  - [ ] CUDA graphs for multi-block prefill through generic padded buckets.
  - [ ] Native block-extend attention. FlashInfer #2722

- [ ] Extend CUDA graph coverage.

  - [x] Fixed-block CUDA graphs. #14203

  - [ ] Piecewise prefill graphs on compatible backends.
  - [ ] Qualify variable-length prefill and graph buckets.

### Phase 3: Models, decoding, and backends

- [ ] Expand model support.

  - [x] LLaDA2.0 model family. #12588
  - [x] SDAR dense and MoE models. #19044
  - [x] DiffusionGemma text and image-input serving. #34061
  - [x] DiffusionGemma FA4 and CUDA graphs on Blackwell. #42239
  - [ ] Route `sglang serve` dLLM launches to the LLM runtime. #40942
  - [ ] Quantized DiffusionGemma checkpoints, FP8 first.
  - [ ] Radix cache and chunked prefill for DiffusionGemma.
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 block routing. #31768
  - [x] LLaDA2.2 insertion/deletion decoding. #31773
  - [ ] LLaDA2.2 routing and editing on Ascend. #32280
  - [ ] Qualify LLaDA2.2 mini and 128K context with a documented launch command.
  - [ ] Nemotron Labs Diffusion with its autoregressive, block-diffusion, and LinearSpec modes. #25803
  - [ ] Dream full-sequence baseline. #36881

  - [ ] Qualify the Fast-dLLM v2 continuation and batching support. @SensenGao #22156
  - [ ] GFusion model support. #29776

- [ ] Extend decoding support.

items.title: num_matched_prefix_tokens stays 0 for cache-agnostic policies (fcfs, lof, random, routing-key)
items.author: phphlio1
items.body_excerpt:
# Issue: `num_matched_prefix_tokens` stays 0 for cache-agnostic policies - load snapshots and cache-hit reporting read zero reuse

## Summary

With `--schedule-policy fcfs` (and the other cache-agnostic policies: `lof`, `random`, `routing-key`), `Req.num_matched_prefix_tokens` stays at 0 for the request's whole lifetime, even though the request does reuse cached prefixes. Every consumer of the field then reads zero reuse.

## Root cause

2 facts combine:

1. `SchedulePolicy.calc_priority` only populates `num_matched_prefix_tokens` at sort time for cache-agnostic policies when `tree_cache.supports_fast_match_prefix()` is true - which is  false for the current radix implementations - so the field is never set there (`python/sglang/srt/managers/schedule_policy.py`).
2. `Req.init_next_round_input` runs the real admission-time re-match (`tree_cache.match_prefix(...)`) and unpacks `prefix_indices` /   `host_hit_length`, but never records the match length into `num_matched_prefix_tokens` - the field keeps its init value 0 (and its retraction reset value 0).

So the scheduler reuses cached prefixes correctly at admission (behavior is fine), but the bookkeeping field stays 0.

## Impact

- `SchedulerLoadInquirer.get_num_waiting_uncached_tokens` computes `req.seqlen - req.num_matched_prefix_tokens` whenever `waiting_queue_prefix_matched()` is true => The uncached waiting-token estimate counts full input lengths, i.e. load snapshots overestimate pending prefill work for cache-agnostic policies.
- Any observability or reporting that reads per-request matched tokens for these policies reads 0.

## Evidence

A 30-minute agentic-replay benchmark run with `--schedule-policy fcfs` (~217 finished requests, 12.9M total input tokens):

- `sum(num_matched_prefix_tokens) == 0` across every request, while an identical-ordering run of the same workload with the sort-time match forced on measured a **91.6% token-weighted prefix hit rate**.
- The fcfs run's own latency/throughput was consistent with real prefix reuse (same ballpark as the matched arm), confirming the runtime reuse happens and only the reported number is wrong.

## Suggested fix

Record the admission re-match length in `init_next_round_input` (read-only, the match already ran and inserts nothing);

```python
self.num_matched_prefix_tokens = min(
    len(self.prefix_indices) + self.host_hit_length,
    self._compute_max_prefix_len(input_len),
)
```

Retraction resets the field to 0, the next admission re-match re-records it. Happy to send a PR with unit tests.

items.title: [Feature] SRT plugins: opt-in fail-fast for required plugins and hooks (`SGLANG_REQUIRED_PLUGINS`)
items.author: piotrm-nvidia
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

## Motivation

SRT general plugins are best-effort, and every failure is logged and skipped:

- `load_plugins_by_group()` logs and continues when a plugin is filtered out by `SGLANG_PLUGINS` / `SGLANG_PLATFORM`
  or when `ep.load()` raises
  ([plugins/__init__.py#L66-L84](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/plugins/__init__.py#L66-L84)).
- `load_plugins()` logs and continues when the plugin's callable raises
  ([#L128-L141](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/plugins/__init__.py#L128-L141)).
- `HookRegistry.apply_hooks()` logs `Failed to apply hooks to %s` and continues
  ([hook_registry.py#L146-L166](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/plugins/hook_registry.py#L146-L166)).
- In the scheduler, `load_plugins()` runs before logging is configured
  ([scheduler.py#L6043](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L6043)
  vs [#L6056](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L6056)),
  so the INFO lines (`Loaded plugin`, `Skipping plugin`) are not visible in the server log.

For a plugin that changes how the model is placed or executed, partial application is worse than none. The server
starts and serves, but without the plugin or without some of its hooks. A stale install, an allowlist typo, or a
renamed hook target is enough to cause this. Examples: a weight-offloading plugin (https://github.com/ai-dynamo/flextensor/issues/6), or a CUDA-graph
persistence plugin (#41791).

A plugin cannot detect this reliably today:

- There is no public way to ask which targets were applied. The only state is the private
  `HookRegistry._hooks` / `_patched`
  ([hook_registry.py#L78-L81](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/srt/plugins/hook_registry.py#L78-L81)),
  which a plugin has to read directly.
- A hook registered after its target was already patched is dropped silently: `apply_hooks()` skips targets already
  in `_patched`.
- If the hook that would run the self-check is the one that failed, no plugin code runs at all.
- A plugin that was filtered out or failed to import cannot report anything.

Diffusion already has the semantics we need (#37547): the selected platform's plugins abort startup on load, callback
or hook-apply failure. It does this through its own `HookRegistry` subclass
([multimodal_gen/runtime/platforms/plugins.py#L82-L85](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/multimodal_gen/runtime/platforms/plugins.py#L82-L85),
[#L181-L192](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/python/sglang/multimodal_gen/runtime/platforms/plugins.py#L181-L192);
failure table in [plugin.mdx#L104-L117](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/v0.5.21/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx#L104-L117)).
SRT has no equivalent, and its failure semantics are not documented.

#41791 added fail-fast for one specific plugin, and the review asked that upstream stay independent of any particular
plugin. This request is the generic, plugin-agnostic version: the operator opts in by naming plugins, and SGLang itself
knows nothing about them.

### Proposal

Default behaviour is unchanged.

1. **`SGLANG_REQUIRED_PLUGINS`** (comma-separated entry-point names, empty by default). It sits in `environ.py` next to
   `SGLANG_PLUGINS`; an env var is used because `load_plugins()` runs before server args are published. `load_plugins()`
   raises an error naming the plugin and the cause when a listed name:
   1. has no entry point in `sglang.srt.plugins`;
   2. is excluded by `SGLANG_PLUGINS` or `SGLANG_PLATFORM`;
   3. raises in `ep.load()`;
   4. raises in its callable;
   5. registered a hook (matched by `HookSource.plugin_name`) whose target failed in `apply_hooks()`, or that was
      registered too late to be applied.

   The launcher process calls `load_plugins()` first, so the error surfaces there, before any scheduler starts.
2. Optional: **a read-only hook status** in place of the private sets (the need behind the withdrawn #38915). Point 1
   alone removes the need for most plugins:
   ```python
   class HookRegistry:
       @classmethod
       def applied_targets(cls) -> frozenset[str]: ...
       @classmethod
       def failed_targets(cls) -> dict[str, BaseException]: ...
   ```
   Optionally, `apply_hooks()` could return the same status. Today it returns `None` and callers ignore it.
3. Optionally, if maintainers prefer it: `HookRegistry.register(..., required: bool = False)`, so a plugin can mark a
   single hook as required from code. `apply_hooks()` would try all targets first, then raise one error listing the
   required targets that failed.

### Acceptance criteria

- With `SGLANG_REQUIRED_PLUGINS` unset, behaviour and logs are unchanged and existing plugin tests pass.
- Each of the cases 1.1–1.5 aborts startup with a message that names the plugin and the cause.
- The abort happens in every process that calls `load_plugins()`, before model load.
- CPU unit tests use fake entry points.
- The SRT row is added to the plugin.mdx failure-semantics table.

This is one of a small set of independent requests listed in https://github.com/ai-dynamo/flextensor/issues/6 (see also #43139, #43144 and
the plugin-facing configuration comment https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/30696#issuecomment-6065847643). It does not depend on them.

items.title: [ROCm][AMD] Qwen3.8-Flash-Next gfx950 / MI355X Performance Optimization
items.author: ChangLiu0709
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

items.title: [RFC]: Limit the use of envvars in vLLM
items.author: zhuohan123
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

vLLM's envvars are on the edge of getting out of control. There are many envvars should instead be configs. Like the attention backend, all2all kernel backend, and even there is a flag to control KV cache layout. envvars are evil because:

1. It is equivalent of using global variables everywhere in the code, which is a bad programming practice.
2. envvars have no advanced structure like, hierarchy, typechecks, etc. 

In summary, I think envvars are the kind of thing that is very easy to add so people tend to add envvars as the shortest path to implement their feature, but this can quickly becomes unmanageable and makes the project very hard to use. 

### Proposed Change.

I think we should:

1. Spend some effort on reviewing the current envvars and move many of them to configs.
2. Have very strict bar on what can be an envvar and question every new envvars in vllm.

items.title: [Docs] Document NIXL KV connector metrics aggregation semantics
items.author: NickLucche
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The NIXL KV connector logs transfer metrics periodically:

```
KV Transfer metrics: Num successful transfers=4, Avg xfer time (ms)=1.381, P90 xfer time (ms)=2.601, Avg post time (ms)=0.672, P90 post time (ms)=0.801, Avg MB per transfer=2.25, Throughput (MB/s)=1629.549, Avg number of descriptors=72.0
```

Currently there is no documentation explaining what these metrics represent, especially in the context of **multi-rank (TP > 1) deployments**. This has already caused confusion among users.

## Current behavior

All metrics are **aggregated across all TP ranks** before summary stats are computed:

1. Each TP rank independently records per-transfer telemetry (`transfer_duration`, `post_duration`, `bytes_transferred`, `num_descriptors`) via `NixlKVConnectorStats.record_transfer()` in [`stats.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py).
2. Stats from all ranks are concatenated via `aggregate()` (`list.extend()`).
3. `reduce()` computes averages, percentiles, and throughput over the **combined** pool of observations from all ranks.

This means:
- **"Num successful transfers"** is the total count across all ranks, not per-rank.
- **"Avg MB per transfer"** is the average over all individual rank-level transfers, not the total bytes moved for a single KV cache transfer operation.
- **"Throughput (MB/s)"** is `total_MB_all_ranks / total_time_all_ranks` — effectively an average per-rank throughput, not the aggregate system throughput.
- **Percentiles (P90)** are computed over the combined distribution of all ranks' transfer times.

This is unintuitive because users may expect metrics to reflect per-engine totals or aggregate system throughput.

## What needs to be documented

1. **Docstrings in `stats.py`**: Add clear documentation to `NixlKVConnectorStats` explaining that stats are aggregated across all TP ranks and what each metric represents in that context.
2. **Inline comments in `reduce()`**: Clarify the semantics of throughput and averages — that they are per-rank averages over the combined observation pool.
3. **Docstrings in `metrics.py`**: Document the `observe()` → `aggregate()` → `reduce()` → `log()` pipeline and the fact that stats arrive pre-aggregated across workers.
4. **(Optional) Docs page**: Add a section to the disaggregated serving documentation explaining how to interpret the KV Transfer metrics log line.

## Relevant files

- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/nixl/stats.py` — `NixlKVConnectorStats` (recording, aggregation, reduction)
- `vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/metrics.py` — `KVConnectorLogging` (observe/log pipeline), `KVConnectorStats` (base class)

## Context

See related discussion: metrics are aggregated across ranks rather than reported per-rank or per-engine. This is a deliberate design choice (fire-and-forget from workers), but it needs to be clearly documented so users can correctly interpret the numbers.

items.title: [RFC]: DeepSeek-V4 Performance Optimization on ROCm (Phase Two)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

> Continue working on phase one: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/41820.

DeepSeek-V4 introduces CSA (Compressed Sparse Attention, `compress_ratio=4`), HCA layers, and a large MoE backbone. A side-by-side trace comparison of the vLLM decode path against vLLM-ATOM on ROCm shows that vLLM still leaves measurable performance on the table. The gaps cluster into three areas:

1. **Unfused mHC kernels.** vLLM runs `mhc_post` and `mhc_pre` as separate kernels, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` as two kernels, while ATOM fuses each pair into a single kernel (`mhc_fused_post_pre` and `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`). Every extra kernel launch on the decode critical path costs launch latency and cache/register thrash.
2. **Serial execution where overlap is possible.** ATOM forks auxiliary HIP streams to run compressor GEMMs (CSA pre-attention), SWA KV insertion (HCA), and the MoE router/shared experts concurrently with the main stream. vLLM executes all of these serially.
3. **Slower attention support kernels.** ATOM replaces the vLLM CSA top-k selection kernels and the post-attention batched GEMMs (`torch.mm` + `manual_unroll`) with dedicated optimized kernels (e.g., `batched_gemm_bf16_kernel`).

An earlier attempt at closing gap #2 — PR #51794, which enables three-stream overlap for CSA pre-attention — is currently a draft: the overlapped region itself is faster when there is no bubble, but some ranks see a much slower tail all-reduce due to inter-rank latency jitter. The un-optimized kernels running in the parallel streams contend for hardware resources and desynchronize ranks. This suggests the correct order of work is: **replace the kernels with ATOM's optimized versions first, then enable stream overlap on top of them.**

## Proposed Change

Port the ATOM-optimized decode path into vLLM's ROCm DeepSeek-V4 implementation, using the ATOM trace as the reference for each change. The work is organized per module:

### CSA:

- [x] **Fuse mHC kernels:** merge `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` into `mhc_fused_post_pre`, and `mhc_pre_big_fuse` + `add_rmsnorm_quant` into `mhc_pre_big_fuse_rmsnorm`. #52737 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse SWA q/kv RMSNorm and q FP8 group quant:** #53540 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Fuse main-compressor and indexer-compressor projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53838 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Pre-attention three-stream overlap:** Before the input GEMMs, fork three HIP streams: (1) **default stream**: fused wqa+wkv GEMM → q/kv RMSNorm → wq_b → qnorm/RoPE → SWA KV insert; (2) **aux stream 0**: main-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → compress kernels (compressed KV cache write); (3) **aux stream 1**: indexer-compressor wkv_gate GEMM → K-cache write. After the join, the indexer weights GEMM, the indexer q-side (wq_b + fused q RoPE+quant), the sparse indexer op (top-k selection), and the MLA attention run serially on the main stream. Each aux stream is a self-contained chain starting from `hidden_states`, so no fine-grained cross-stream dependencies are required. **This item stays disabled (draft) until the kernels in the parallel streams are replaced with ATOM's**.
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50866 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51794 @shen-shanshan 
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54571 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61378 @shen-shanshan 
- [ ] **Support FP4 indexer:**
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56834 @LiuYinfeng01
  - [ ] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60834 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Remove MQA temporary fix:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55808 @shen-shanshan 
- [x] **Replace top-k kernels:** between `gluon_deepgemm_fp8_paged_mqa_logits_preshuffle` and the core `sparse_attention`, replace the vLLM top-k implementation with ATOM's fused sparse-indexer kernels. #52882 @Fangzhou-Ai 
- [x] **Support FP8 attention output projection:** https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54894 @LiuYinfeng01 

### HCA:

- [x] **Pre-attention two-stream overlap:** for `c128a` layers (which have no indexer), run the main KV compression concurrently with SWA token insertion on an auxiliary stream. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56853 @shen-shanshan 

### MoE:

- [x] **Router and shared-experts dual-stream overlap:** run the router computation concurrently with the shared experts on a second stream, then join before the routed experts. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/56098 @mawong-amd 
- [x] Enable AITER heterogeneous fused MoE:
  - [x] TP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53161 @Fangzhou-Ai 
  - [ ] DP: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54134 (not needed now, prefer to use dual-stream MoE for DP) @LiuYinfeng01
- [x] Enable mega MoE: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/59685 @micah-wil 

### Others:

- [x] Prefill optimization:
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54855 @jiacao-amd 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57773 @shen-shanshan 
  - [x] https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58405 @ZhengGong-amd

items.title: [Feature]: Allow pooling tasks (token_embed / token_classify) to reuse prefix cache while returning full hidden-state sequences
items.author: xxyyy
items.body_excerpt:
### The problem

On vLLM 0.29.0, pooling requests with `task="token_embed"` or `task="token_classify"` are **forcefully excluded from prefix-cache reads**, even when prefix caching is explicitly enabled and the caller explicitly requests it.

The mandatory behavior is in `vllm/pooling_params.py` (`_merge_default_parameters`, present in v0.29.0 through current `main`):

```python
if self.skip_reading_prefix_cache is None:
    # If prefix caching is enabled,
    # the output of all pooling may less than n_prompt_tokens,
    # we need to skip reading cache at this request.
    if self.task in ["token_embed", "token_classify"]:
        self.skip_reading_prefix_cache = True
    else:
        self.skip_reading_prefix_cache = False
```

When the caller leaves `skip_reading_prefix_cache` as `None` (the default), it is forced to `True` for these two tasks. There is no supported way for an application to opt in to cache reads while keeping the pooling task.

### Why full hidden states + prefix caching are needed together

Our workload is multi-candidate classification with a sequence-classification adapter (`vllm-jev`, serving Open-Jev-2B style decision heads). For each HTTP request:

1. The prompt is built as `fixed instructions + fixed candidate list (up to ~18 candidates) + per-request state`, so **the leading ~400+ tokens are identical across requests** and only the trailing state differs.
2. The adapter submits one pooling request per candidate (or a deduplicated set of shared-prefix sequences) with `task="token_embed"`, because the decision head needs **the hidden states at specific readout positions** of the full sequence — a scalar `classify` output is not sufficient.
3. Many candidates share the same leading tokens, and the fixed instruction/criteria block is repeated across every request. This is exactly the workload prefix caching is designed for.

With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back):

- `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests;
- the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation;
- using `--decision-template` style reordering so that the fixed text truly leads the prompt does not change this (the skip happens before any block matching).

With the forced skip, every request recomputes the entire prompt. Measured on an RTX 4090 (vLLM 0.29.0, prefix caching enabled, same `cache_salt`, identical prompts re-submitted back-to-back):

- `metadata.cached_tokens` is always `0` for both `token_embed` and `classify` pooling requests;
- the engine-level `Prefix cache hit rate` metric does occasionally report small non-zero values (2.6%–5.1%), so the cache subsystem itself is alive — but per-request `num_cached_tokens` stays 0 and our throughput matches the "no reuse" expectation;
- using `--decision-template` style reordering so that the fixed text truly leads the prompt does not change this (the skip happens before any block matching).

If prefix-cache reads were allowed for `token_embed` requests, the shared leading blocks (instructions + candidate list ≈ 400+ tokens per request, ×18 candidate variants deduplicated by shared prefixes) would be served from cache, which for our benchmark shape roughly halves the per-request prefill compute.

### Why full hidden states + prefix caching are needed together — the general pattern

The pattern behind this request is **"encode once, read out at many positions"**: a decoder runs the prompt once, and lightweight heads (linear probes, small MLPs) read the hidden states at one or more token positions to produce decisions. This is how a growing family of classification/routing models works on top of decoder backbones. For these models:

- a scalar `classify` output is insufficient — the head needs hidden vectors at specific positions;
- the prompts typically share a large fixed prefix (instructions, schema, candidate definitions) with only a small varying payload;
- request rate is high (classification/routing/moderation workloads), so prefill compute dominates.

All three properties make prefix-cache reuse the single biggest performance lever for this model class, which is why the current forced skip hurts disproportionately.

### Why simply forcing `skip_reading_prefix_cache = False` breaks today

We understand the guard exists for a reason. With cache hits, the scheduler marks the hit tokens as already computed, and the pooling runner processes only the non-cached tail — so `token_embed` would return hidden states for fewer positions than the prompt has tokens, while downstream consumers (decision heads over readout positions, token-level classifiers) require **one hidden vector per prompt token, position-aligned**.

So the missing piece is not just the flag: the V1 pooling path (`vllm/v1/worker/gpu/pool/pooling_runner.py`) has no mechanism to reconstruct position-aligned full-sequence hidden outputs when part of the prompt was served from cache.

### Proposed solutions (any one would unblock this workload)

1. **Fill the gap in the pooling runner**: when a `token_embed`/`token_classify` request has prefix-cache hits, still run (or reconstruct) the hidden states for the cached prefix positions so the output remains position-aligned with the full prompt. Conceptually the KV cache already contains the states for those tokens; the runner would need to re-emit their hidden activations from cache rather than skipping them.
2. **Opt-in flag**: expose `skip_reading_prefix_cache=False` as a documented, caller-owned choice for pooling tasks (as it already is for generation tasks), with a clear caveat that the caller must tolerate/align partial hidden outputs. Applic

### 🐛 Describe the bug When the secondary tier says a key is absent, AsyncLookupManager caches that and keeps it until no request references the key. A new request for the same key in that window gets the cached absent and never probes. That works fine for a private tier but not a shared one (fs root_dir, obj). Another instance can write the block right after the probe. With steady traffic on a common prefix some request always holds the key, so this instance keeps missing blocks that are already on disk. Repro on main, cpu only. The set stands in for the shared tier, and adding the key is another instance writing the block: ```python import time from vllm.v1.kv_offload.base import ReqContext, make_offload_key from vllm.v1.kv_offload.tiering.async_lookup import AsyncLookupManager shared_tier = set() probes = 0 class SharedTierLookup(AsyncLookupManager): def batch_lookup(self, keys, req_context): global probes probes += 1 return [k in shared_tier for k in keys] def resolve(mgr, key, req_id): while (found := mgr.lookup(key, ReqContext(req_id=req_id))) is None: mgr.flush() time.sleep(0.01) return found mgr = SharedTierLookup(tier_type="fs") key = make_offload_key(b"prefix-block-0", 0) print("r1:", resolve(mgr, key, "r1"), "probes:", probes) shared_tier.add(key) print("r2:", resolve(mgr, key, "r2"), "probes:", probes) mgr.cleanup("r1") mgr.cleanup("r2") print("r3:", resolve(mgr, key, "r3"), "probes:", probes) mgr.shutdown() ``` observed: ``` r1: False probes: 1 r2: False probes: 1 r3: True probes: 2 ``` expected: ``` r1: False probes: 1 r2: True probes: 2 r3: True probes: 3 ``` r2 never reaches the backend, and same with the real fs tier: two processes, each with its own `FileSystemTierManager` on one shared `root_dir`. A stores 4 chunks while B's r1 is alive.

items.title: [Bug]: --enable-prompt-embeds sizes OPT-350m embeds at hidden_size 1024, but OPT embeds at word_embed_proj_dim 512
items.author: chrikrah
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

```text
vLLM main c75cb63cd2bb8e0dc62608e9930d8b953ee3b422, imported from the source tree (VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu)
torch 2.14.1+cpu, transformers 5.19.0, Python 3.12.6
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`facebook/opt-350m` embeds tokens at `word_embed_proj_dim` = 512. `OPTDecoder.forward` (`model_executor/models/opt.py:279`) then runs `project_in` up to `hidden_size` = 1024. With `--enable-prompt-embeds`, the rest of vLLM sizes embeds at 1024:

- `renderers/embed_utils.py:98` checks `prompt_embeds` against `get_hidden_size()`. It refuses 512 and accepts 1024, which `project_in` cannot take.
- `get_inputs_embeds_size()` (`config/model.py:1626`) reads only `projection_dim` and `projection_size`, so it also returns 1024. `gpu_model_runner.py:530` sizes the `inputs_embeds` buffer with it. `gpu_model_runner.py:3546` then writes 512-wide `embed_input_ids()` rows into that buffer.

No width works, and the engine should fail at startup: `profile_run` calls `_dummy_run`, whose prompt-embeds branch (`gpu_model_runner.py:5941`) passes the 1024-wide buffer to `forward`.

```python
import io, pybase64, torch
from vllm.config import ModelConfig
from vllm.renderers.embed_utils import safe_load_prompt_embeds

mc = ModelConfig(model="facebook/opt-350m", enable_prompt_embeds=True, dtype="float32")
hf = mc.hf_text_config
print(f"hidden_size={hf.hidden_size} word_embed_proj_dim={hf.word_embed_proj_dim}")
print(f"get_hidden_size()={mc.get_hidden_size()} get_inputs_embeds_size()={mc.get_inputs_embeds_size()}")

def enc(t):
    b = io.BytesIO(); torch.save(t, b); return pybase64.b64encode(b.getvalue())

proj_in = torch.nn.Linear(hf.word_embed_proj_dim, hf.hidden_size, bias=False)  # OPT project_in
for d in (hf.word_embed_proj_dim, hf.hidden_size):
    for name, fn in (("validation", lambda: safe_load_prompt_embeds(mc, enc(torch.randn(4, d)))),
                     ("project_in", lambda: proj_in(torch.randn(4, d)))):
        try:
            fn(); print(f"width {d} {name}: ok")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"width {d} {name}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

buf = torch.zeros(8, mc.get_inputs_embeds_size())  # runner inputs_embeds buffer
buf[torch.tensor([0, 1])] = torch.zeros(2, hf.word_embed_proj_dim)  # embed_input_ids rows
```

```text
$ VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH=. python opt_embeds.py
hidden_size=1024 word_embed_proj_dim=512
get_hidden_size()=1024 get_inputs_embeds_size()=1024
width 512 validation: VLLMValidationError: `prompt_embeds` hidden_size 512 does not match the model's hidden_size 1024. (parameter=prompt_embeds)
width 512 project_in: ok
width 1024 validation: ok
width 1024 project_in: RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (4x1024 and 512x1024)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "opt_embeds.py", line 23, in <module>
RuntimeError: shape mismatch: value tensor of shape [2, 512] cannot be broadcast to indexing result of shape [2, 1024]
# not run: a GPU engine or profile_run; the last line stands in for gpu_model_runner.py:3546
```

I'd add `word_embed_proj_dim` to the names `get_inputs_embeds_size()` reads, which only OPT has, so the runner buffer drops to 512. For the request check I'd validate against `word_embed_proj_dim` where it exists and keep `get_hidden_size()` otherwise. Pointing `embed_utils.py:98` at `get_inputs_embeds_size()` wholesale would be shorter, but it moves CLIP and SigLIP to `projection_dim`, which their `forward()` slices back to `hidden_size` (`clip.py:984`).

@DarkLight1337 which accessor should own the true input width after #29741? Once you pick, I can open the PR with a test on the opt-350m config.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [ ] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
  - Issue and PR search for `word_embed_proj_dim`, `get_inputs_embeds_size` and `prompt_embeds` finds no OPT report. The chatbot was not asked.

items.title: [Bug] Native connector worker death leaves L2 adapter pending maps and L1 read locks stuck
items.author: Writtic
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

Please label as `bug`.

**Summary**

`ConnectorBase`'s worker loop can exit with requests still queued, and nothing tells the Python side. Every `future_id` submitted to that worker then sits in `NativeConnectorL2Adapter`'s pending maps for the life of the process, and for stores it also pins the L1 read locks the in-flight task holds.

Raised in review on #4211 by @maobaolong. Filing it separately as agreed there, since the fix belongs to the C++ completion contract rather than the adapter.

**Details**

The adapter pairs every insert into `_pending_ops`, `_pending_store_sizes`, and `_pending_store_tasks` with a removal: the submit failure path cleans up its own entries, and the demux thread pops all three when a completion arrives. The maps grow without bound only when a submitted `future_id` never produces a completion.

`worker_loop_for_queue` in `csrc/storage_backends/connector_base.h` has two such paths:

1. `create_connection()` throws before the request loop starts. The outer `catch` prints to stderr and the worker returns, leaving its queue undrained.
2. A non-`std::exception` escapes the per-tile `catch (const std::exception&)`, unwinds to `catch (...)`, and kills the worker. That tile never reaches `handle_tile_completion`.

Both report through `fprintf(stderr, ...)` instead of the logger, so a dead worker is easy to miss.

For stores the cost is larger than dict growth. `StoreController` records `read_locked_keys` per in-flight task and releases them on completion, so a task that never completes holds L1 read locks until the process exits and those chunks cannot be evicted.

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

Every submitted `future_id` gets exactly one completion, including when its worker dies. Options worth discussing:

- On worker exit, drain the queue and push a failed `Completion` for each pending request.
- Widen the per-tile catch to `catch (...)`, so an unknown exception fails one tile instead of the worker.
- Report worker death through the logger and a metric, not only stderr.

**Actual Outcome**

The maps grow without bound and the store task never completes. #4211 adds `lmcache_mp.l2_adapter_pending_entries`, a gauge over the three maps per adapter, which makes this visible: a series that keeps climbing without returning to zero is this leak.

items.title: [Documentation Request] vLLM kv_load_failure_policy doesn't apply to load failures in L2 adapters
items.author: RedL0tus
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**
Please label your issue so that it can easily be easily categorized under [LMCache Onboarding](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/1882)

**Summary**
[kv_load_failure_policy](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/api/vllm/config/kv_transfer/#vllm.config.kv_transfer.KVTransferConfig.kv_load_failure_policy) doesn't seem to apply to remote KV data load failures in L2 adapters.

**Details**
vLLM supports setting kv_load_failure_policy, which defines the behavior during KV load failures. However, this configuration option doesn't seem to apply to L2 adapters. We've tested the `nixl_store` L2 adapter and the `s3` L2 adapter with injected errors, and LMCache seems to treat L2 load failures as cache misses instead of failures.

is this an intentional design choice? It would be great to document the expected behavior of failures at different cache levels in LMCache.

**Steps / Reproduction (if applicable)**
1. Start LMCache with L2 adapter set to `nixl_store` with OBJ backend, or `s3`.
2. Start vLLM, use LMCache for KV cache offloading and internal prefix caching disabled with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`.
3. Send data to vLLM and Intercept all GetObject calls to the S3 endpoint.

**Expected Outcome / Goal**
With `"kv_load_failure_policy": "fail"`, requests with external cache hits should return error code.

**Actual Outcome (if applicable)**
LMCache log errors to the console, vLLM proceed to serve all requests with recomputed KV data as if it's only a cache miss.

**Additional Context**
This issue was first discovered by [Anish Sana](mailto:anish.sana@hpe.com) under HPE's internal testing.
