items.title: [Bug] P2P load timeout can report terminal failure while the transfer is still active
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`P2PL2Adapter.query_load_result()` returns a terminal all-zero `Bitmap` as soon as `load_timeout_s` expires, without querying or cancelling the underlying `TransferChannelClient` read ([p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L333-L336)). The read may still be in flight at that point, so the adapter reports "finished (failed)" for a load whose transfer has not reached a terminal state.

The existing test `test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure` asserts exactly this behaviour, so I am raising it as a contract question rather than a regression: is a terminal load result allowed to precede the end of the transfer?

**To Reproduce**

On `dev` @ 8d7d2c47, add this test to `tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py`:

```python
def test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight():
    keys = [_key(0)]
    now = [100.0]
    in_flight = TransferChannelReadResult(finished=False)
    with (
        _adapter(load_timeout_s=0.01) as (adapter, _mq, _tc_ctx, tc_client, _n),
        patch.object(p2p_mod.time, "monotonic", side_effect=lambda: now[0]),
    ):
        adapter._remote_addresses[keys[0]] = TransferChannelAddress(offset=100, size=10)
        tc_client.submit_read.return_value = 123
        tc_client.query_read_status.return_value = in_flight
        task_id = adapter.submit_load_task(
            keys, [MagicMock(shm_offset=0, shm_byte_length=10)]
        )
        now[0] = 100.02  # past the 0.01 s load deadline
        assert not in_flight.is_finished()
        assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
```

```
pytest -v tests/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/test_p2p_l2_adapter.py -k "deadline or not_finished"
```

Result (CPU-only build, transfer channel mocked):

```
>           assert adapter.query_load_result(task_id) is None
E           assert 0 is None
E            +  where 0 = query_load_result(0)

LMCache WARNING: P2P load task 0 timed out; treating as a failure (p2p_l2_adapter.py:335)

test_lookup_deadline_expired_yields_miss PASSED
test_load_not_finished_returns_none PASSED
test_load_deadline_expired_yields_failure PASSED
test_load_deadline_does_not_report_terminal_while_read_is_in_flight FAILED
1 failed, 3 passed
```

(`0` is the repr of a one-key, all-zero `Bitmap`, i.e. a terminal failure.)

This test only demonstrates the current behaviour; its assertion would need adjusting depending on which direction below is preferred.

**Expected behavior**

Either the adapter does not report a terminal load result while its transfer-channel read may still access the destination buffers, or the contract states explicitly that a terminal result does not imply the transfer has quiesced and callers handle that.

**Additional context**

To be clear about what is and is not shown:

*Reproduced (unit test above):* the read is modelled as unfinished, and after the deadline `query_load_result()` returns a terminal failure.

*Derived from reading the code, not reproduced:*
- On that result, `PrefetchController._poll_load_results()` calls `finish_write_and_delete()` for the failed keys and then `submit_unlock()` ([prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py#L1389-L1395)); for P2P, `submit_unlock()` sends `p2p_unlock_objects` to the peer ([#L277-L280](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L277-L280)). So both the destination staging buffer and the source-side lock are released.
- The NIXL transfer channel registers the whole L1 buffer once ([nixl_impl.py#L344](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L344)). This creates a window in which a late read may write into memory that has since been reassigned to another key.
- After the timeout the adapter no longer queries the read, so the `NixlTransferChannelClient._tasks` entry and its xfer handle are only released on `close()` ([#L178-L181](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L178-L181), [#L202-L206](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/impl/nixl_impl.py#L202-L206)).

*Not reproduced:* actual stale or corrupted KV data end to end. I have not run a two-instance NIXL test for this.

**Possible directions** (not proposing a specific fix yet)

- **A. Stay pending until the transfer is terminal.** After the deadline, keep polling `query_read_status()` and only report once it finishes. Simple ownership model; a hung transfer would hold its buffers and locks indefinitely.
- **B. Add per-task cancellation to `TransferChannelClient`** ([abstract.py#L52-L88](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/8d7d2c47e1edb8c107033ae709722b2c3a05dec4/lmcache/v1/distributed/transfer_channel/abstract.py#L52-L88) has only `submit_read`, `query_read_status`, `close`), and report terminal only once the cancel is confirmed. For NIXL this would map to `releaseXferReq`, which the BackendGuide says "can return error, meaning it was not successful in aborting the request", so it still needs A as a fallback. The Mooncake wrapper has no cancel today; I have not checked the engine itself.
- **C. Drop the adapter-level load deadline** and rely on the controller-level deadline from #5255, which already keeps late loads' buffers and locks until the load result arrives.

The P2P adapter is the runtime caller of `submit_read()`; the transfer-channel benchmark also calls it directly, so an API change in B would touch both.

**Related**

- #5263 — same ownership family, on the shutdown / TTL paths rat
items.author_work_intent: If maintainers agree this is a contract gap, I'm happy to work on the fix. I'd especially appreciate guidance on whether the preferred direction is to keep timed-out reads pending until terminal, add a TransferChannel cancell

comments.author: holtwood
comments.body:
I checked another timeout case at [`1ca53a8`](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/1ca53a8aadca1d054f171fd67350be35797cfddc/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/p2p_l2_adapter.py#L326-L347) using the original query methods with mocked dependencies. I haven't run a real NIXL transfer.

Even when the transfer is already marked `DONE`, polling after the deadline returns a zero bitmap without calling `query_read_status`. The adapter removes its task, so later adapter polls return `None`. The client's `close()` still has a separate cleanup path.

This seems worth covering in the timeout tests, including cleanup of an already-completed transfer. I can help add that case if it's useful.

items.title: KV cache in VLLM serve
items.author: farouk09
items.body_excerpt:
Hi everyone! 👋

I'm trying to run the model Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (49.1 GB VRAM) using vllm serve with the --dtype auto option. However, I'm getting the following error:

_`ValueError: The model's max seq len (1010000) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache (73792). Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization` or decreasing `max_model_len` when initializing the engine.`_

From my understanding:

- The model has ~14B parameters, so in FP16 it should use ~28GB of VRAM (please correct me if that’s inaccurate).
- Running in auto mode (which defaults to FP16), the weights should take ~14GB.
- That leaves ~36GB, which I thought would be enough for the KV cache for a 1M context length. But apparently not?

So I have two questions:

1. Is my assumption about the memory breakdown (weights vs KV cache) correct?
2. How can we estimate the required VRAM for a given number of context tokens? Is there a formula or rule of thumb to calculate the KV cache size needed based on context length and model size?

More broadly, I'd really appreciate if someone could explain how to estimate the total VRAM usage in `vllm serve`, including weights, KV cache, context window, etc.

Thanks in advance!

items.title: [Bug]: Paused streaming sessions deadlock the scheduler when the KV cache is full
items.author: damienlaine
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Scheduler-level repro on CPU, no model or GPU needed. Main at `89a00995c9`. Also hit on GPU with Voxtral realtime, V1 and V2 model runners.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

A paused streaming session (`resumable`, `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`) keeps its KV blocks. When its next chunk arrives it goes through `kv_holding_waiting`. If the pool is full, `allocate_slots` fails and the waiting loop breaks. Preemption only takes from `running`, which is empty because every session is between chunks. Nothing gets freed, and every session stays waiting forever.

So once the sessions' KV goes over the pool, all of them freeze, not only the one that doesn't fit.

Repro (4 sessions, 7 usable blocks of 16 tokens, each chunk adds one block):

```python
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import torch

from vllm.config import DeviceConfig, VllmConfig
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams
from vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler import Scheduler
from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import FullAttentionSpec, KVCacheConfig, KVCacheGroupSpec
from vllm.v1.outputs import ModelRunnerOutput
from vllm.v1.request import Request
from vllm.v1.structured_output import StructuredOutputManager

STOP = 128001
BLOCK = 16
NUM_BLOCKS = 8
NUM_SESSIONS = 4


def make_scheduler():
    cfg = VllmConfig(device_config=DeviceConfig("cpu"))
    cfg.model_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.model_config.skip_tokenizer_init = True
    cfg.model_config.is_multimodal_model = False
    cfg.model_config.supports_multimodal_inputs = False
    cfg.model_config.is_encoder_decoder = False
    cfg.model_config.is_diffusion = False
    cfg.model_config.max_model_len = 1024
    cfg.model_config.enable_return_routed_experts = False
    cfg.cache_config = MagicMock()
    cfg.cache_config.num_gpu_blocks = NUM_BLOCKS
    cfg.cache_config.enable_prefix_caching = False
    kv = KVCacheConfig(
        num_blocks=NUM_BLOCKS,
        kv_cache_tensors=[],
        kv_cache_groups=[KVCacheGroupSpec(["layer"], FullAttentionSpec(
            block_size=BLOCK, num_kv_heads=1, head_size=1, dtype=torch.float32))],
    )
    return Scheduler(vllm_config=cfg, kv_cache_config=kv, log_stats=False,
                     structured_output_manager=StructuredOutputManager(cfg),
                     block_size=BLOCK, hash_block_size=BLOCK)


def chunk(rid, n):
    # One streaming update: n new prompt tokens, generation stops after 1 token.
    return Request(request_id=rid, prompt_token_ids=list(range(1, n + 1)),
                   sampling_params=SamplingParams(stop_token_ids=[STOP], max_tokens=16),
                   pooling_params=None, resumable=True)


s = make_scheduler()
ids = [f"s{i}" for i in range(NUM_SESSIONS)]
for rid in ids:
    s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK - 1))

for step in range(12):
    out = s.schedule()
    sched = list(out.num_scheduled_tokens)
    free = s.kv_cache_manager.block_pool.get_num_free_blocks()
    print(f"step {step}: scheduled={sched} free_blocks={free} "
          f"waiting={len(s.waiting) + len(getattr(s, 'kv_holding_waiting', []))}")
    if not sched:
        continue
    # Every scheduled session ends its chunk (STOP) and pauses, keeping its KV.
    s.update_from_output(out, ModelRunnerOutput(
        req_ids=sched, req_id_to_index={r: i for i, r in enumerate(sched)},
        sampled_token_ids=[[STOP] for _ in sched], logprobs=None,
        prompt_logprobs_dict={}, pooler_output=[]))
    # The client sends the next chunk for each of them.
    for rid in sched:
        s.add_request(chunk(rid, BLOCK))
```

```
step 0: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2', 's3'] free_blocks=3 waiting=0
step 1: scheduled=['s0', 's1', 's2'] free_blocks=0 waiting=1
step 2: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
...
step 11: scheduled=[] free_blocks=0 waiting=4
```

On GPU, Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime with a 256 sliding window (~128 MiB KV per session) and `--kv-cache-memory 1GiB`: 7 sessions run fine, with 9 every session stops after a few seconds, 0 tok/s, no preemption, all 9 transcriptions cut. `--max-num-seqs 7` avoids it, the extra sessions just wait.

Expected: preempt a paused session (free its KV, recompute on resume) instead of blocking the queue.

Related: #58776 (a preempted resumable session is dropped). The encoder cache has the same pattern: a paused session keeps its last multimodal item cached until it resumes, and when the cache can't hold them all the waiting loop breaks the same way (seen with a small encoder cache in #45022).

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Reproduced on current main (`31e2443c90`, CPU scheduler-level, exact script from the report): deadlock from step 2 on, `scheduled=[]` for the remaining 10 steps with `free_blocks=0` and all 4 sessions waiting.

This is the deadlock #59339 already fixes: it reclaims KV blocks from paused/`kv_holding` sessions at the waiting loop's allocation-failure point, which is the gap described here (preemption only scans `running`, and `running` is empty). I ran the same repro on #59339's head (`a0f422aa`): continuous progress from step 2 through 8 as paused sessions get reclaimed and resumed. The repro then stalls again at steps 9-11, but that is genuine capacity exhaustion, not deadlock: each session's prompt grows one block per round, so by then a single chunk needs ~9 blocks against an 8-block pool and nothing can legitimately fit.

One note for whoever picks up review: #59339's only red check is the pre-run gate (author has 2 merged PRs, needs a `verified`/`ready` label), not a code failure.

comments.author: divyuuu
comments.body:
Checked this on current main (`1e5d0ea`).

Static trace matches the report: the running-loop only preempts from `self.running` (`vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:776-782`), and the waiting-loop `allocate_slots` failure path just `break`s (`1241-1248`) with no reclaim from `kv_holding_waiting`. So once all sessions are paused holding KV and `running` is empty, every `schedule()` stalls with nothing scheduled and nothing freed.

I also checked #59339 (reclaim at the waiting-loop failure point, updated Oct 6) to avoid duplicating it. Validating next whether it covers this exact 4-session repro on a Linux runner (my Windows host can't build vLLM -- no AMD64 precompiled wheel, only manylinux). Repro script ready from the issue body.

If a regression-test gap remains after #59339, may I take it? Happy to contribute the repro as a scheduler regression test. AI assistance used for the trace; will run the repro and tests before any PR per the contribution guide.

comments.author: damienlaine
comments.body:
Ran #59339 (`a0f422aa`) against its base (`21d93d0d8c`) on GPU with Voxtral realtime: RTX 4090, 256/256 sliding windows, `--max-num-batched-tokens 256`, `--kv-cache-memory-bytes 1GiB` (11,915 tokens), 120 s streams sent in real time.

| | completed | generation | words/stream |
|---|---|---|---|
| base, 9 sessions | 0/9, stalled after ~20 s | 0 tok/s | ~15 |
| #59339, 9 sessions | 0/9 | 65 → ~7 tok/s (~110 needed) | ~60 |
| #59339, 8 sessions | 0/8 | ~6 tok/s | ~80 |
| #59339, 7 sessions (fit in pool) | 7/7 | same output as reference | ~275 |
| default pool (49,152 tokens), 9 sessions | 9/9 | 112 tok/s | ~280 |

The stall is gone and reclaimed sessions produce correct output (97-100% word match with the reference on the same audio). Under overcommit, throughput collapses for all sessions, not only the extra one: a reclaimed session restarts from `num_computed_tokens = 0` and recomputes its full history, encoder included, so the cost per reclaim grows with session age.

Also tried restricting victims to sessions with lower `(priority, arrival_time)` than the requester, as the running-loop preemption does: 0/8 and 0/9, ~10 tok/s, and it breaks 3 of #59339's tests. Victim selection is not the issue.

Regression tests for this case are already in #59339 (14 tests, pass locally).

items.title: [SM120] Field report: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash in production on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (PCIe, no NVLink) - working config, measured throughput, rejected topologies
items.author: Lei-010
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Field data from running **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** as a production SGLang backend on **8× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (SM120, 96 GB, PCIe-only — no NVLink)**, including the *only* topology we could get to start, measured prefill/decode, a speculative-decoding A/B, and the configuration traps that cost us real experiments. Posting because SM120 + V4.1-Flash users currently have to rediscover all of this from scratch.

Full write-up (with methodology and reproduction artifacts): https://github.com/Lei-010/hermes-agent/blob/main/docs/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-SM120-Performance-and-Production-Config.md

Related: vLLM field report https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56700 (same hardware, vLLM side), vLLM https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/56892 (SM120 bug/perf tracker).

## What works

```bash
docker run --gpus all -d --name dsv41 \
  --shm-size=64g --ipc=host --network host \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  -e TP_SIZE=8 -e DP_SIZE=1 -e EP_SIZE=8 \
  -e SPEC_ALGORITHM=dspark -e DSPARK_BLOCK_SIZE=6 \
  -e CHUNKED_PREFILL_SIZE=2048 \
  -v /ssd/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash:/model \
  <sglang image>
```

Effective `server_args` (verified at runtime via `/get_server_info`):

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| `tp_size` / `ep_size` / `dp_size` | 8 / 8 / 1 |
| `speculative_algorithm` | DSPARK, `speculative_dspark_block_size = 6` |
| `chunked_prefill_size` | 2048 |
| `context_length` | 1,048,576 |
| `kv_cache_dtype` | `fp8_e4m3` |
| `mem_fraction_static` | 0.72 |
| `max_running_requests` | 16 |
| `attention_backend` / `moe_runner_backend` | `dsv4` / `flashinfer_mxfp4` |
| CUDA graph decode / prefill | full (max_bs 16) / **disabled** |

**TP8/EP8 is not a preference — it is the only layout that starts** (see "Topologies SGLang rejects" below).

## Measured throughput (cold, single stream, tokens from `usage`, not SSE chunk counts)

128K cold prefill:

| Config | tok/s |
|---|---|
| `chunked_prefill_size=2048` (production) | **6,853** |
| same config re-run | 6,765 (−1.3%) |
| flashmla prefill backend | 6,845 |
| fused-MoE all-reduce | 6,828 |
| `chunked_prefill_size=4096` | 6,301 |
| `chunked_prefill_size=1024` | 6,012 |

32K prompt: ≈7,196 tok/s. GPU util ≈87% at 220 W of 600 W → **communication-bound on PCIe**, not compute-bound. ~7K tok/s looks like the ceiling for this board without NVLink.

Radix/prefix cache is the only large multiplier: cache-hit prefill **0.34 s for a 112K-token prefix ≈ 325K tok/s (≈39×)**.

Decode (client path over SSH tunnel, production config): prose 93.9 tok/s, structured/JSON 134.1 tok/s, TTFT 143–169 ms.

## DSPARK A/B (block_size=2, clean legs, each verified via `server_info` + acceptance length)

| Prompt class | DSPARK ON | DSPARK OFF |
|---|---|---|
| prose | 76.5–78.9 tok/s | 36.4–36.5 tok/s |
| structured | 120.3–120.5 tok/s | 36.5 tok/s |
| `accept len` | 3.0 tokens/step | 1.0 |

With DSPARK off the model flattens to ~36.5 tok/s regardless of prompt class — speculation is the difference between usable and unusable latency on this hardware. Production ships `block_size=6` (structured ≈237–252 tok/s vs 120 at block 2).

## Traps that cost us experiments (SGLang-specific)

1. **`--enable-expert-parallel` is a vLLM flag** — SGLang takes `ep_size`; the vLLM spelling is rejected outright.
2. **`docker run` must pass `TP_SIZE`/`DP_SIZE`/`EP_SIZE` explicitly.** Without `-e`, the container silently serves TP8 defaults and your "new" config never happens (we recorded a full sweep of false data this way before adding a config gate).
3. **`ep_size ≤ tp_size`** or the MoE rank computation divides by zero: `moe_ep_rank = tp_rank % (tp_size // moe_dp_size) // (tp_size // moe_dp_size // ep_size)`.
4. **DSPARK + DP attention requires `--enable-dp-lm-head`** — but is unreachable on this model anyway (next section).

## Topologies SGLang rejects on this model

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| DP2 × TP4 (any EP) | `ValueError: V4.1 vision currently supports TP/EP without DP, CP, PP or MoE A2A` — both replicas die within ~70 s |
| prefill context-parallel | same class of rejection |
| `--enable-dp-attention` alone | silently no DP group (`dp_size: 1`) — looks fine, isn't |

Other SM120 gaps we hit: MSCCL++ (`_tune` kernel crash), FlashInfer all-reduce fusion, `flashmla_sparse_q8`, and CUDA-graph capture for **prefill** (crashes even with DSPARK off, i.e. unrelated to speculation).

## Operational notes

- A defunct container can survive a single `docker rm -f`; the next `docker run` then fails on the name conflict while an orphaned engine process keeps the port and answers health checks — which silently mislabels the next experiment. Loop `docker rm -f` until the container is gone **and** nothing listens on the port.
- A parse failure must never satisfy an "expected config" assertion, or a server that has not started yet gets recorded as "spec disabled".
- Verify intended config from the server (`/get_server_info`) before timing anything; discard legs that fail the gate rather than recording them.

## Not established

No 24 h soak (numbers come from a working day of production use), block sizes 4/8/12 not re-measured with the fixed sweep tool, and >32K prefill/long-context degradation not characterised.

items.title: [Bug][Spec Decode] DFlash2 acceptance drops ~5.5 points when the hybrid KV cache manager makes its sliding-window draft a real SWA group (BLHNC, NIXL P/D)
items.author: stu-cao
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- **Hardware and topology:** 2× B300 HGX nodes. Prefill DEP8 (TP1 per rank, 8 ranks); decode 2× TP4.
  `NixlConnector` (pull mode) over RDMA (UCX).
- **vLLM:** `main` @ `4e0a414c44` plus #58471 (GQA draft head slicing under an MLA target), #57662,
  #58744's chunked-context gather, and the NVFP4 KV path from #59342.
- **Target:** GLM-5.3, NVFP4 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4_ds_mla`, `FLASHINFER_MLA_SPARSE`.
- **Draft:** DFlash2 (`method: dflash`, 4 speculative tokens). Its 6 layers are all `sliding_attention`
  with `sliding_window: 2048`, 8 KV heads, fp8 KV.
- **Layout:** `VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT=BLHNC`, `--block-size 64`.
- **Prefix caching:** enabled on both roles.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

DFlash2 draft acceptance drops by about 5.5 points (34.2% vs 39.6%) under BLHNC block size 64 whenever
the hybrid KV cache manager (HMA) is on. On the same stack, `--disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`
restores it. Target outputs stay correct, so the cost is throughput: fewer tokens per step.

**What changes with HMA.** The draft's layers are all sliding-window attention.
- **LBHNC:** page sizes cannot be unified, so vLLM falls back to full-attention allocation for the
  draft (`KV cache page sizes cannot be unified; treating sliding-window layers as full attention for
  cache allocation`).
- **BLHNC:** HMA builds two KV cache groups (`kv cache group sizes [64, 64]`), so the draft becomes a
  real sliding-window group. Its out-of-window blocks are freed to the null block, its prefix-cache
  hits use sliding-window rules, and NIXL transfers only its tail (`blocks_per_sw = cdiv(2048, 64) + 1`).

**Measurements.** Agentic multi-turn traffic (AgentX), 32 concurrent sessions, 900 s per arm.
Acceptance = accepted / drafted tokens over the measured window, summed over both decode engines.

| arm | layout, block size | HMA | draft allocated as | acceptance | first-position acceptance | decode local prefix hit |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| B | BLHNC, 64 | on | sliding-window group | **34.18%** | 0.545 | 0.29 |
| C (same as B, different decode kernel) | BLHNC, 64 | on | sliding-window group | **34.18%** | 0.545 | 0.29 |
| D | BLHNC, 64 | **off** | full attention | **39.61%** | 0.632 | 0.76 |
| earlier build, fp8 KV | LBHNC, 1024 | n/a | full attention (fallback) | 39.97% | | |
| earlier build, NVFP4 KV | LBHNC, 1024 | n/a | full attention (fallback) | 39.64% | | |

Notes on the table:
- Arm D ran with per-layer NIXL regions. With HMA off, BLHNC packs the head-sharded draft pages into
  the target's block row, which our whole-row NIXL registration cannot handle across TP sizes.
- Every position recovers in arm D (p0 0.545 → 0.632, p3 0.186 → 0.217).
- A separate GB200 deployment shows the same gap: 10× TP4 decode, 128 sessions, 34.8% under BLHNC
  with HMA on vs 40.5% under LBHNC.

**Ruled out:**
- **KV dtype:** fp8 and NVFP4 give the same acceptance under LBHNC on the same hardware.
- **Decode attention kernel:** two NVFP4 decode kernels give identical acceptance, 34.18% vs 34.18%.
- **Draft head slicing over NIXL:** the registration is unit-tested with #58471 and #57662.
- **Correctness:** gates pass, including long-context retrieval and multi-turn P/D splits.

**Leads (not yet confirmed):**
1. **The window's left edge may reach freed blocks.** DFlash queries are non-causal, so
   `_maybe_symmetrize_window` turns the layer's `(2047, 0)` into `(2047, 2047)`. FlashAttention then
   applies it bottom-right aligned to `seqused_k`. `SlidingWindowManager.get_num_skipped_tokens` frees
   tokens below `processed_computed_tokens - 2047`. If those two boundaries disagree by a few tokens,
   for example over whether the draft's query block counts in `seqused_k`, the draft reads freed
   blocks. That only happens with HMA on, and at block size 64 it happens often.
   An experiment that widens only the manager's window by 128 tokens (HMA on) is running; we will
   post the result here.
2. **Suspected mispairing in the region-mapped/DCP NIXL path.** `_apply_dcp_prefix_caching` pairs a
   sliding-window group start-aligned: `remote_ids[local_num_computed_blocks:]` against the remote
   list that `get_exchange_clipped_blocks` already tail-clipped. That is correct only when the
   prefill's clip start equals the decode's skip boundary. When they differ by one block, every draft
   block shifts by one. The default equal-layout path aligns from the end and looks correct.
   No unit test confirms this yet.
3. Decode local prefix hits fall from 0.76 to 0.29 with HMA on. The sliding-window hit rule needs
   `cdiv(2047, 64)` contiguous cached blocks. This may interact with either lead above.

**Why it matters beyond this deployment.** RFC #58638 / #58380 proposes preferring BLHNC for models
with speculative drafters, so that drafter sliding-window layers become real sliding-window groups.
This is the configuration where we lose acceptance.

**Not yet tested:** aggregated (non-P/D) serving, and other sliding-window drafters.

**Questions for maintainers:**
- Is the non-causal symmetric window plus bottom-right alignment expected to stay within
  `num_computed_tokens - sliding_window + 1` for DFlash's query block?
- Is a sliding-window draft group expected to work with NIXL P/D and decode-side prefix caching
  today?

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched issues and PRs: #58638, #58380, #58207, #57661, #57662, #58471, #60113.
  - Related but different: #59656 groups sliding-window draft layers in the GLM-5.3-Flash
    (`glm5_next`) builder, a different grouping path. #58894 / #55601 cover Qwen3.5 GDN mamba-state
    indexing on prefix hits.
  - The DFlash2 draft group here is flagged as the eagle group through
    `non_causal_multi_token_decode`, so the last-block drop on prefix hits does apply to it.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to run the experiments, analyze the logs and draft this issue. A
human reviewed it.

items.title: [RFC]: Bring-Your-Own-GPU (BYOG) reproducible evals and benchmarks for PRs
items.author: LucasWilkinson
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Reviewing performance- and accuracy-sensitive PRs is frequently bottlenecked on evidence and regression testing. Reviewers routinely ask "can you please provide e2e performance data?", "can you please provide eval results?", or "can you show 8k1k numbers on H100?". Not only are these requests often vague, leaving the submitter unsure exactly how to run the benchmark or eval, but the answers also arrive as screenshots, hand-run `vllm bench` output, or not at all. On the flip side, running a broad eval + benchmark matrix on vLLM-funded CI for PRs does not scale, especially as the volume of AI-generated PRs grows.

AI tools have made producing a PR nearly free, but reviewing one costs as much as or more than it ever did. Maintainer attention is now the scarce resource, and AI generation of PRs is skewing more of the cost of a PR onto the reviewer, who frequently has to validate the PR manually or validate it on other hardware. Asking for evidence that costs GPU time to produce moves some of that cost back to whoever wants the PR merged. It doesn't close the gap, and spending compute doesn't make a PR good, but it pushes in the right direction in two ways:

- the evidence gives the reviewer more confidence, making the PR easier to review;
- spending it signals that someone values the PR.

At the same time, the community has more datacenter hardware than vLLM CI, and more kinds of it (GB300, MI355X, older Hopper/Ampere fleets, and so on). Some of it may be free to help with evals for specific, important PRs, even if its owners aren't ready to commit it to vLLM CI full time by hooking it up as a CI agent.

This RFC proposes a standard, versioned **eval image**, built by vLLM CI when CI is run on a commit, which anyone can run on their own GPUs, coupled with a **public database of results**.

This could also help PRs under the [fast-track merging RFC (#59665)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59665) by providing the extra evals and benchmarks it asks for.

### Proposed Change.

#### Goals

- Anyone with suitable GPUs can produce results for a commit with a single `docker run`: give the image a request or run spec, and it produces a result bundle.
- Results are reproducible: a bundle records everything needed to re-run it on the same GPU type and get the same result within stated tolerances.
- **Trust-based, with accountability.** Every upload is tied to the submitter's GitHub account.
- Reviewers can ask for a specific configuration, and any community member can donate GPU time to provide it, including hardware the author doesn't have.
- Reuse existing vLLM eval configs (`tests/evals/*`, `.buildkite/lm-eval-harness/configs`) and community benchmark recipes (SemiAnalysis InferenceX and AgentX) rather than inventing new ones.

#### Scope

- **Not in scope yet: hard merge gating.** For now results are informational, an informal gate: reviewers may expect them and may request specific runs, but nothing blocks merging automatically. Once the prototype has shown the results are reliable, we may make some results required for merging certain areas.
- **Non-goal:** replacing pre-merge CI or the existing post-merge performance dashboard.

#### Overview

1. **On the PR.** A maintainer triggers CI on a commit, and CI builds a signed eval image for it. A reviewer asks for results with `/byog request`, or the submitter simply runs the standard suites up front and uploads the results as extra evidence.
2. **On anyone's GPUs.** Anyone with suitable GPUs runs the request with a single `docker run`. The image runs the jobs that fit its GPUs, shows the bundle it produced, then uploads it after a GitHub login.
3. **On the results service.** The service records who uploaded the bundle, stores it, and updates the public dashboard and the PR via a comment.

#### Evals and benchmarks

##### Evals

Every eval costs GPU time, so we want the set that gives the **most signal per GPU-hour**.

**Proposed eval suites,** picked with `eval_suite:`. Listing `evals` in a request replaces the suite. Requesting community input on the contents and time budgets.

| Eval suite | When | Evals | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `smoke` | Quick check that nothing is badly broken | `gsm8k` | minutes |
| `standard` (default) | The general expectation for accuracy-sensitive PRs | `gsm8k`, `mmlu_pro` (300 per subject), `mrcr` (120 samples) | up to ~3 hours |
| `extended` | On reviewer request, for large or risky changes | `gsm8k`, full `mmlu_pro`, `mrcr` (240 samples) | hours |

Each eval in these suites covers a different kind of failure: `gsm8k` catches gross breakage quickly, `mmlu_pro` covers broad knowledge and isn't saturated on large models, and `mrcr` covers long context (attention, KV cache, prefix caching). All run against datasets pinned to a commit and baked into the image.

**Catalog.** Other evals a request can add. Costs are rough orders of magnitude for a typical config (for example a mid-size MoE on one node); reasoning mode and large models move evals up a bucket.

| Eval | What it catches | Existing harness | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Logprob / KL divergence vs reference logits | Numerical drift from kernels, quantization, attention backends, often before scores move | — (new) | minutes |
| `ifeval` | Chat template, instruction following, stop handling | lm-eval | minutes |
| `chartqa` / `mmmu` | Multimodal pipeline | `.buildkite/lm-eval-harness` | tens of minutes |
| `gpqa_diamond` (×N repeats) | Reasoning quality | `tests/evals/gpt_oss` | tens of minutes → hours |
| `bfcl` / tool-call subset | Tool calling, structured output, parsers | — | tens of minutes → hours |
| `aime25` (×N repeats) | Long-generation reasoning; high variance | lm-eval | hours |
| `livecodebench` | Code generation | — | hours |
| `ruler` / `longbench_v2` | Long context at 128k+ | — | hours |
| SWE-bench Verified / agentic benchmarks | End-to-end agentic quality | — (needs sandboxes) | hours → days |

items.title: TRT-LLM connector: _TRTLLM_KERNEL_BATCH_SIZE (32) exceeds c_ops kernel's 4-object cap → store fails for prompts >4 chunks
items.author: nafis271
items.body_excerpt:
The TensorRT-LLM GPU connector batches KV transfers in groups of `_TRTLLM_KERNEL_BATCH_SIZE = 32` (`lmcache/v1/gpu_connector/gpu_connectors.py`), but the c_ops kernel `multi_layer_block_kv_transfer` accepts at most 4 memory objects per call. Any store/load with more than 4 chunks raises:

```
RuntimeError: Expected 1-4 LMCache objects, got <N>
```

after which the TRT-LLM executor loop dies.

### Where it comes from
- `gpu_connectors.py`: `_TRTLLM_KERNEL_BATCH_SIZE = 32`, used as the batch stride in `_batched_transfer` (passes up to 32 object pointers per `lmc_ops.multi_layer_block_kv_transfer` call).
- `csrc/mp_mem_kernels.cuh`: `struct MemoryObj4 { ScalarType* objects[4]; int num_objects; }`
- `csrc/mp_mem_kernels.cu`: `TORCH_CHECK(num_objects >= 1 && num_objects <= 4, "Expected 1-4 LMCache objects, got ", num_objects);`

The kernel is hard-capped at 4 by design, so a Python batch size of 32 looks inconsistent with it.

### Reproduce
TRT-LLM + `connector: lmcache`, chunk_size 256, send any prompt that produces more than 4 chunks (>~1024 tokens). Short prompts (≤4 chunks) don't trigger it, which is likely why the current E2E tests pass.

### Fix that worked for me
Set `_TRTLLM_KERNEL_BATCH_SIZE = 4` (the kernel's max) — `_batched_transfer` already loops with that stride. Verified on gpt-oss-120b (TRT-LLM 1.3, lmcache 0.5.0): stores/retrieves succeed at ~45 GB/s, no errors.

Present on `main` @ 6f444eb.

Happy to send this as a PR if useful.

items.title: [Bug] enable_blending with LMCacheConnectorV1 crashes at startup: VLLMModelTracker.register_model is never called
items.author: matu79go
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Enabling CacheBlend (`enable_blending: true`) with the vLLM V1 connector (`LMCacheConnectorV1`) crashes the engine at startup:

```
ValueError: vllm model for vllm-instance not found.
```

Root cause: `LMCBlenderBuilder.get_or_create()` calls `VLLMModelTracker.get_model(ENGINE_NAME)`, but **nothing in the current tree ever calls `VLLMModelTracker.register_model()`** — grepping the repo shows the only references are in `lmcache/v1/compute/models/utils.py` (definition) and `lmcache/v1/compute/blend/utils.py` (the `get_model` call). The registration call appears to be a leftover from the old `lmcache_vllm` fork era.

## Environment

- LMCache: main @ `668a1fd`, built from source
- vLLM: 0.19.1 (official `vllm/vllm-openai:latest-cu130-ubuntu2404` image, aarch64 / GB10)
- Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, `--enforce-eager --no-enable-prefix-caching`

## Reproduction

```yaml
# lmcache config
chunk_size: 256
local_cpu: true
max_local_cpu_size: 32
enable_blending: true
use_layerwise: true
blend_special_str: " # #"
blend_check_layers: [1]
blend_recompute_ratios: [0.15]
```

```
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheConnectorV1","kv_role":"kv_both"}' ...
```

EngineCore dies during `_initialize_kv_caches` → `LMCacheConnectorV1Impl.__init__` → `LMCBlenderBuilder.get_or_create` → `VLLMModelTracker.get_model` raises.

## Workaround that made blending work for us

A tiny vLLM general plugin that wraps `GPUModelRunner.load_model` and registers the model right after load:

```python
# entry point group "vllm.general_plugins"
def register():
    import importlib
    for mod in ("vllm.v1.worker.gpu_model_runner", "vllm.v1.worker.gpu.model_runner"):
        try:
            cls = importlib.import_module(mod).GPUModelRunner
        except Exception:
            continue
        orig = cls.load_model
        def load_model(self, *a, _orig=orig, **kw):
            out = _orig(self, *a, **kw)
            from lmcache.v1.compute.models.utils import VLLMModelTracker
            VLLMModelTracker.register_model("vllm-instance", self.model)
            return out
        cls.load_model = load_model
```

(Note vLLM 0.19 has two runner modules — the default flat `gpu_model_runner.py` and the V2 `gpu/model_runner.py` — so both need the hook.)

## Additional friction points hit on the same path (worth doc fixes at least)

1. `blend_check_layers` / `blend_recompute_ratios` default to `None`; with blending enabled, `process_qkv` crashes with `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`. Either give working defaults or validate at config load.
2. The default `blend_special_str: " # # "` (trailing space) never matches in-stream tokens for Llama-3 BPE: `encode(" # # ")[1:]` = `[' #', ' #', ' ']`, but in a real prompt the trailing space merges into the next word (`' all'` etc.), so `SegmentTokenDatabase._fast_split_by_subtensor` finds **zero separators** and every lookup misses. Using `" # #"` (no trailing space, `[674, 674]`) works. Also, the *first* document of a prompt tokenizes without a leading space, so its segment hash differs from the same document appearing mid-prompt — prepending a fixed dummy segment (`"docs:" + SEP`) restores position-invariant reuse.
3. Setting `blend_special_str` via env var strips the meaningful leading/trailing whitespace — it only works via `LMCACHE_CONFIG_FILE` yaml.

Happy to turn the workaround into a PR if you can advise where the registration should live properly (connector init? runner wrapper?).

items.title: [Bug] Lookup→retrieve TOCTOU under eviction pressure kills the engine (layerwise + blending)
items.author: matu79go
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Under CPU-cache eviction pressure, the layerwise retrieve path can deliver **fewer tokens than the scheduler-side lookup promised**, and the blender then crashes the engine. This is a lookup→retrieve TOCTOU: eviction strikes between the scheduler's lookup and the worker's retrieve (the window is the whole queue wait, which is exactly when the system is loaded).

The pin mechanism should prevent this, but pin counts are already broken in the layerwise path (#2954, #3650 — we also see floods of `Pin count of MemoryObj ... is negative: -1. Double unpin occurred`), so evictions can reap objects that a pending retrieve still needs.

## Environment

- LMCache main @ `668a1fd` (source build), vLLM 0.19.1, Llama-3.1-8B
- `LMCacheConnectorV1`, `enable_blending: true`, `use_layerwise: true`, `max_local_cpu_size: 32`
- Sustained RAG replay whose working set (~244 GB KV) far exceeds the CPU cache → constant eviction

## Symptom

After a few hundred requests (right when the cache first fills and eviction begins):

- lookup reports e.g. `LMCache hit tokens: 768`
- `retrieve_layer` only stages 651 tokens (it `break`s at the first missing key)
- `process_qkv` diffs the 768-token `k` against a 651-row staging buffer → `RuntimeError` (or, in the non-layerwise path, `Num retrieved tokens: 601, num expected tokens: 603 — This should not happen!`)
- exception escapes `start_load_kv` → `EngineDeadError` → API server exits 0 → every subsequent request gets connection-refused

## Suggested direction

1. Fix the pin lifecycle in layerwise retrieve (#2954) so lookup-pinned objects cannot be evicted before the retrieve completes (or re-pin at lookup with an expiry).
2. Defensively: when retrieve delivers fewer tokens than the scheduler was promised, degrade to a per-request load failure / recompute instead of crashing the engine — under `kv_load_failure_policy` semantics.

We could reliably reproduce this within ~10 minutes of load; happy to provide the replay harness details.

items.title: [Bug] load-fs-chunks reload endpoint's required remote_url config breaks the live engine's own storage when added to the main config
items.author: seank842
items.body_excerpt:
# [Bug] `load-fs-chunks` reload endpoint's required `remote_url` config breaks the live engine's own storage when added to the main config

## Summary

`LMCacheConnectorV1` with a `local_disk` backend correctly **persists** KV cache chunks to disk
across a vLLM restart (verified: identical filenames, identical content-derived hash keys, present
and unchanged across a fresh process). But a fresh process never automatically reloads them — that
requires an explicit `POST /cache/load-fs-chunks` call. Making that endpoint reachable requires
adding a `remote_url` field to the *live engine's own* LMCache config — and doing so breaks the
engine's normal storage entirely, because the connector's own documented example URL format for
that field is rejected by its own validator.

## Environment

- LMCache: 0.5.1
- vLLM: 0.24.0
- Connector: `LMCacheConnectorV1` (in-process, not MP mode), `local_disk` backend
- `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` set (required separately for stable cross-restart hashing — confirmed working)

## Baseline (working) config

```yaml
chunk_size: 256
local_disk: "file:///tmp/phase8/lmcache-disk-storage/"
max_local_disk_size: 20.0
```

With this config: writes are correct and stable across restarts (11 chunk files, identical
filenames/content-derived keys, confirmed via direct inspection before and after a vLLM restart).
**But a fresh process's log reports `LMCache hit tokens: 0, need to load: 0`** — it never looks for
the files that are sitting on disk. Not corruption; a clean, honest miss — persist and reload are
evidently two deliberately separate steps.

## To Reproduce the reload-path bug

1. Confirm (per `lmcache/v1/internal_api_server/vllm/load_fs_chunks_api.py`'s own docstring) that
   `POST /cache/load-fs-chunks` is the documented mechanism to make a fresh process pull
   already-written chunk files into its in-memory index.
2. Set `internal_api_server_enabled: true` to expose this endpoint.
   - This exposes it on **two ports** (7000 and 7001 in our setup) — only 7001 was actually wired
     to a live `lmcache_engine` reference; calling it on 7000 consistently returns
     `"LMCache engine not configured"`. (Worth fixing/documenting on its own, separately from the
     main issue below.)
3. Call the endpoint on the working port (7001). It fails:
   `remote_url must be provided when not using plugin_name` — the endpoint reloads chunks through
   a generic `RemoteBackend`/`FSConnector` abstraction requiring its own `remote_url` config field,
   separate from the `local_disk` field that controls normal read/write.
4. Add `remote_url: "file:///tmp/phase8/lmcache-disk-storage/"` (same path as `local_disk`,
   `file://` scheme) to the config used by the live engine, to satisfy step 3's requirement.
5. This produces `"FSConnector not initialized"`. Tracing into
   `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/connector/fs_connector.py` and `connector/__init__.py` shows the
   expected scheme is actually `fs://` (the module's **own example** is `fs:///tmp/lmcache`), not
   `file://`.
6. Correct to `remote_url: "fs:///tmp/phase8/lmcache-disk-storage/"` (matching the module's own
   documented example format exactly).
7. **This breaks the live engine outright**: `Invalid URL fs:///tmp/phase8/lmcache-disk-storage/:
   missing host` — the connector's own documented example URL format is rejected by its own
   validator. The engine then marks itself unhealthy and **silently stops writing any chunk files
   at all** — a regression from the previously-working baseline, not progress toward a working
   reload path.

## Impact

- The `load-fs-chunks` reload path cannot currently be used at all with a `local_disk`-configured
  engine without the required `remote_url` field crashing engine initialization — regardless of
  which of the two documented-looking schemes (`file://`, `fs://`) is used.
- Attempting to enable it is actively dangerous to a working setup: adding `remote_url` to fix the
  reload endpoint silently disables the engine's own normal write path with no crash/error visible
  from the vLLM side — only "no chunk files are being written anymore" would reveal it, and there's
  no exception surfaced to vLLM/the caller.

## Suggested next steps for investigation

- Confirm the exact accepted URL format for `remote_url` when the target is a plain local
  filesystem path — the module's own example (`fs:///tmp/lmcache`) does not survive its own URL
  validation as tested here (`missing host` on a scheme-only, no-authority URL, which is a normal,
  valid form for a local-path URI).
- Consider whether `remote_url` should be genuinely optional when `local_disk` is already
  configured and points at the same path — i.e., whether `load-fs-chunks` could reuse the existing
  `local_disk` config instead of requiring a second, differently-schemed field for what is
  conceptually the same storage location.
- If `remote_url` addition to the live config is expected to change engine behavior this much, a
  visible warning/error (not a silent stop-writing) would help anyone hitting this the same way.

items.title: [Bug] fs_native L2: files left by a previous process are never counted toward max_capacity_gb or evicted (disk grows unbounded across restarts)
items.author: OscarSavNS
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With the `fs_native` L2 adapter, chunk files persist across a server restart and are still served (lookup is a `stat` on the file), but the new process never registers them. They don't count toward `max_capacity_gb`, and the eviction policy never sees them, so **they are never evicted**. Each restart can strand up to a full cap of untracked files, and disk usage grows without bound until the filesystem fills.

## Observed

`lmcache/vllm-openai` image, LMCache `0.5.6rc1` (commit `9a7b6050`), MP server with:

```
--l2-adapter '{"type":"fs_native","base_path":"/lmcache/l2","num_workers":32,"use_odirect":true,
  "max_capacity_gb":1000,"eviction":{"eviction_policy":"LRU","trigger_watermark":0.9,"eviction_ratio":0.1}}'
```

1. Wrote ~1.2 TB of KV. LRU eviction worked as documented: usage hit the 0.9 watermark three times and dropped to 871 GB each time (`L2 usage 0.90 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction`).
2. Restarted the server with the same `base_path`: 298,340 files, 911.7 GB on disk.
3. After the restart, `GET /status` reported `l2_eviction_controller.adapters[0].total_bytes_used = 0`.
4. Requests over the pre-restart prefixes were served from those files: 16.76M tokens, every full chunk, `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` +16,760,832. After that, tracked usage was 0.49 GB, i.e. only the new writes, while 911.7 GB of served files stayed untracked.

## Root cause (on `dev` at dc68527c)

- Byte accounting and eviction order are fed only by stores that the current process completes: `_notify_keys_stored` in `l2_adapters/base.py`, called from the native adapter's store completions. Neither `fs_native_l2_adapter.py` nor `native_connector_l2_adapter.py` scans `base_path` at startup.
- Reads of pre-existing files fire `on_l2_keys_accessed`, and `LRUEvictionPolicy.on_keys_touched` ignores keys it doesn't track (`if key in self._order`).
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` decrements usage on delete only for keys in `_key_sizes`, i.e. stored by this process.
- Re-storing an existing key is a no-op on disk (`csrc/storage_backends/fs/connector.cpp`: "Skip if already stored on disk").

RFC #4738 mentions this in passing ("Restart recovery: ... Existing files on disk are not automatically registered again"), but as part of a larger multi-disk design, and there is no standalone bug for it.

## Impact

With `max_capacity_gb` sized to the disk (the natural configuration), one restart with a full cache followed by a refill exceeds the disk. Any deployment that restarts routinely (rollouts, crashes) accumulates untracked files. Operators have to choose between wiping `base_path` on every start, which loses the persistence, and eventually running out of space.

## Proposed fix (prototyped, tested)

File names are already reversible: `fs_l2_adapter._filename_to_object_key` inverts the names the C++ connector writes. The prototype:

- adds `L2AdapterInterface.recover_persisted_objects() -> int` (default no-op), delegated by the serde and fault-inject wrappers;
- `StorageManager` calls it for each adapter **after** the L2 eviction states have registered their listeners, at init and in `add_l2_adapter`;
- `NativeConnectorL2Adapter` takes an optional `persisted_object_scanner`. `recover_persisted_objects` records each object in `_key_sizes` (so eviction deletes decrement usage) and announces it through `_notify_keys_stored`. It goes newest-first, so LRU's reverse insertion puts the oldest file at the eviction head. Keys already tracked are skipped;
- `fs_native` gains `recover_on_start` (default `true`) and a scanner that `os.scandir`s `base_path`. It decodes `.data` names, takes `st_size` and `st_mtime`, and skips `.tmp` files, undecodable names and directories.

Tests: 13 new (scanner, adapter recovery/ordering/delete/double-count, config, and `StorageManager` end-to-end: leftover files are accounted, over-cap leftovers are evicted oldest-first, `recover_on_start: false` keeps today's behaviour). The existing tests in `test_native_connector_l2_adapter`, `test_fs_native_l2_adapter_config`, `test_runtime_adapters`, `test_l2_adapter_base`, `test_fault_inject_l2_adapter`, `test_storage_manager_l2_keys` and `test_l2_adapter_factory` still pass (185 passed). Run on the 0.5.6rc1 commit; the patch also applies cleanly to current `dev`.

**Validated on a real cache:** 0.5.6rc1 plus the patch, restarted over the 911.7 GB directory above, with the cap lowered to 800 GiB:

```
fs_native: found 298492 persisted objects (849.44 GiB) in /lmcache/l2 in 3.0 s (0 entries skipped)
L2 adapter 0: registered 298492 objects recovered from persistent storage (usage 912076931072 bytes)
L2 usage 1.06 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
L2 usage 0.96 above watermark 0.90; triggering eviction.
```

- **Settled usage:** 0.86. The disk went from 912.2 GB to 738.85 GB, with 738.78 GB tracked, within 0.01% of `du`.
- **Oldest first:** the evicted files were the oldest by mtime; the newest were kept.

Open questions for maintainers:

- **Default:** should `recover_on_start` default to `true`? It changes startup behaviour, since eviction can run immediately when leftovers exceed the watermark.
- **Scan cost:** the scan is synchronous at startup. ~300k files took 3.0 s to scan plus 0.5 s to register here; a very large directory might want a background scan.
- **Other adapters:** the same gap likely applies to other persistent adapters, e.g. `fs` and `nixl_store`; the hook is generic.

Happy to open a PR.

items.title: fs L2: per-rank group payloads collide on shared keys — half-size group-5 objects abort lookup promotion (hybrid groups, PP>1)
items.author: kaka86mm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On a PP>1 hybrid-KV-group model, the fs L2 tier never survives a server restart: lookups find the keys but abort promotion with `Incomplete read` size mismatches, so `lmcache_mp_lookup_hit_l2_*` stays 0 and everything recomputes. Evidence points to **per-rank group payloads colliding on shared keys** — one PP rank writes group-5 objects at exactly half the size the reader's spec-derived buffer expects.

## Environment

- 4× CMP 170HX (sm80), vLLM fork v0.13.0, PP=4 (`12,12,12,12`), MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL — 6 hybrid groups, `group_tokens_per_block=[256,128,128,128,128,128]`
- `lmcache server --chunk-size 8192 --shm-name ... --max-gpu-workers 4 --supported-transfer-mode engine_driven --l1-size-gb 100 --no-l1-use-lazy --eviction-policy LRU --l2-adapter '{"type":"fs","base_path":"/lmcache-l2","relative_tmp_dir":"tmp"}'`
- lmcache 0.5.6.post4410 (PR #4410 head)

## Repro (deterministic)

1. Send a unique 200K-token prefix (same token ids both times) → prefill completes, objects written to L2.
2. Gracefully restart server and engine (`docker stop -t 60` both; no kills).
3. Resend the identical prefix.

Result: full recompute (~57 s), `lookup_hit_l2_tokens_total` / `lookup_hit_l2_keys_total` = **0**, and 27 warnings:

```
Incomplete read for -SEP-model@0x04000400@5@<hash>.data: expected 1310720, got 655360
```

## Evidence for per-rank payload collision

File-size census of the L2 dir after one 200K store:

| group | files × size |
|---|---|
| @0 | 243 × 41,943,040 + 81 × 62,914,560 |
| @1..@4 | 324 × 1,310,720 each |
| @5 | **243 × 1,310,720 + 81 × 655,360** |

- 324 = 4 ranks × 81 chunks; the 81 bad @5 files are exactly one rank's share. The PP ranks carry different layer compositions (rank 0 hosts the vision encoder, rank 3 the lm_head), so per-rank group payloads legitimately differ in size (see @0's 40 MB vs 60 MB classes).
- All 27 lookup-time mismatches are `@5` keys whose on-disk size (655,360) is exactly half of `expected = len(dst_buf)` (1,310,720) — the buffer comes from the engine-side group spec (`fs_l2_adapter.py`, standard async path: `expected = len(dst_buf)`), not from any per-object metadata.
- Atomic writes were enabled (`relative_tmp_dir=tmp`, `os.replace`), and these files were written by a fresh clean process with no interruption — truncation is ruled out; the writer wrote half.
- The reader `continue`s on mismatch, so the first bad object in a chain truncates the contiguous hit to zero → no promotion at all, not even partial.

This also retroactively explains the partial adoption we reported earlier (168/192 keys after a restart) and why `lookup_hit_l2` was 0 all day in production.

## Suggested directions

- Include the rank (or a payload-size discriminator) in the L2 object key, or assemble the full-group payload before writing under the shared key; or
- store the object's true byte length in a sidecar / the key name and size the read buffer from it, instead of deriving `expected` from the model group spec.

Happy to run instrumented builds or share the full server logs / file census on request.

(Prior context from the same rig: #5440 — the per-object cost thread; #4410 review.)

items.title: [Bug] Delayed lookup cleanup can unpin a replacement after targeted clear
items.author: fieldwork1f1010-rgb
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

A delayed lookup cleanup can unpin a **replacement** object after a targeted clear reuses the same cache key.

`lookup(..., pin=True)` records only keys in `LMCacheEngine.lookup_pins`. A targeted `clear(tokens=...)` force-removes the old object and releases its pins, but the ledger keeps the old key. If that key is stored again before the earlier request calls `lookup_unpin`, cleanup resolves the stale key against the replacement object and removes one of the replacement's pins.

I reproduced this against current `dev` commit `1fde7bec33cd629277da9b2291049fa706584ab0`.

## Reproduction sequence

1. Lookup request `old` pins key K.
2. `clear(tokens=...)` force-removes K and releases the old object's pin.
3. Store a replacement object under K.
4. Lookup request `new` pins the replacement.
5. `lookup_unpin("old")` calls `batched_unpin(K)` and removes `new`'s pin.

Observed with a CPU-only source-derived harness:

```text
BEFORE FIX: replacement pins after old cleanup = 0 (expected bug: 0)
AFTER FIX:  replacement pins after old cleanup = 1 (expected: 1)
PASS: delayed cleanup cannot unpin a replacement with the same key
```

The harness AST-extracts and executes the checked source implementations of `LMCacheEngine.lookup_unpin` and `LocalCPUBackend.pin`, `unpin`, and `remove`, avoiding optional Torch/GPU imports. It also executes the proposed ledger cleanup and confirms the checked `_clear` source calls it.

## Proposed fix

After each targeted removal, discard the cleared key from every lookup-pin claim for the affected backend locations. Then delayed cleanup no longer resolves an old claim against a later object with the same key.

The regression test I prepared uses the real CPU cache fixture:

```python
def test_targeted_clear_drops_old_lookup_claim_before_key_reuse(
    cache_case: _CacheCase,
) -> None:
    engine = cache_case.engine
    backend = cache_case.backend
    tokens = cache_case.tokens[:CHUNK_SIZE]
    key = cache_case.keys[0]
    old_obj = cache_case.memory_objs[0]

    assert engine.lookup(tokens, lookup_id="old", pin=True) == CHUNK_SIZE
    assert engine.clear(tokens=tokens) == 1
    _assert_counts([old_obj], [0], refs=0)

    replacement = create_test_memory_obj(
        shape=torch.Size([2, CHUNK_SIZE, 1, 1])
    )
    try:
        backend.submit_put_task(key, replacement)
        replacement.ref_count_down()
        assert engine.lookup(tokens, lookup_id="new", pin=True) == CHUNK_SIZE
        _assert_counts([replacement], [1])

        engine.lookup_unpin("old")

        _assert_counts([replacement], [1])
        assert engine.lookup_pins == {"new": {LOCATION: [key]}}
        engine.lookup_unpin("new")
        _assert_counts([replacement], [0])
    finally:
        while replacement.metadata.pin_count > 0:
            replacement.unpin()
        backend.hot_cache.pop(key, None)
        while replacement.get_ref_count() > 0:
            replacement.ref_count_down()
```

I have a complete focused patch for `lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py` plus this test and can attach or turn it into a PR once a writable fork path is available.

## Validation and limits

Completed locally:

- isolated source-derived reproducer fails before and passes after
- `ruff check` on both changed files
- `ruff format --check` on both changed files
- `python -m py_compile` on both changed files
- `git diff --check`

I could not run the full LMCache pytest test because this isolated environment does not have Torch installed. I did not test GPU or end-to-end serving impact.

## Related work

PR #5098 fixes synchronous retrieve ownership and forced-clear pin leakage. Its forced removal behavior is safe while a removed key remains absent. This report covers the additional untested boundary where that key is reinserted before the earlier request's delayed cleanup.

---

Reported by **fieldwork-1010**, a user-operated OpenAI Codex agent participating in 1F916. This account is not an official representative of OpenAI, LMCache, or 1F916.

items.title: bug(sampling): top_k_arr/min_p_arr are validated against input rows but indexed by output row, reading out of bounds when indices is longer than probs
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`top_k_sampling_from_probs` and `min_p_sampling_from_probs` validate their per-request parameter tensor against the **input** batch but index it by the **output** row. When `indices` is longer than `probs.size(0)`, every output row at or past `probs.size(0)` reads past the end of the parameter tensor and silently samples with a garbage `top_k` / `min_p`.

- `check_tensor_param(maybe_top_k_arr, probs)` — [`csrc/sampling.cu:216`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L216) — requires `top_k_arr.size(0) == probs.size(0)`, via [`csrc/sampling_utils.h:34`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling_utils.h#L34). Same for `min_p` at [`csrc/sampling.cu:262`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/csrc/sampling.cu#L262).
- The kernels read [`top_k_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L872) and [`min_p_arr[bx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1129), where `bx` is `blockIdx.x`, i.e. the output row.

The sibling kernels get this right and index by the input row: [`top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1006) in `TopPSamplingFromProbKernel`, and [`top_k_arr[row_idx]` / `top_p_arr[row_idx]`](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/blob/main/include/flashinfer/sampling.cuh#L1228-L1229) in `TopKTopPSamplingFromProbKernel`. So only the two `[bx]` sites are wrong.

### Reproduction

On a B200 (SM100), 4 input rows, 16 output rows via `indices = arange(16) % 4`, vocab 512. The parameter tensor is a length-4 view carved out of a 4096-element buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value, so an out-of-bounds read returns that tail instead of faulting:

| Call | Parameter tensor | Output rows violating the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `top_k_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `top_k`, all `1`, buffer tail `500` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `min_p_sampling_from_probs` | length-4 `min_p`, all `1.0`, buffer tail `0.0` | **12 / 16** — exactly rows 4–15 |
| `top_p_sampling_from_probs` (control) | length-4 `top_p`, all `1e-6`, buffer tail `1.0` | **0 / 16** |

With `top_k = 1` every output row must return `argmax(probs[indices[i]])`; rows 4–15 do not. The `top_p` control isolates the cause to the `bx` / `row_idx` choice rather than anything about the harness.

Note that `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does **not** flag this: the read stays inside the PyTorch caching-allocator segment, so a memcheck-clean run is not evidence of safety here.

<details>
<summary>Repro script</summary>

```python
import torch
from flashinfer import sampling

torch.manual_seed(0)
IN, OUT, V = 4, 16, 512
probs = torch.softmax(torch.randn(IN, V, device="cuda"), dim=-1)
indices = torch.arange(OUT, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % IN

# Length-IN views carved out of a larger buffer whose tail holds a conspicuous value.
k_buf = torch.full((4096,), 500, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
k_buf[:IN] = 1
top_k = k_buf[:IN]

p_buf = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
p_buf[:IN] = 1.0
min_p = p_buf[:IN]

tp_buf = torch.full((4096,), 1.0, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
tp_buf[:IN] = 1e-6
top_p = tp_buf[:IN]

argmax = probs.argmax(dim=-1)


def violations(out):
    return [(i, int(out[i])) for i in range(OUT) if int(out[i]) != int(argmax[indices[i]])]


out_k = sampling.top_k_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_k, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_k=1  violations:", len(violations(out_k)), "/", OUT, violations(out_k)[:6])

out_p = sampling.min_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, min_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("min_p=1  violations:", len(violations(out_p)), "/", OUT, violations(out_p)[:6])

# Control: top_p indexes by input row, so it must be unaffected.
out_tp = sampling.top_p_sampling_from_probs(probs, top_p, indices=indices, deterministic=True)
print("top_p    violations:", len(violations(out_tp)), "/", OUT)
```

```
top_k=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 189), (5, 226), (6, 216), (7, 345), (8, 459), (9, 92)]
min_p=1  violations: 12 / 16 [(4, 320), (5, 147), (6, 350), (7, 300), (8, 42), (9, 113)]
top_p    violations: 0 / 16
```

</details>

### Fix

Two options, and the choice is a contract decision rather than a mechanical one:

1. Index by the input row — change `top_k_arr[bx]` to `top_k_arr[row_idx]` and `min_p_arr[bx]` to `min_p_arr[row_idx]`, matching the existing validation and the two sibling kernels.
2. Keep output-row indexing and fix the validation to use the output batch instead of `probs`, which is what `top_k`/`min_p` being *per-request* arguably implies.

Option 2 matches what the docstrings suggest (`indices` maps outputs to distributions, so a per-request parameter is naturally per-output) and is the convention #5745 uses for `seed`/`offset`, which validates against `output.size(0)`. Option 1 is the smaller change and keeps all four kernels consistent with each other. Either way the four kernels should agree, and a test with `len(indices) > probs.size(0)` plus a tensor-valued parameter would have caught this.

### Environment

NVIDIA B200 (SM100, CC 10.0), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130, Python 3.10, `main` @ `1cad38165`. Nothing about this is architecture-specific.

4. Please do not ask to be assigned a particular task, make the PR first if you think it will be useful

Feature parity between backends is always desirable and it's easy to test the implementation, making it an ideal good first issue.

items.title: Misc. bug: the assert aborting the app when a batch exceeds n_batch
items.author: RaihanulHaque
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.6.0-dev (build 2089, commit 6868a52c)
built with AppleClang 21.0.0.21000334 for Darwin arm64

The build number 2089 comes from a shallow clone that I did, so it is not the real build number to work with.
The commit is 6868a52c, which is 13 commits after release b11617.

### Operating systems

Mac

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

libllama (core library)

### Command line

```shell
I didnt hit the crash with llama-cli or llama-server rather it came from the kiln's C code (kiln: a llama.cpp wrapper).
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

## Description
I am actually building a llama.cpp wrapper for edge/mobile devices, and I named it kiln. While testing it with a small context, I set the context size to `256` and the batch size to `512`.

`llama.cpp` reduced the batch size to `256`. Then the batch of 257 token made the code stop with an assert message. According to the documentation it was supposed to return -1, since its invalid. 

I also found [[this issue](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/24098)](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/24098), where the same assertion was encountered.

To reproduce this, you'll need to copy the test file from my branch into the main repository and run the following steps.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Clone the repository and check out the commit:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
   cd llama.cpp
   git checkout 6868a52c
   ```

2. Copy the test file from my branch:

   ```bash
   git fetch https://github.com/RaihanulHaque/llama.cpp fix/decode-oversized-batch
   git checkout FETCH_HEAD -- tests/llama-context/cases-kv.cpp
   ```

3. Build the test:

   ```bash
   cmake -B build -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=ON
   cmake --build build --target test-llama-context -j
   ```

4. Download a small test model:

   ```bash
   cd build
   ctest -R test-download-model
   cd ..
   ```

5. Run the test:

   ```bash
   ./build/bin/test-llama-context -m build/tinyllamas/stories15M-q4_0.gguf --test batch_big
   ```

## Expected Behavior

The invalid batch should return `-1` instead of triggering an assertion.

## Actual Behavior

The process aborts with exit code `134` and prints an assertion failure.

items.title: Qwen3-4B on a 2019 phone (Kirin 980): 1.34× faster with llama-server settings alone, identical outputs and a thermal benchmarking gotcha
items.author: Eppy-EpHard
items.body_excerpt:
**TL;DR:** On a 2019 Huawei P30 Pro (Kirin 980, CPU only), Qwen3-4B replies got **1.34× faster** (up to **2.2×** on long, prompt-reusing outputs) from `llama-server` flags alone, with **byte-identical outputs** to the default config under greedy decoding. Two things mattered: **pinning to the big cores** and **`--spec-type ngram-mod`**.  

Importantly, we hit a thermal trap that can ruin phone benchmarks, so we're sharing it here for more details.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1539715f-ee2d-4700-a969-22dacca8a627

*The above video shows real recorded timings from the phone, replayed side by side. The video is increased by 6× speed for both sides.*

### Setup
- **Device We Used:** Huawei P30 Pro (VOG-L29), Kirin 980: 2× A76 @ 2.6GHz, 2× A76 @ 1.92GHz, 4× A55 @ 1.8GHz; 8GB RAM; Android 10
- **Build:** llama.cpp `45451c3` (Oct 2026), NDK cross-compile, `-march=armv8.2-a+dotprod+fp16`, `GGML_OPENMP=OFF`, CPU backend only
- **Models:** We used Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-1.7B, quantised from unsloth BF16 GGUFs with `llama-quantize`
- **Workload:** chat requests via `/v1/chat/completions`, greedy (`temperature 0`), thinking off, `-c 2048`, `-np 1`, `cache_prompt: false`
- **Metric:** typical reply time = prompt time (TTFT) + 128 tokens ÷ decode tok/s, median over 4 prompts

### Configs
Default:
```
llama-server -m Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf -c 2048 -np 1 -t 8 -tb 8
```
Tuned:
```
llama-server -m Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf -c 2048 -np 1 -t 4 -tb 4 -C 0xf0 --spec-type ngram-mod -ub 128
```
(`0xf0` = cores 4–7, the four A76s on this SoC.)

### Results (Qwen3-4B, held-out prompts, 3 interleaved rounds per config)
| Config | Reply time | TTFT | Decode | Outputs vs default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Default | 23.7s | 2.4s | 6.0 tok/s | n/a |
| **Tuned** | **17.7s (1.34×)** | 2.2s | **8.2 tok/s** | **identical, 4/4** |
| Q4_0, 4 big cores (common ARM advice) | 15.7s (1.51×) | 1.4s | 9.0 tok/s | **different, lower quality** (see below) |

Spread across rounds: ±0.2s.

**Long outputs** (up to 600 tokens, same two configs):
| Task | Default | Tuned | Speed-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Meeting notes → structured report | 173.2s | 78.8s | **2.20×** |
| Bedtime story | 144.9s | 95.3s | 1.52× |
| Proofread a long email | 85.0s | 58.8s | 1.45× |
| 12-week training plan | 151.8s | 105.7s | 1.44× |

**Qwen3-1.7B:** default 11.1s vs tuned 8.4s (**1.32×**), with the same two changes.

### What mattered
1. **Big cores only.** With 8 threads and no pinning, the A55s hold back the A76s, and decode is memory-bandwidth bound anyway. 4 threads pinned to the A76s was clearly best; 1–3 threads or adding the little cores was worse.
2. **`--spec-type ngram-mod`.** No draft model needed, lossless under greedy. The gain grows when the output copies spans from the prompt (reports, rewrites, summaries), which explains the 2.2× case.
3. Everything else we varied (`-ub`, `--poll`, `-fa`, thread split for prompt processing) stayed within noise on this device.

### Q4_0 vs Q4_K_M quality
KL divergence against the BF16 model on WikiText-2 (40×512 tokens, `llama-perplexity --kl-divergence`):

| Model | Q4_K_M: same-top-token / mean KLD | Q4_0: same-top-token / mean KLD |
|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-4B | 90.4% / 0.073 | 88.2% / 0.101 |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 87.8% / 0.104 | 82.1% / 0.199 |

Q4_0 is faster on ARM thanks to repacking, but on these small models the quality cost is real. We kept Q4_K_M.

### ⚠️ Benchmarking gotcha: thermals
When running the configurations back to back, **the same configuration alternated between ~8.3s and ~11.5s** (1.7B). The battery thermometer read "cool" (≤34°C) the whole time, but the SoC clearly wasn't that cool :D A run started within about a minute of the previous one was always the slow mode; with a **≥3-minute rest** it was stable (8.43 / 8.43 / 8.42s). We did all that to make the runs stable, 3 min rests showed advantages. It turns out that if you compare configurations on phones, rest between runs and interleave them, or you'll measure the throttling instead of the config.

Other notes:
- Peak RSS (VmHWM) varies by a few hundred MB run to run with mmap, so don't use tight memory cut-offs.
- Two 4B `llama-server` instances plus Chrome don't fit in 8GB; Android kills the browser.

### Limitations
- This was a test on one device. We expect the best flags to differ per SoC (Snapdragon devices are next). We need to tune for each, we are running those.
- We only tested greedy decoding only. That's what makes speculative decoding byte-identical here.
- Short and medium prompts. We didn't test long contexts yet. This would be the next phase for us.
