items.title: [Bug]: Intermittent XGrammar request termination with V2 DFlash probabilistic drafting and block rejection
items.author: tomasruizt
items.body_excerpt:
[Machine-written]

### Environment

Upstream main at `a7b7bc1fbe1f5c4e47c53b0f02a3ecfbcd8054b9`, Model Runner V2, one H100 80GB per server, TP=1, PP=1. Python 3.12.12, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, xgrammar 0.2.8, transformers 5.19.0, flashinfer-python 0.7.0.post1, NVIDIA driver 580.126.09. Source checkout with precompiled extensions.

### Observed failure

A valid structured JSON request was terminated during generation with Qwen3-4B, DFlash probabilistic drafting, block rejection sampling and async scheduling. The schema has category/priority enums and free-text advice. Sampling was temperature=1, top-k=50, top-p=0.9, max_tokens=512, with an explicit per-request seed and thinking disabled.

Three 61-request runs at concurrency 1 and two 540-request runs at concurrency 16 completed. During the third concurrency-16 run, the server logged:

```text
[backend_xgrammar.py:201] Failed to advance FSM for request chatcmpl-b2055da1fad0f46b-a7547c73 for tokens 0. Please file an issue.
[scheduler.py:2199] Unexpected: grammar rejected tokens [756, 414, 0] for request chatcmpl-b2055da1fad0f46b-a7547c73. Terminating request.
[serving.py:203] Request chatcmpl-b2055da1fad0f46b failed with an internal error during generation
```

The streaming client received `{"message":"Internal server error","type":"InternalServerError","param":null,"code":500}`. This was an error in the SSE stream, not an observed initial HTTP 500 response. Tokens `[756, 414, 0]` decode to `",\n`, five spaces, and `!`.

**This report does not claim an engine crash.** The benchmark runner raised on the failed request and then explicitly sent SIGTERM to its server. We did not check server health between that original failure and the runner's shutdown.

### Reproduction status

The original run on October 12, 2026 **did fail**. Its measured batches were:

| Original run | Requests planned | Observed failures | Outcome |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Concurrency 1, repeats 1–3 | 183 (3 × 61) | 0 | All three completed |
| Concurrency 16, repeats 1–2 | 1,080 (2 × 540) | 0 | Both completed |
| Concurrency 16, repeat 3 | 540 | 1 | Aborted at the first observed failure |

Warmup and pilot requests are excluded from this table. The failed batch did not complete, and its completed-request count was not retained. **We cannot infer a failure rate of 1/540.** The confirmed observation is one failed request during that third concurrency-16 batch, logged at `16:52:32` in the server log.

I have not obtained a reliable minimal reproducer. The table below covers only the **subsequent clean reduction attempts**, not the original failing run. Those attempts completed 26,742 requests without reproducing the error:

| Attempt | Requests | Failed |
|---|---:|---:|
| Original schema, concurrency 16, initial rerun | 1,620 | 0 |
| Original schema, new seeds, concurrency 16 and 64 | 10,800 | 0 |
| Two-choice and single-field schemas, concurrency 1, 16 and 64 | 6,144 | 0 |
| Original schema, warmup/pilot stages and workload order, including concurrency 64 | 8,178 | 0 |

The reduction runner kept the server alive after requests and checked `/health` after every batch. All those health checks returned 200. These passing attempts do not establish recovery after the original failure, nor prove the bug is fixed.

The commands and self-contained client below reproduce the workload conditions, **not a guaranteed failure**. Prefix caching is disabled and the same server is reused across repeats. The exact failing request's index/seed was not retained by the original fail-fast runner.

```bash
export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B \
  --served-model-name benchmark --host 127.0.0.1 --port 19213 \
  --max-model-len 2048 --max-num-seqs 64 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --disable-uvicorn-access-log --async-scheduling \
  --structured-outputs-config '{"backend":"xgrammar"}' \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16","num_speculative_tokens":15,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block"}'
```

### Request-side workload

Save the client below as `repro.py`, then run it in a second terminal while the server above is running:

```bash
python -m pip install aiohttp
BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:19213 python -u repro.py
```

It sends three 61-request batches at concurrency 1, then three 540-request batches at concurrency 16, with warmup requests before each stage. The client includes the full prompt, JSON schema and per-request sampling seeds. It reports request failures and server health without shutting down the server.

<details>

items.title: [Bug]: NixlConnector P/D: first handshake per remote engine stalls all DP decode ranks (THP compaction in `_build_fa_remote`); late reads after lease expiry return HTTP 200
items.author: simon-veitner-redhat
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.31.0 (`vllm/vllm-openai:v0.31.0`), numpy 2.2.6, NIXL over UCX
- 2 nodes, 8x H200 each, Linux 6.x, THP `enabled=madvise`, `defrag=madvise`
- Most of host RAM (more than 60%) is pinned in `/dev/shm` by the OffloadingConnector CPU tier and Engram

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On the first P/D traffic after startup, a decode rank's first NIXL handshake with a prefill engine can stall the whole decode instance for seconds to minutes (up to about 45 min in our runs). With the default 30 s `kv_lease_duration`, the prefill frees the KV unread. The decode later reads the freed blocks and returns HTTP 200.

The cause is the descriptor build on the handshake path combined with numpy's huge page advice:

1. For each new remote engine, `NixlBaseConnectorWorker.add_remote_agent` (`nixl/base_worker.py:2438` at v0.31.0) calls `_build_fa_remote` (`:2065-2112`). It builds one descriptor per block per KV region of the whole remote pool with numpy (`np.arange`, `np.empty((n, 3))`, `np.concatenate`). With a large KV pool this is several million descriptors and about 100 MB of fresh arrays per handshake.
2. numpy calls `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` on large allocations. With THP `enabled=madvise` and `defrag=madvise`, the first touch of each 2 MB range runs synchronous direct compaction.
3. When most host RAM is pinned, compaction almost always fails (`compact_fail` rises with `compact_stall`), and each fault costs milliseconds to seconds.
4. The faulting thread holds the mmap lock, so the worker's other threads block too.
5. With DP + EP, all decode ranks meet in the all-reduce of `sync_cudagraph_and_dp_padding` (`v1/worker/gpu/dp_utils.py:77`) every step. One stalled worker stops all ranks, so other requests cannot start their handshakes and no rank sends lease heartbeats.

The duration depends on memory fragmentation at that moment, so the same setup is sometimes fine.

#### Evidence

Fresh servers, no warm-up, 30 s lease, 10 concurrent cold requests:

| numpy huge pages | Handshake thread system CPU per worker | Client warmup | Expired leases / invalid reads |
|---|---|---|---|
| default (on) | 0.5 to 69.6 s | 89 s | 8 / 8, all HTTP 200 |
| `NUMPY_MADVISE_HUGEPAGE=0` | 0.26 to 0.80 s | 25 s | 0 / 0 |

A py-spy profile of one decode worker put 263 of 286 samples in `add_remote_agent` inside `_build_fa_remote`, mostly memcpy under `np.concatenate`. The NIXL calls themselves took about 0.2 s per handshake.

Prefill log:

```
(Worker_DP5_EP5) WARNING 10-14 18:59:20 [base_worker.py:3074] Releasing expired KV blocks for request <id> which were retrieved by 0 remote worker(s) before lease expired.
(Worker_DP5_EP5) ERROR 10-14 19:00:00 [pull_worker.py:663] Potentially invalid KV blocks for unrecognized request <id> were retrieved by a decode worker. They may have expired.
```

#### Expected behavior

- A handshake should not stall the engine. The remote descriptors should not cost O(remote pool) fresh memory per remote engine. Prefill engines share one block layout and differ only in base addresses, so the descriptors could be built once, or only for the blocks a request reads.
- At minimum, the connector should not request huge pages for these arrays.
- Lease heartbeats should start before the handshake finishes, and a read after lease expiry should fail the request instead of returning HTTP 200 (#61229, PR #61549).

#### How to reproduce

This script repeats the numpy work of `_build_fa_remote` for 4.3M descriptors and prints the time and the compaction counters:

```python
import sys, time, numpy as np
def vm():
    return {k: int(v) for k, v in (l.split() for l in open("/proc/vmstat"))
            if k in ("compact_stall", "compact_fail", "thp_fault_alloc")}
n, regions = 4_300_000, 100
v0, t0 = vm(), time.perf_counter()
parts = []
for i in range(regions):
    addrs = np.uint64(0x7F0000000000 + i * 2**33) + np.arange(n // regions, dtype=np.uint64) * np.uint64(19008)
    out = np.empty((addrs.shape[0], 3), dtype=np.uint64)
    out[:, 0] = addrs; out[:, 1] = 19008; out[:, 2] = 0
    parts.append(out)
arr = np.concatenate(parts)
v1 = vm()
print(round(time.perf_counter() - t0, 3), "s", {k: v1[k] - v0[k] for k in v0})
```

On a decode node next to a running vLLM instance: 0.96 s with 94 failed compaction stalls by default, 0.11 s with no stalls under `NUMPY_MADVISE_HUGEPAGE=0`.

To see it in vLLM, run a P/D pair (DP8 + EP8 per node) on hosts with most memory pinned, using NixlConnector in pull mode plus the OffloadingConnector CPU tier:

```bash
--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MultiConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"connectors":[
  {"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_role":"kv_both"},
  {"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec","cpu_bytes_to_use":<bytes>}}]}}'
```

Send concurrent first requests to cold rank pairs through any P/D proxy. Watch the system CPU of each decode worker's `vllm-nixl-handshake-initiator` thread and `compact_stall` in `/proc/vmstat`, then repeat with `NUMPY_MADVISE_HUGEPAGE=0`.

#### Workarounds

- `NUMPY_MADVISE_HUGEPAGE=0` in the server environment.
- A longer `kv_lease_duration` on the prefill.
- One warm-up request per prefill and decode rank pair, sequentially, before real traffic.

#### Related

- #61229 and PR #61549: lease expiry during a pending READ makes the decode consume overwritten KV silently. Same consequence; our trigger is a slow first handshake.
- #60019: synchronous O(num_blocks) NIXL peer registration in the P2P offload tier stalls the rank.
- #53095: push connector leases expire under concurrency with the same `retrieved by 0 remote worker(s)` message.

This report was drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code) from our logs and reviewed by the submitter.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page

Follow-up for #5118 after #5125.

#5125 enabled Ruff `G004` repo-wide and added temporary `per-file-ignores` for the files/directories that still build logging messages with f-strings. This issue is one small slice of that cleanup queue.

Claiming: please comment `/claim` and wait for assignment so we avoid duplicate PRs.

## Scope

Convert only the logging f-strings in:

- `lmcache/v1/storage_backend/nixl_storage_backend.py` (10 G004 findings)

Counts above were measured on `dev` at `dd5dfca` with `ruff check --isolated --select G004`.

## Expected change

items.title: What is the first practical limit of persistent KV across Agent steps?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. Recent sampling and decode-interface work led me to a question about long-running local Agent workloads.

Persistent KV could reduce repeated prefill, but only if cache identity, layout, eviction and framework boundaries stay correct as models, adapters and stages change. Which condition is most likely to invalidate the idea in practice: layout incompatibility, model or tokenizer changes, fragmentation, eviction quality loss, scheduler interference, or missing cross-framework contracts?

One counterexample or minimum test would be especially useful. @yzh119

— Rui, Psync.labs

comments.author: eprogressing
comments.body:
For an agent that changes adapters or rewrites its prompt between steps, I would check **cache identity/correctness before fragmentation or scheduling**. That is a conditional priority, not a measured ranking of workloads.

A concrete counterexample is switching from adapter A to adapter B while retaining A's KV. If B changes the value projection (or earlier hidden states), identical token IDs and identical tensor shapes do not make those cached values valid for B. Similarly, editing earlier tool results breaks reuse past the unchanged token prefix in an ordinary causal transformer. Rendering the same conversation differently can also change that prefix.

I would start with this small integration test:

1. Under A, prefill a short token prefix P, then process suffix S using the cached prefix. Compare the next-token logits with a fresh A forward pass on P+S, within an appropriate numerical tolerance.
2. Use a distinct, nonzero B adapter that affects `v_proj`. Repeat with a fresh B prefill as the reference. Your cache manager should reject A's cache; forcibly reusing it is the negative control, which can expose a discrepancy.
3. Edit one early token in P and verify that cache lookup stops at the unchanged prefix. Check logits, rather than just generated text: argmax can hide a difference.

This is consistent with [vLLM's prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/), which keys blocks using the parent hash, block tokens and extra hashes such as LoRA IDs. Adapter IDs also need versioning/invalidation if their weights can change in place.

After that, check the storage contract separately: [FlashInfer's KV layout documentation](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) specifies NHD/HND layouts and page metadata. Matching semantics alone does not make a buffer portable between frameworks.

Prepared with Codex assistance from the linked documentation. The integration test above was initially a proposal; the execution update below now supplies an actual mechanism test. Is your agent retaining one model/adapter with append-only history, or switching adapters and rewriting history?


---
**GPU experiment update (2026-10-11):** I ran the actual Transformers/PEFT forward path on an A100-SXM4-40GB, plus CPU controls: Torch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, PEFT 0.21.2. This is a random three-layer Llama (hidden 64, four attention heads/two KV heads), with rank-four v_proj LoRA; it does not exercise FlashInfer's attention kernel or a production agent cache manager.

Across seeds 0/1/2, CPU/CUDA and float32/float64, all 72 comparison expectations held. Correct same-adapter reuse, an adapter-name change with exactly zero update, and reuse limited to the two tokens preceding a prefix edit agreed with fresh forwarding (maximum absolute logit error <=1.49e-7; predeclared tolerances float32 1e-5 / float64 1e-10). Forcibly reusing A's KV with nonzero B produced max-absolute differences 0.2205–0.2727; retaining the old full prefix after the edit produced 0.1082–0.2622. Each stale-cache case changed argmax in only 4/12 trials, so comparing all logits matters. Each path used a newly created cache with asserted sequence lengths.

This supports the specific correctness counterexample, not a universal ranking against fragmentation/scheduling. It does not measure answer quality, throughput, cross-framework layout compatibility, or automatic rejection by a cache manager. [Reproduction scripts, full inputs/logits, versions and results](https://gist.github.com/eprogressing/84db3e068aabbe449f8629a3f362a6e5). Prepared with Codex assistance; these runs were actually executed.

comments.author: no4ni
comments.body:
**Документация: Работа с `llama.cpp` b6286 (август 2025)**

**1. Изменения в архитектуре и API**

*   **Изменение публичного API:** Прямой доступ к внутренним библиотекам `ggml` и `gguf` через их заголовочные файлы (`ggml/ggml.h`, `ggml/gguf.h`) **больше не является публичным или рекомендуемым**. Функции вроде `gguf_init_from_file`, `gguf_get_n_tensors` и т.д. скрыты.
*   **Унификация API:** Всё взаимодействие с моделью, её метаданными и тензорами теперь должно происходить **только** через унифицированный API, предоставляемый в **`include/llama.h`** (и `include/llama-cpp.h` для C++).
*   **Изменение структуры `include`:** Публичные заголовки теперь находятся непосредственно в `include/`. Внутренние заголовки `ggml` перемещены в `ggml/include/`.

**2. Создание собственного примера/приложения (например, `qedit`)**

*   **Расположение:** Поместите исходный код примера (например, `qedit.cpp`) и его `CMakeLists.txt` в подкаталог `examples/<имя_примера>/` внутри корня проекта `llama.cpp`. Например: `llama.cpp/examples/qedit/`.
*   **`CMakeLists.txt` примера:**
    ```cmake
    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
    project(<имя_примера> CXX) # Замените <имя_примера> на имя вашего проекта

    set(TARGET <имя_примера>)
    add_executable(${TARGET} <имя_файла>.cpp) # Замените <имя_файла>.cpp на имя вашего .cpp файла

    target_compile_features(${TARGET} PRIVATE cxx_std_17)

    # Указываем include-путь к llama.h
    target_include_directories(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include    # папка с llama.h
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/common   # Если используете заголовки из common
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/ggml/include # Только если требуется прямой доступ к внутренним ggml (не рекомендуется)
    )

    # Линкуем необходимые библиотеки
    target_link_libraries(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        # common     # Если используете утилиты из common
        llama        # ОСНОВНАЯ библиотека, предоставляющая API из llama.h
        # ggml       # Обычно не нужно явно указывать, так как llama зависит от ggml.
                     # Но можно оставить для ясности.
        # ggml-cuda  # НЕ НУЖНО. Отдельная цель ggml-cuda НЕ СОЗДАЕТСЯ.
                     # Функциональность CUDA интегрирована в основную библиотеку ggml.
        ${CMAKE_THREAD_LIBS_INIT} # Если требуется
    )
    ```
*   **Использование API:** В коде вашего примера используйте только функции, объявленные в `include/llama.h`. Примеры функций:
    *   `llama_backend_init()`, `llama_backend_free()`: Инициализация/деинициализация бэкенда.
    *   `llama_model_default_params()`: Получение параметров модели по умолчанию.
    *   `llama_load_model_from_file()`: Загрузка модели.
    *   `llama_model_meta_count()`, `llama_model_meta_key_by_index()`, `llama_model_meta_val_str_by_index()`: Доступ к метаданным модели.
    *   `llama_model_n_embd()`, `llama_model_n_ctx_train()`, `llama_model_n_params()`: Получение информации о модели (некоторые могут требовать активного контекста).
    *   `llama_free_model()`: Освобождение модели.

**3. Сборка проекта `llama.cpp`**

*   **Конфигурация CMake:**
    *   Используйте CMake для генерации проекта сборки.
    *   Для включения поддержки CUDA используйте опцию `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` (устаревшая `LLAMA_CUBLAS=ON` больше не поддерживается).
    *   Пример команды для Visual Studio 2022:
        ```bash
        cmake .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_COMMON=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
        ```
*   **Сборка библиотек:**
    *   При включении `GGML_CUDA=ON` и `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` (по умолчанию для MSVC):
        *   Исходники CUDA (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/*`) добавляются в сборку основной библиотеки `ggml`.
        *   Создаются файлы `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.dll` (содержит и CPU, и CUDA код) и `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.lib` (библиотека импорта для этой DLL).
    *   Основная библиотека `llama.lib` зависит от `ggml.lib`. Линковка с `llama.lib` предоставляет доступ ко всей функциональности, включая CU

items.title: Feature Request: Hexagon FP8 weight support and DiT optimizations for HTP v79+
items.author: happyyzy
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

[Hexagon] FP8 weight support and DiT-oriented optimizations for HTP v79+


  ### Motivation

  We have implemented and validated an FP8 inference path for diffusion transformers on Qualcomm Hexagon HTP v79+ devices, including Snapdragon 8 Elite / SM8750.

  The goal of this issue is to discuss how to upstream the generic pieces into llama.cpp incrementally, particularly the FP8 type plumbing, Hexagon weight repacking, and HMX FP8 GEMM support.

  ### Implementation

  The current v79+ path includes:

  - Loading standard `F8_E4M3` weights from safetensors.
  - One-time `set_tensor` repacking into the HMX 32x32 tiled weight layout.
  - FP8 W8A16 GEMM using HMX.
  - Fused Q/K RMSNorm and RoPE.
  - A generic segmented-K matrix multiplication used by FLUX.2/Klein `linear2` in single stream blocks.
  - FP16 VAE activations.
  - Implicit-GEMM convolution.
  - Fused GroupNorm, affine transform, and SiLU.
  - Fused upscale and convolution.

  This enables complete on-device text encoding, DiT sampling, and VAE decoding at resolutions from 1024x1024 through 2048x2048.

  ### FP8 HMX execution

  The FP8 GEMM uses the v79 HMX:

  - `activation.hf`
  - `weight.f8`

  instruction path with FP32 accumulation.

  The HMX operation:

  ```text
  cvt.hf = acc(2)
```

  applies the architectural 1/256 conversion when storing the accumulator as FP16.

  The HVX output epilogue compensates by multiplying by 256. The same FP32 epilogue also folds in:

  - The FP32 scale associated with the model's FP8 weight tensor.
  - Any scalar multiplication represented by the surrounding GGML graph.

  This avoids an additional tensor pass and adds negligible overhead to the GEMM store stage.


  ### Results and integration

  The stable-diffusion.cpp integration, benchmark comparison, commands, and image-quality examples are available here:

  https://github.com/leejet/stable-diffusion.cpp/pull/1970

items.title: rpc : single-threaded accept loop starves every connection after the first
items.author: shikanime
items.body_excerpt:
**Environment**
- 2x AMD Strix Halo, 10 GbE link. llama.cpp master `8ea29024` (2026-09-11), identical build on the llama-server (router) leader and the ggml-rpc-server worker. Reproduced identically on `18443257a3` (2026-09).
- Leader runs llama-server in router mode: each model child opens its own long-lived RPC connection to the worker (`--rpc <worker>:50052`).

**Repro**
Load a second model while a first model's RPC connection stays open (router mode: any two models; a single model + anything else works too). The second model's child hangs in warmup forever. A dense 27B loads and serves fine — it is merely the *first* connection. Local protocol repro: connect A, HELLO, hold A open; connect B, HELLO -> B never gets a reply (timeout). With the fix below, B replies instantly.

**Observed (production + local)**
- Leader child (second model): main thread blocked in `recv(fd, buf, 8, 0)` (`/proc/<pid>/syscall` = `45 0x3 ... 0x8 ...`), i.e. waiting for an 8-byte reply header, indefinitely. It never gets past the HELLO handshake.
- Worker: the second connection is ESTABLISHED in the kernel backlog — `/proc/<pid>/net/tcp` shows the listen socket and a pending connection row with **inode 0** and unread rx bytes; the worker's single thread is inside `rpc_serve_client` for the *first* connection, blocked in `recv(&cmd, 1)`.

**Analysis**
`ggml_backend_rpc_start_server` serves clients in a single accept loop:

```
while (true) {
    auto client_socket = server_socket->accept();
    ...
    rpc_serve_client(backends, cache_dir, client_socket);   // blocking
    printf("Client connection closed\n");
}
```

`rpc_serve_client` runs until that connection closes. In router mode the first model's connection is long-lived (held for the model's lifetime), so the loop never returns to `accept()` and every later connection starves in the kernel backlog — the client's HELLO is never answered and its lockstep `recv(8)` blocks forever. Not MoE-specific: any second long-lived connection wedges; it only *looks* MoE-shaped because dense models usually load first.

**Fix (PR attached)**
Serve each connection on its own detached thread. `rpc_server` is already constructed per connection inside `rpc_serve_client` (`rpc_server server(backends, cache_dir);`), so per-connection state is isolated; the shared `backends` handles are the same objects the single-threaded loop already used. Verified locally: A held open, B's HELLO answered in 0.00s; handler-failure path still closes the socket (RST) as before.

**Notes**
- Not related to `--cache`, tensor bounds, or the client-side assert from #28739 — a prior hypothesis that a failing handler `return` wedges the client was disproven by repro (the server closes the socket there).

items.title: Misc. bug: Incorrect free VRAM causes spill into shared memory on AMD GPU on Windows
items.author: sadam266
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama-server.exe --version
version: 0.6.0-dev (build 11429, commit d81235049)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Other? (Please let us know in description), Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

Other (Please specify in the next section)

### Command line

```shell
llama-server.exe --list-devices
llama-server.exe --model Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-noMTP-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18116 --threads 1 --cpu-mask 0xFFF000 --poll 0 --cache-ram 0 --n-gpu-layers 999 --override-tensor token_embd.weight=ROCm0 --flash-attn on --load-mode dio --fit-target 1536 --parallel 1 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Description
On Windows the HIP backend reports free VRAM without subtracting other processes usage.

For instance: on my RX 7900 XTX:
`--list-devices` says 24410 MiB free, while Task Manager shows ~2 GB already used and WSL with ROCDXG on the same machine reports 22599 MiB.
`--fit-target` then over-allocates, WDDM spills into shared memory and prompt processing drops significantly, in my particular test, it dropped from 1137 to 121 t/s.

### Steps to reproduce:
1. Windows, AMD GPU, load on VRAM e.g. desktop
2. `llama-server --list-devices`
 -> shows free VRAM close to total VRAM.
4. Load a model that nearly fills VRAM with `--fit-target 1536` or smaller, send a large prompt ~5K+ tokens
-> shared GPU memory grows, RAM utilisation by `llama-server` process grows, prompt processing speed drops

### Solution idea
librocdxg (WSL) computes free as local heap minus BytesResident from D3DKMTQueryStatistics. Doing the same in ggml_backend_cuda_device_get_memory prevents the spill.

``` cpp
for (ULONG i = 0; i < nb_segments; i++) {
    segment.QuerySegment.SegmentId = i;
    D3DKMTQueryStatistics(&segment);
    if (seg_info.SegmentProperties.SegmentType == D3DKMT_QUERYSTATISTICS_SEGMENT_TYPE_MEMORY) {
        resident += seg_info.BytesResident;
    }
}
*free = std::min(*free, *total - resident);
```

I've implemented that solution locally and the free VRAM perfectly matches that of Task Manager Performance metrics

items.title: Eval bug: Vulkan: MiniMax-M2 prompt processing collapses at long context with ubatch above 128 on Strix Halo (gfx1151); long submits trigger amdgpu "device lost"
items.author: jakehardee-wq
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama.cpp build 23b0202a1 (11552), Vulkan backend

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

Minisforum MS-S1 MAX P495: Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, Radeon 8065S (RADV STRIX_HALO, gfx1151), 192GB LPDDR5X-8533. BIOS UMA set to 512MB, GTT raised to 170GB with ttm.pages_limit.

### Models

unsloth MiniMax-M2.7 UD-IQ4_XS (100.96 GiB, 228.69B params)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With the Vulkan backend, MiniMax-M2 prompt processing at 32k depth gets dramatically slower as ubatch grows past 128. At the default ubatch of 512 it is about 6x slower than at 128, and individual GPU submissions run long enough to trip the amdgpu job timeout.

llama-bench, pp512, Vulkan (t/s):

| ubatch | depth 0 | depth 32768 |
|--:|--:|--:|
| 32 | 54.6 | 42.6 |
| 64 | 78.9 | 55.7 |
| 128 | 124.0 | 77.5 |
| 256 | not tested | 51.5 |
| 512 (default) | 309.3 | 13.3 |

At depth 0, larger ubatch is faster as expected. At depth 32768 the trend inverts sharply above 128.

Context that suggests this is specific to the Vulkan path for this model:

- Same model and machine on a ROCm build (c83f3058), ubatch 128: pp512 is 246.4 at depth 0 and 151.0 at depth 32768. No collapse.
- DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (UD-IQ3_S) on the same Vulkan build does not show it. pp512 at depth 32768 is 107.7 at ubatch 512, and pp2048 at depth 32768 is 137.6 at ubatch 2048. Larger is faster at every depth.
- gpt-oss 120B MXFP4 on the same Vulkan build: pp512 at depth 32768 is 384.8 at the default ubatch.

### Crash (device lost)

With the default amdgpu lockup timeout, the depth 32768 MiniMax run at ubatch 512 crashes:

    radv/amdgpu: The CS has been cancelled because the context is lost. This context is innocent.
    ggml_vulkan: device lost on Vulkan0
    terminate called after throwing an instance of 'vk::DeviceLostError'
      what():  vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost

The same crash also happened in llama-server with a dense model (Qwen3.8 27B Q8_0) once the context reached n_tokens = 82576.

Adding the kernel parameter amdgpu.lockup_timeout=60000 prevents the crash, and the same run then completes at 13.3 t/s. So the crash looks like a consequence of a single submission taking longer than the default timeout, which matches the slow large-ubatch path above. Lowering ubatch to 128 also avoids it and is much faster.

### Steps to reproduce

    llama-bench -m MiniMax-M2.7-UD-IQ4_XS-00001-of-00004.gguf -p 512 -n 0 -d 0,32768 -ub 32,64,128,512 -r 1 -o md

Run once with the default amdgpu.lockup_timeout to see the crash, and once with amdgpu.lockup_timeout=60000 to get the full table.

### Workaround

ubatch 128 for this model, plus amdgpu.lockup_timeout=60000 as a safety net.

items.title: Eval bug: CUDA illegal memory access (MUL_MAT) on RTX 5090 with cohere2moe
items.author: tugrultamturk
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

Although I encountered this while using Ollama, the crash happens directly inside the bundled `llama-server.exe` binary during evaluation, not in the Ollama wrapper. 

You can reproduce this natively without Ollama by running `llama-server` on an RTX 5090 with any cohere2moe GGUF model and a context size of 8192:

llama-server.exe --model <path_to_cohere2moe_gguf> -c 8192 --flash-attn auto -b 1024 -ub 1024

Once the server loads, send a standard completion/chat request. The server will immediately crash inside `ggml_cuda_compute_forward` with "MUL_MAT failed / illegal memory access".

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

RTX5090

### Models

north-mini-code-1.0

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Here is what I found during my tests:
- The model works perfectly on Ollama v0.32.1 (which uses an older llama.cpp backend).
- It consistently crashes on Ollama v0.32.3 and later builds.
- Context size used: 8192
- Interestingly, turning off Flash Attention (`--flash-attn` off) prevents the crash. It seems there is a bug with how Flash Attention handles MoE matrix multiplication (`ggml_cuda_compute_forward` / `MUL_MAT`) specifically on Compute 12.0 (Blackwell).
- The exact same GGUF runs fine on macOS via MLX, so the model file itself is perfectly healthy.

### First Bad Commit

I haven't performed a `git bisect` on the llama.cpp repository itself since I am using the pre-compiled binaries from the Ollama project. 

However, I can pinpoint the exact release window for the regression:
- Last known working build: Ollama v0.32.1
- First failing build: Ollama v0.32.3

The bad commit was introduced during the upstream `llama.cpp` bump that was integrated into Ollama between those two specific releases.

### Relevant log output

ggml_cuda_compute_forward: MUL_MAT failed
CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
C:\...\ggml\src\ggml-cuda\ggml-cuda.cu:108: CUDA error
  current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_compute_forward at C:\...\ggml\src\ggml-cuda\ggml-cuda.cu:2422

items.title: Eval bug: NemotronForCausalLM with decoupled head_dim (head_dim != n_embd / n_head) fails to load ("error loading model: check_tensor_dims: tensor ... has wrong shape")
items.author: Jeronymous
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-cli --version
version: 0.6.0-dev (build 11610, commit 091b6a7fc)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux aarch64
```

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

The failure is backend and harware independent, because it happens during model loading (tensor-dimension check), before any compute.
It happens both on GPU and CPU.

### Models

Model can be downloaded at: https://dl.labs.linagora.com/files/models/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-KD-Math-Instruct-1.1-GGUF/Luciole-8B-KD-Math-Instruct-1.1-Q4_K_M.gguf (4.87 GiB)
It is a quantification of this model https://dl.labs.linagora.com/files/models/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-KD-Math-Instruct-1.1
We plan to make public these models on Hugging Face soon.

| property | value |
|---|---|
| hidden_size (`n_embd`) | 3840 |
| num_attention_heads (`n_head`) | 48 |
| **head_dim** (explicit) | **128** |
| num_key_value_heads (`n_head_kv`) | 8 |
| n_head * head_dim (q width) | **6144** (!= n_embd) |
| n_head_kv * head_dim (k/v width) | 1024 |
| num_hidden_layers | 28 |

The produced GGUF stores this correctly (`gguf` reader excerpt):
```
general.architecture            = nemotron
nemotron.embedding_length       = 3840
nemotron.attention.head_count   = 48
nemotron.attention.head_count_kv= 8
nemotron.attention.key_length   = 128      <- decoupled head_dim
nemotron.attention.value_length = 128
nemotron.block_count            = 28
```

and the tensor itself is the correct width:
```
blk.0.attn_q.weight : [3840, 6144]   (= n_embd x (n_head*head_dim))
```


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

#### Problem description

Two related problems affect **nemotron** models whose attention **`head_dim` is decoupled** from `hidden_size / n_heads` (i.e. `head_dim * n_head != hidden_size`), such as this Luciole model (`hidden_size = 3840`, `n_head = 48`, `head_dim = 128`, so `head_dim * n_head= 6144`). Both stem from the assumption `n_embd == n_head * head_dim`, which does not hold here.

**1. The model fails to load (loader bug).**
The loader sizes the Q/K/V (and O) projections from `n_embd` instead of `n_head * head_dim`, so the tensor-shape check rejects the (correct) wider `attn_q` tensor (expected `{3840, 3840}`, got `{3840, 6144}`). The GGUF is well-formed and carries the correct `nemotron.attention.key_length` / `value_length` metadata (both 128); the loader just ignores it. This is the same class of decoupled-head_dim issue already handled for the `llama` / `qwen2` architectures (e.g. Mistral-Nemo, where `head_dim * n_head != hidden_size`), but the `nemotron` loader does not honor it.

**2. The RoPE dimension is wrong in the GGUF (converter bug).**
Independently, the `nemotron` converter computes the partial-RoPE dimension as `int(partial_rotary_factor * hidden_size) // n_head` instead of `partial_rotary_factor * head_dim`. These two formulas agree when `head_dim == hidden_size / n_head`, but diverge for a decoupled head_dim. For this model (`partial_rotary_factor = 0.5`), the converter writes:
> nemotron.rope.dimension_count = int(0.5 * 3840) // 48 = 40

whereas the correct value is `0.5 * 128 = 64`. Since this value is baked into the GGUF metadata, it is a second, independent bug: even once the loader is fixed, the model would apply RoPE over 40 dimensions instead of 64 (wrong positional encoding, degraded output).
So Luciole-8B-KD-Math-Instruct-1.1-Q4_K_M.gguf given as an example would have to be reconverted with a fixed loader.

#### Steps to reproduce

Try to load the GGUF:

```bash
$ llama-cli --run -m Luciole-8B-KD-Math-Instruct-1.1-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 0 -p "Hello" -n 8

[...]
llama_model_load: error loading model: check_tensor_dims: tensor 'blk.0.attn_q.weight'
  has wrong shape; expected   3840,   3840, got   3840,   6144,      1,      1
llama_model_load_from_file_impl: failed to load model
common_init_: failed to load model '.../Luciole-8B-KD-Math-Instruct-1.1-Q4_K_M.gguf'
```

*Minimal synthetic repro*

Build a tiny `nemotron` config with a decoupled head_dim, e.g. `hidden_size=256`, `num_attention_heads=4`, `head_dim=128` (so `n_head*head_dim = 512 != 256`), random weights; convert to GGUF; load. It fails the same way (`attn_q` expected `256,256`, got `256,512`).

### Root cause and suggested fix

In the `LLM_ARCH_NEMOTRON` tensor creation, the Q/K/V (and O) projections are sized from `n_embd` and the `n_embd == n_head * head_dim` assumption, so the expected `attn_q` shape is `{n_embd, n_embd}` = `{3840, 3840}`. For this model `n_head * head_dim = 6144 != n_embd = 3840`, so the (correct) `{3840, 6144}` tensor is rejected.

There are two independent things to fix, matching the two problems above.

**1. Loader (tensor shapes).**
Use `n_embd_head_k`/`n_embd_head_v` (read from `key_length`/`value_length`) and the head counts, as the `llama`/`qwen2` loaders already do.
Roughly, in the nemotron path of `llm_load_tensors` (src/llama-model.cpp):

```cpp
const int64_t n_embd_head_k = hparams.n_embd_head_k;   // from key_length (128)
const int64_t n_embd_head_v = hparams.n_embd_head_v;   // from value_length (128)
layer.wq = create_tensor(tn(LLM_TENSOR_ATTN_Q, "weight", i), {n_embd, n_head    * n_embd_head_k}, 0);
layer.wk = create_tensor(tn(LLM_TENSOR_ATTN_K, "weight", i), {n_embd, n_head_kv * n_embd_head_k}, 0);
layer.wv = create_tensor(tn(LLM_TENSOR_ATTN_V, "weight", i), {n_embd, n_head_kv * n_embd_head_v}, 0);
layer.wo = create_tensor(tn(LLM_TENSOR_ATTN_OUT, "weight", i), {n_head * n_embd_head_v, n_embd}, 0);
```

and ensure the nemotron attention build-graph reshapes Q/K using `n_embd_head_k` rather than `n_embd / n_head`.

**2. Converter (RoPE dimension).**
In the nemotron converter (`convert_hf_to_gguf.py`), the partial-RoPE dimension is derived from `hidden_size`, which is wrong for a decoupled head_dim. It should be derived from `head_dim`:

```python
# before (wrong for decoupled head_dim): int(partial_rotary_factor * n_embd) // n_head
head_dim = self.hparams.get("head_dim", n_embd // n_head)
self.g

items.title: Eval bug: CUDA: MUL_MAT_ID via MMVQ fails with "invalid argument" on Turing when device code is compiled for an older arch (e.g. 61-virtual)
items.author: DukeNukem-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.6.0-dev (build 11616, commit e7268bf6a)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64

Environment: 11× GTX 1660 Super (TU116, cc 7.5), CUDA 12.9, Ubuntu 24.04. llama.cpp e7268bf6a, built with -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="61-virtual;80-virtual". Model: ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF (IQ3_XXS).

Symptom: some prompts abort at the start of processing or generation:

```
CUDA error: invalid argument
current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_kernel_launch at ggml-cuda/common.cuh:1715
... ggml_cuda_mul_mat_vec_q(...)
```

Reproducible with a minimal chat request ("hello", 11 prompt tokens). Dense models are unaffected.

Cause: in mmvq.cu, the host-side get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch(type, cc) uses the device's real compute capability (7.5 → get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch_turing_plus, IQ3_XXS = 7), while the device-side get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch_for_device() uses `__CUDA_ARCH__`. With PTX for 6.1 JIT-compiled on Turing, that's 610, which falls through to get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch_pascal_older (IQ3_XXS = 4). For MoE batches of 5–7 tokens, the host launches a configuration the compiled kernel doesn't support.

Confirmed by: a native -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75 build doesn't crash (but is ~5× slower at prompt processing on these cards, so not a practical workaround). The one-line patch below fixes the 61-virtual build, with no speed loss:

```
diff
 int get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch(ggml_type type, int cc) {
     // NVIDIA: P100, Volta, Ada Lovelace, and Blackwell always use MMVQ for MUL_MAT_ID.
     if (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc)) {
+        cc = ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc);

```
Other host-side decisions keyed on cc, where the device code uses `__CUDA_ARCH__`, may have the same mismatch.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

CPU: Intel Core i7-9700K
GPUs: 11x NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 Super (TU116, compute capability 7.5, 6 GB each), layer split across all 11
Driver 595.99.02, CUDA toolkit 12.9, Ubuntu 24.04


### Models

ISTA-DASLab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GSQ-RCO-GGUF, IQ3_XXS (MoE). Dense models (Qwen3.8-27B) are unaffected.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Build: -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="61-virtual;80-virtual"
(61-virtual is used deliberately: on these cards it gives ~5x faster prompt processing than a native sm_75 build.)

Server: llama-server -m <IQ3_XXS shard 1> -lm mmap -lzm on -ngl 999 -fa on -c 32768 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 -np 2 -ub 256 --jinja

Steps: send a minimal chat request, e.g. {"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}],"stream":true}
(11 prompt tokens). The server aborts with "CUDA error: invalid argument" in ggml_cuda_mul_mat_vec_q. Some longer prompts also crash, others do not.

Cause: in mmvq.cu, the host-side get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch(type, cc) uses the device's real compute capability
(7.5 -> get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch_turing_plus, IQ3_XXS = 7), while the device-side get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch_for_device()
uses __CUDA_ARCH__, which is 610 for PTX compiled for 6.1 and JIT-compiled on Turing. 610 falls through to
get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch_pascal_older (IQ3_XXS = 4). For MoE batches of 5-7 tokens, the host launches a configuration
the compiled kernel does not support.

Confirmed by:
- A native -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=75 build does not crash (but is ~5x slower at prompt processing on these cards).
- This one-line patch fixes the 61-virtual build, with no speed loss:

```diff
 int get_mmvq_mmid_max_batch(ggml_type type, int cc) {
     // NVIDIA: P100, Volta, Ada Lovelace, and Blackwell always use MMVQ for MUL_MAT_ID.
     if (GGML_CUDA_CC_IS_NVIDIA(cc)) {
+        cc = ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc);
```

Other host-side decisions keyed on cc, where the device code uses __CUDA_ARCH__, may have the same mismatch.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

  current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_kernel_launch at ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh:1715
  cudaGetLastError()
libggml-cuda.so.0(ggml_cuda_error(...))
libggml-cuda.so.0(ggml_cuda_mul_mat_vec_q(ggml_backend_cuda_context&, ggml_tensor const*, ggml_tensor const*, ggml_tensor const*, ggml_tensor*, ggml_cuda_mm_fusion_args_host const*))
libggml-base.so.0(ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async)
libllama.so.0(llama_context::graph_compute(ggml_cgraph*, bool))

items.title: [RFC]: Master rolling upgrade has no index-preserving path today, and no readiness signal predicts a safe promotion
items.author: gongwei-130
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

There is currently **no upgrade path for the Master that preserves the cache index** — not rolling, not stop-and-restore. We measured all three available paths on two clusters running `0.3.13` and each one loses the index, by three different mechanisms.

This is filed as a new RFC rather than a comment on #1920 because #1920 is closed and, more importantly, because its **"Current Capabilities" section describes a baseline that does not hold in `0.3.13`**. Three of the capabilities it builds on are broken, and one of them makes #1920's own proposed Master Upgrade Flow unsafe as written. The design work in #1920 is good and mostly orthogonal to this; what is missing is a promotion-safety baseline underneath it. #1920 should be reopened as the design track; this RFC is about the precondition.

## What we measured

Two Kubernetes clusters, `kvcacheai/mooncake:0.3.13` (digest `sha256:51d695314243f3a35615784634ac4fd4bfd5f1aca316df997383a0617169b780`), etcd-backed HA, 2 masters, 3 and 7 store clients, `enable_snapshot` tested both ways.

| Upgrade path | Result | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| `RollingUpdate` the master Deployment, promote the new standby | **index lost** — 200 keys → 0, and 300 keys → 0 on the second cluster | two distinct causes, below |
| `Recreate` both masters | **index lost** | OpLog replication is standby-to-primary state transfer, not persistence; with `enable_snapshot=false` there is nothing on disk |
| `enable_snapshot=true`, restart, restore | **objects lost** (segments and `Replica::next_id_` return) | filed as #3761 |

Store-client and compute-client rolling upgrades are fine — see "What already works" below. The blocker is entirely the Master.

## The load-bearing problem: neither available readiness signal predicts a safe promotion

We tried the obvious mitigation — create the standby, let it soak under live traffic, then promote — and it failed too. Two attempts, two different causes:

**Attempt 1, a freshly created standby has no baseline.** It reports itself fully synced in **7 microseconds**, having replayed nothing, while the live primary was at sequence 206:

```
17:49:59.719648  oplog_applier.cpp:117        OpLogApplier: recovered from sequence_id=0, expected_sequence_id set to=1
17:49:59.719655  standby_state_machine.cpp:245 Standby state transition: SYNCING -> WATCHING (event: SYNC_COMPLETE)
```

It starts at zero, declares `SYNC_COMPLETE`, and watches *forward* — it never replays history. That is consistent with the documented Standby Bootstrap sequence ("from the snapshot's `last_included_seq`, or from 1 if no snapshot"), so with no snapshot there is nothing to build on. Arguably a design limit rather than a bug — but a promotable one, which is the problem.

**Attempt 2, a soaked standby fails as well, and this one is a bug.** This standby had been up nine minutes *before* the data was written, had `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id 1920`, `ha_oplog_applied_entries_total 1953`, and had watched every one of the 300 puts:

```
I hot_standby_service.cpp:560]      Promoting Standby to Primary. Applied seq_id: 1920, lag: 0 entries
I hot_standby_service.cpp:588]      Standby promoted to Primary successfully. All remaining OpLog entries have been synced.
E master_service.cpp:3198]          RestoreFromStandbySnapshot: overlapping memory descriptors
E master_service_supervisor.cpp:401] Standby restore failed: INVALID_PARAMS
```

The standby **had** the state. Promotion reported success. Then the restore validator rejected the entire `PromotionContext` on one inconsistency and the index came out empty. Filed separately as #3760. Note this sits *on top of* #3527 and #3354, both already inside `0.3.13` — the error string only exists because of #3354 — so it is not a stale-version problem.

**The consequence for orchestration: `ha_oplog_standby_lag = 0` is not a go signal.** It read 0 throughout *both* failed attempts. It means "not behind on the stream I am watching", and says nothing about whether the restore will be accepted. The only honest number was the standby's own `master_key_count = 0`, and there is no signal at all for "my `PromotionContext` will survive validation". Those two `E` lines are the sole evidence, and **no metric exposes the failure**.

**This is why #1920's Master Upgrade Flow does not hold today.** That flow is:

> Start new-version Standby → wait for `IsReadyForPromotion()` → StepDown old Primary → new Standby wins election → Clients auto re-mount → remove old container

Both of our failed attempts would have satisfied any readiness predicate expressible from the observable state — the fresh standby reaches `WATCHING`/`SYNC_COMPLETE` in 7 µs, and the soaked one reported `lag: 0` with 1953 entries applied. A graceful StepDown API makes the transition *deterministic*; it does not make it *safe*. If `IsReadyForPromotion()` is satisfied by `WATCHING` state (which the observable state machine suggests, though we have not read that predicate), the flow reliably destroys the index. Worth confirming before that design is implemented on top.

## Proposed changes

Ordered by what unblocks what. (1) and (2) are the precondition; (3) and (4) are independently useful and already have issues.

### 1. Validate the promotion context *before* the point of no return, and abort rather than serve empty

Today validation runs after `Promoting Standby to Primary` has already succeeded and the old leader is gone, so a validation failure has no recovery path — it produces a serving master with an empty index and no error surface.

- Run `RestoreFromStandbySnapshot`'s validation as a dry run while the standby is still a standby.
- On failure, **refuse promotion** and leave the existing leader in place. Losing an election attempt is recoverable; losing the index is not.
- Separately, prefer partial restore over total discard: one bad memory descriptor should drop that descriptor, not 300 keys (this is the #3760 ask).

### 2. Expose an honest promotability predi

items.title: [Track]: [Store] Land the tenant-first MasterService migration in staged PRs
items.author: Aionw
items.body_excerpt:
This issue tracks how the `MasterService` half of RFC #3670 lands in `main`. #4370 carries the whole migration as one PR (+7.3k/−6.6k), which is too large to review, so the work is split into 17 PRs. Each PR builds, passes the tests and is correct on its own, and the order below is the order they can merge in. The code for the whole series is already written. Each PR is cut from the finished end state, so reviewing it means reviewing that slice of a design that is already complete, not code still in progress. Review comments are welcome on any PR in the series, and on this issue for the overall plan. Anyone whose review suggestion is adopted is added as a co-author of the PR that takes it. ## Status Last updated 2026-10-14. In the dependency graph below, green is merged and yellow has an open PR. | Step | PR | State | |---|---|---| | 4. Tenant quota control plane | #4563 | Merged | | 1. Per-key `ObjectState` | #4562 | Merged | | 3. Dynamic replication controller | #4589 | Merged | | 5. Object route | #4585 | Open | | 2. Promotion candidate tracker | #4586 | Open | | everything else | — | Waiting on its dependencies | Step 9 now waits only on step 2 (#4586). Step 8, the next step that builds on #4563, also needs step 6 (namespace layer), which comes after step 5. ## Design ### Before: shard-level ownership ```mermaid flowchart TB MS["MasterService"] --> SH subgraph SH["1024 MetadataShards (hash of tenant and key, one lock each)"] TS["TenantState
one per shard and tenant"] TS --- MD["metadata map
ObjectMetadata + TenantQuotaLedger"] TS --- SM["7 per-key side maps
+ lease map"] end subgraph SIDE["Also inside MasterService"] GD["GroupDomain
all groups, one lock"] OL["ObjectOperationLock
4096 striped mutexes"] EV["BatchEvict · NoFBatchEvict
EvictTenantMemoryForQuota"] end SH -->|"census of every shard, every pass"| EV ``` - **Ownership.** A shard holds fragments of many tenants. Each `TenantState` in it keeps the object map plus seven separate per-key maps (processing keys, replication, offload and promotion tasks, promotion candidates, dynamic-replication pending records and cooldowns) and a map of dynamic-replication leases. items.title: [Question] How to force certain computations to occur in float16?
items.author: vedantroy
items.body_excerpt:
I have the following kernel:
```python3
@triton.jit
def unmasked_blend_kernel(
    img1_ptr, img2_ptr, ratio: float, total_items: int, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr
):
    block_idx = tl.program_id(0)
    offset = block_idx * BLOCK_SIZE
    item_element_idxs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    img1_item_ptrs = img1_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs
    img2_item_ptrs = img2_ptr + offset + item_element_idxs

    if offset + BLOCK_SIZE > total_items:
        mask = item_element_idxs < total_items % BLOCK_SIZE
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out, mask=mask)
    else:
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs)
        out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2
        tl.store(img1_item_ptrs, out)
```

Given that this kernel is blending 2 uint8  tensors, I figured it would make sense to do the computation ` out = ratio * img1 + (1.0 - ratio) * img2`  since I don't need high precision.

However, I can't figure out how to force the Triton compiler to do the computations in FP16.
I tried doing:

```python3
        img1 = tl.load(img1_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
        img2 = tl.load(img2_item_ptrs, mask=mask, other=0).to(tl.float16)
```
but from looking at the generated PTX, it just seems like the float16s are just converted to float32s before the multiplication 
occurs.

Is there a way I can force the Triton  compiler  to make the multiplications float16? (Or is this impossible for a good reason;  i.e maybe this is not what I actually want)?

items.title: Block-wise Scatter-Reduce :  __getitem__ / __setitem__ errors
items.author: olivier-peltre
items.body_excerpt:
While trying to implement a scatter-add reduction inside a kernel, I get errors related to `tensor.__{get,set}item__`. 

As far as I understand, indexing features in triton are either limited or new and I'd like some advice on how to find a satisfactory workaround :slightly_smiling_face: 

Here is a sample code and descriptions of errors: 

```py
    ...
    # load indices and values
    idx = tl.load(idx_ptr + j + row)
    values = tl.load(values_ptr + begin + block)     
    # prepare output 
    out = tl.zeros((BLOCK_HEIGHT, OUT_WIDTH), values.dtype)
    mask = tl.full((OUT_WIDTH,), 0, tl.int1)

    # reduce on axis -1 in horizontal for-loop (FAILS) 
    offset = idx[0]
    for k in tl.static_range(BLOCK_WIDTH): 
        idx_k = idx[k] - offset
        mask[idx_k] = 1 
        out[:,idx_k] += values[:,k]
    
    # store output (atomic lock in case of small global height)
    tl.atomic_add(out_ptr + idx_0, out, mask) 
```
- when trying to access indices I get e.g.  line `offset = idx[0]` I get: 
    ```
    > `offset = idx[0]`
    ValueError("unsupported tensor index: constexpr[0]")
    ```
    is this intended?
    
    I can obviously replace this by `tl.load(idx_ptr + j (+k))`  as workaround
    
- I further get upon calling setitem:
    ```
    > mask[idx_k] = 1
    AssertionError()
    ```
    Overlooking the source, I guess this is because `tensor` doesn't have a `__setitem__` method, though throwing `AttributeError` would be more informative.
    
- I assume the following
  ```
  out[:, idx_k] += val[:,k]
  ```
  would fail for the same reason, though I could probably work around this with `tl.where`.  I'm also unsure whether the shared memory (?) accumulator `out` shouldn't be transposed for performance befor the final `store` instruction. 
  

But more generally, what would you recommend? Maybe this has been done somewhere else? 
Any form of advice greatly appreciated :pray: 

I'm tagging you here @apgoucher and @Mogball, as I wonder whether your recent #5262 PR could help on this subject. 


### Note

I'm looking into whether triton could help scale-up scatter-add kernels, after having noticed large runtime discrepancies between jax and torch implementations (torch ~4x faster) though both scale bad to large input sizes. I'm hoping that aligning loads to 128B sector sizes while putting more work on each warp (as opposed to a naive implementation relying solely on atomics) could improve the scaling in the large input size limit.

I'm also wondering whether leveraging cuda `__shfl_sync` semantics wouldn't be necessary to get satisfactory results on this (which would probably fall out of triton's scope). Though I'm still looking for a good triton implementation first!

items.title: Python 3.14t: C extension missing Py_MOD_GIL declaration causes GIL re-enable warning
items.author: kdt2014
items.body_excerpt:
### Description
Triton 3.5.0 provides binary wheels for Python 3.14t (free-threaded build), but the C extension module `triton._C.libtriton` does not declare GIL compatibility, causing Python to re-enable the GIL with a warning.

### Environment
- Python version: 3.14.0 free-threading build
- Triton version: 3.5.0
- Platform: Linux x86_64
- Installation: `pip install triton` (cp314t wheel)

### Current Behavior
When importing Triton in Python 3.14t:
```python
import triton._C.libtriton
```

Output:
```
RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load module 
'triton._C.libtriton', which has not declared that it can run safely without the GIL.
```

### Expected Behavior
The C extension should declare its GIL compatibility status using the `Py_mod_gil` slot in the module definition, as described in [PEP 703](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/).

### Reproduction Steps
```bash
python3.14t -c "import triton._C.libtriton"
```

### Suggested Fix
Add the appropriate `Py_mod_gil` declaration in the C extension module initialization:
```c
static PyModuleDef_Slot module_slots[] = {
    {Py_mod_gil, Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED},  // or Py_MOD_GIL_USED if needed
    {0, NULL}
};
```

### Additional Context
- Since Triton already builds and distributes cp314t wheels, adding the GIL declaration would complete the free-threaded support
- This affects users trying to leverage true parallel execution in Python 3.14t
- The warning can be suppressed with `PYTHON_GIL=0`, but proper declaration is the correct solution

### References
- PEP 703: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/
- Python 3.14 free-threading docs: https://docs.python.org/3.14/howto/free-threading-extensions.html
```

items.title: Floating-point `%` loses the sign of an exact zero remainder
items.author: merlinsun
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

For floating-point operands, Triton's `%` lowers through the floating remainder operation. On the tested build, the exact-zero result loses the sign of the dividend: `-0.0 % 3.0` is stored as `+0.0` for both f32 and f64. Other finite remainder values in the same probe matched the reference.

Minimal f32 reproducer:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr):
    i = tl.arange(0, 2)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + i)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + i)
    tl.store(out_ptr + i, x % y)

x = torch.tensor([-0.0, 0.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
y = torch.tensor([3.0, 3.0], device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
out = torch.empty_like(x)
kernel[(1,)](x, y, out)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(out, out.view(torch.int32))
```

Expected first result: `-0.0` (f32 bits `0x80000000`). Observed: `+0.0` (bits `0x00000000`). The same mismatch was observed for f64. `TRITON_INTERPRET=1` passes this isolated `%` test.

### Environment details

Triton https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/commit/4fd7cc5cfd0a84acfeb5dadb1578dffa409903fc on A800

items.title: Compiler crash:LLVM AMDGPU MachineVerifier report "Virtual register defs don't dominate all uses"
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Compiling a legal, deterministic Triton GEMM kernel aborts the process during LLVM AMDGPU codegen: LLVM's post-RA MachineVerifier rejects the generated MIR and calls `abort()`. The same kernel compiles and runs correctly with `num_warps=2` or `num_stages=1/3`; the crash requires `num_warps=1, num_stages=2`.
**Likely cause**
`num_stages=2` enables software pipelining, which clones the A-tile address computation (`V_XOR_B32_e32 112, %3212`) into the prologue and the loop body. A late machine pass (register allocation / live-range splitting / COPY insertion) then makes both clones define the same virtual register `%9951`, without materializing one definition at a common dominator. The epilogue use is reachable from a path that bypasses each definition (bb.4 bypasses the loop-body def in bb.5; bb.1 bypasses the prologue def in bb.2), so no def dominates the use and MachineVerifier aborts. Correct behavior would be distinct vregs per path, or a single merged definition at the common dominator (bb.3).

**Error log excerpt**
Output before crash
REPRO_START M=31 N=63 K=33 BLOCK=128x128x32 num_warps=1 num_stages=2 grid=(1, 1)

LLVM MachineVerifier error (process SIGABRT, exit code 134)
*** Bad machine code: Virtual register defs don't dominate all uses. ***
- function:      gemm
- v. register:   %9951
LLVM ERROR: Found 1 machine code errors.

Definitions/uses of bad virtual register %9951
```
1952:  bb.2   %9951:vgpr_32 = COPY %9347:vgpr_32       def 1 (prologue path)
2254:  bb.5   %9951:vgpr_32 = COPY %9346:vgpr_32       def 2 (loop-body path)
3346:  bb.9   %9348:vgpr_32 = COPY %9951:vgpr_32       use 1 (inside loop; reachable only via bb.5)
4244:  bb.15  %9349:vgpr_32 = COPY %9951:vgpr_32       use 2 (epilogue; reachable via both bb.4/bb.5 paths)
```


Sources of the two definitions
(the same A-tile address computation was cloned twice by software pipelining)
1951:  %9347:vgpr_32 = V_XOR_B32_e32 112, %3212:vgpr_32, ...; 22_gemm_llvm_verifier_min_repro.py:56:18
2253:  %9346:vgpr_32 = V_XOR_B32_e32 112, %3212:vgpr_32

Dominance relationship (two incoming paths to bb.15)
```
bb.3 -> bb.5 -> (loop: bb.7..bb.9) -> bb.10 -> bb.6 -> ... -> bb.15
bb.3 -> bb.4 -> bb.6 -> ... -> bb.15
```
def 2 is in bb.5, but the bb.4 path bypasses bb.5; def 1 is in bb.2, but another path via bb.1 bypasses bb.2
=> the use in bb.15 has no dominating definition, so the verifier is correct to reject it

Exit code
134 (SIGABRT)

**Reproducer**
```
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def gemm(_fz_switch_ptr, _fz_switch_output_ptr, A, B, C, M, N, K, BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_K: tl.constexpr):
    opaque_values = tl.load(_fz_switch_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2))
    opaque_zero, opaque_one = tl.split(opaque_values)
    opaque_true = opaque_zero < opaque_one
    n_id = tl.program_id(1)
    a_offset_m = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N), dtype=tl.float32)
    for k in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):
        offset_k = k + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_K)
        a_tile = tl.load(A + a_offset_m[:, None] * K + offset_k[None, :], mask=(a_offset_m[:, None] < M) & (offset_k[None, :] < K), other=0.0)
        if opaque_true:
            tl.store(_fz_switch_output_ptr + tl.arange(0, 2), tl.min(tl.reshape(tl.arange(0, 4), (2, 2)) + opaque_one, axis=1) + opaque_values)
        b_tile = tl.load(B + (n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :] + offset_k[:, None] * N, mask=((n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :] < N) & (offset_k[:, None] < K), other=0.0)
        acc += tl.dot(a_tile, b_tile)
    if opaque_true:
        tl.store(C + a_offset_m[:, None] * N + (n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :], acc.to(tl.float16), mask=(a_offset_m[:, None] < M) & ((n_id * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N))[None, :] < N))


def _main() -> None:
    device = "cuda"  # ROCm uses the cuda namespace; no CPU fallback possible.
    M, N, K = 31, 63, 33
    num_warps = int(os.environ.get("NUM_WARPS", "1"))
    num_stages = int(os.environ.get("NUM_STAGES", "2"))
    BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K = 128, 128, 32

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.rand(M, K, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    b = torch.rand(K, N, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    c = torch.rand(M, N, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    switch = torch.tensor([0, 1], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
    scratch = torch.empty(2, dtype=torch.float32, device=device)

    grid = (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_M), triton.cdiv(N, BLOCK_N))
    print(
        f"REPRO_START M={M} N={N} K={K} BLOCK={BLOCK_M}x{BLOCK_N}x{BLOCK_K} "
        f"num_warps={num_warps} num_stages={num_stages} grid={grid}",
        flush=True,
    )
    gemm[grid](
        switch, scratch, a, b, c, M, N, K,
        BLOCK_M=BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N=BLOCK_N, BLOCK_K=BLOCK_K,
        num_warps=num_warps, num_stages=num_stages,
    )
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("REPRO_DONE (no crash; use NUM_WARPS=1 NUM_STAGES=2 to trigger)", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _main()

### Environment details

```
# Environment: 
- AMD MI308X (gfx942) 
- ROCm 7.2.3
- torch 2.14.0+rocm7.2
- triton-rocm 3.8.0.

items.title: [Gluon] Warp-specialized lowering emits different setmaxnreg instructions within one warpgroup
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

When a warp-specialized kernel sets `worker_num_regs` and a warpgroup holds more than one partition, the warps of that warpgroup execute different `setmaxnreg` instructions. The partitions include the no-op padding partitions that `AllocateWarpGroups` adds, so a single 1-warp worker partition is enough to trigger this.

PTX ISA 9.4 §9.7.21.5 (`setmaxnreg`) requires all warps of a warpgroup to execute the same `setmaxnreg` instruction, and makes the behavior undefined otherwise. For the mandatory `.aligned` qualifier, it allows `setmaxnreg` in conditional code only when every thread of the warpgroup evaluates the condition identically. Here the instructions have the same text but are distinct instructions, reached by a branch whose condition differs across the warpgroup.

The pattern comes from the lowering (permalinks at main `0d4e0a0`):
- `padToMaxWarpGroups` pads the worker partitions to whole warpgroups ([AllocateWarpGroups.cpp L39–L87](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/AllocateWarpGroups.cpp#L39-L87)). Every partition in a warpgroup then gets the same count, the warpgroup's maximum ([L220–L242](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/AllocateWarpGroups.cpp#L220-L242), [L265–L272](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/AllocateWarpGroups.cpp#L265-L272)).
- `rewritePartitionRegions` calls the target's `reallocRegisters` at the start of each partition region and at each `warp_return` ([WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp L391–L393](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L391-L393), [L423–L425](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L423-L425)). On NVIDIA, that emits a `setmaxnreg` ([ConvertWarpSpecializeToLLVM.cpp L231–L238](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/third_party/nvidia/lib/TritonNVIDIAGPUToLLVM/ConvertWarpSpecializeToLLVM.cpp#L231-L238)).

So partitions that share a warpgroup reach the same count through different instructions. The dispatcher chooses each warp's partition with a switch on a per-warp state byte; in the example below, that switch is a `brx.idx` jump table.

**Example.** Tutorial `python/tutorials/gluon/08-warp-specialization.py`, `elementwise_add_warp_specialized_kernel`, compiled with Triton 3.8.0 for sm_90a, using the wrapper's default arguments:
- `XBLOCK=32`, `YBLOCK=64`;
- 2 load and 2 store buffers;
- `num_warps=4`, `maxnreg=128`;
- worker partitions `[1, 1]` warps with `[24, 24]` registers.

Warps 0–3 run the default partition. Warps 4–7 form one warpgroup holding the 2-warp padding partition, the load partition and the store partition. The default warps store the selector word `0x01000202` (line 127, before the barrier at 128), so warps 4–7 read 2, 2, 0, 1. Excerpt of the generated PTX, with line numbers from our file:

```
127:  st.shared.b32   [global_smem+49376], 16777730;   // selectors 2,2,0,1 for warps 4..7
...
314:  setmaxnreg.dec.sync.aligned.u32   24;           // all of warps 4..7
316:  ld.shared.b8    %r14, [%r16+49372];              // %r16 = global_smem + warp index
321-325:  $L_brx_0: .branchtargets $L__BB0_5, $L__BB0_9, $L__BB0_13, $L__BB0_18;   // selector 3 = exit
326:  brx.idx         %r14, $L_brx_0;
327: $L__BB0_5:                                        // selector 0: warp 6 (load)
328:  setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32   24;
...
426: $L__BB0_9:                                        // selector 1: warp 7 (store)
427:  setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32   24;
...
303: $L__BB0_13:                                       // selector 2: warps 4, 5 (padding)
305:  setmaxnreg.inc.sync.aligned.u32   24;
```

Warps 4 and 5 execute the instruction at 305, warp 6 the one at 328, and warp 7 the one at 427, all within one warpgroup. The exits differ the same way: 308 for warps 4 and 5, 424 for warp 6, and 522 for warp 7.

The same holds in every warp-specialized kernel we compiled from the Gluon tutorials with Triton 3.8.0:
- tutorial 08: the add kernel with `num_warps=8` (warps 8–11 split the same way), and the matmul kernel for sm_100a;
- tutorial 10: `matmul_accumulate_kernel`, sm_100a;
- tutorial 11: `mma_scaled_warp_specialized_kernel`, sm_100a.

In the sm_100a kernels, the extra warps execute a common `setmaxnreg.inc 256` in the dispatcher. Each partition then executes its own `setmaxnreg.dec 24`.

**A second instance of the same rule.** PTX also requires all warps of the warpgroup to synchronize explicitly after a `setmaxnreg` before any of them executes the next one. Each partition's exit `setmaxnreg` branches straight back to the dispatcher's `setmaxnreg`, with no barrier in between: 424 → 314, 522 → 314 and 308 → 314. In the lowering, each `warp_return` becomes barrier, realloc, branch ([L420–L426](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L420-L426)), and the switch loop starts with realloc, barrier ([L443–L445](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/0d4e0a0ceae18cecacf582b9c6f557847a772bdf/lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/WarpSpecializeUtility.cpp#L443-L445)). So warp 6 can execute 314 while warp 7 is still in the store partition.

**To reproduce.** On a Hopper GPU, run the tutorial's `test_elementwise_add_warp_specialized` with `num_warps=4`, then `grep -n setmaxnreg` the kernel's `.ptx` in the Triton cache.

We found this with a PTX-level checker on a Gluon GEMM of our own, and traced the tutorial PTX by hand. No GPU run.

**Expected behavior.** Every warp of a warpgroup executes the same `setmaxnreg` instruction, and the warpgroup synchronizes between

items.title: [FuseNestedLoops] flatten=True advances outer loop-carried indices on inner iterations
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With `tl.range(..., flatten=True)`, the kernel below returns wrong integers: a value carried from two outer iterations back is combined with the index from one iteration back. With `flatten=False` it matches the Python reference. This reproduces on Triton 3.5.1, 3.8.0 and main (`0d4e0a0c`).

### Reproducer

```python
import sys
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def flow_nested(X, Y, Z, Indices, Data, C, N, T, D, U, enabled,
                BLOCK: tl.constexpr, LOOP_STAGES: tl.constexpr,
                INNER_STAGES: tl.constexpr, FLATTEN: tl.constexpr,
                UNROLL: tl.constexpr, DISALLOW: tl.constexpr):
    pos = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    valid = pos < N
    now = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    delayed_one = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    delayed_two = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    checksum = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_x = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_y = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_z = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_idx = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    old_valid = tl.full((BLOCK,), False, tl.int1)
    older_z = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    older_idx = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
    older_valid = tl.full((BLOCK,), False, tl.int1)
    for t in tl.range(0, T, num_stages=LOOP_STAGES, flatten=FLATTEN,
                      loop_unroll_factor=UNROLL, disallow_acc_multi_buffer=DISALLOW):
        if enabled and t % 3 != 1:
            g1 = tl.load(Data + pos * D + old_idx,
                         old_valid & (old_idx >= 0) & (old_idx < D), other=0).to(tl.int32)
            delayed_one += tl.where(old_valid, (old_x * old_y + g1) * (t + 1), 0)
        if enabled and t % 2 == 0:
            g2 = tl.load(Data + pos * D + older_idx,
                         older_valid & (older_idx >= 0) & (older_idx < D), other=0).to(tl.int32)
            delayed_two += tl.where(older_valid, (2 * older_z + g2) * (t + 1), 0)
        x = tl.load(X + t * N + pos, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
        y = tl.load(Y + t * N + pos, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
        z = tl.load(Z + t * N + pos, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
        idx = tl.load(Indices + t * N + pos, valid, other=0)
        now += x * y + z * (t + 1)
        checksum += y * (pos + 1) + idx * (t + 1)
        inner_old = tl.zeros((BLOCK,), tl.int32)
        inner_valid = tl.full((BLOCK,), False, tl.int1)
        for s in tl.range(0, U, num_stages=INNER_STAGES, flatten=FLATTEN,
                          loop_unroll_factor=UNROLL, disallow_acc_multi_buffer=DISALLOW):
            neighbor = (pos + s + 1) % N
            inner_z = tl.load(Z + t * N + neighbor, valid, other=0).to(tl.int32)
            if enabled and (t + s) % 2 == 0:
                checksum += (inner_z + x * (s + 1)) * (t + 1) * (s + 1)
            if enabled and s % 2 == 1:
                checksum += tl.where(inner_valid, inner_old * (s + 1), 0)
            inner_old = inner_z
            inner_valid = valid
        older_z = old_z
        older_idx = old_idx
        older_valid = old_valid
        old_x = x
        old_y = y
        old_z = z
        old_idx = idx
        old_valid = valid
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos, now, valid)
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos + 1, delayed_one, valid)
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos + 2, delayed_two, valid)
    tl.store(C + 4 * pos + 3, checksum, valid)


def reference(X, Y, Z, I, Data, N, T, D, U):
    out = []
    for p in range(N):
        now = d1 = d2 = ck = 0
        old = older = None  # (x, y, z, idx) of the previous / second-previous outer iteration
        for t in range(T):
            if t % 3 != 1 and old:
                d1 += (old[0] * old[1] + Data[p * D + old[3]]) * (t + 1)
            if t % 2 == 0 and older:
                d2 += (2 * older[2] + Data[p * D + older[3]]) * (t + 1)
            x, y, z, idx = X[t * N + p], Y[t * N + p], Z[t * N + p], I[t * N + p]
            now += x * y + z * (t + 1)
            ck += y * (p + 1) + idx * (t + 1)
            inner_old = None
            for s in range(U):
                inner_z = Z[t * N + (p + s + 1) % N]
                if (t + s) % 2 == 0:
                    ck += (inner_z + x * (s + 1)) * (t + 1) * (s + 1)
                if s % 2 == 1 and inner_old is not None:
                    ck += inner_old * (s + 1)
                inner_old = inner_z
            older, old = old, (x, y, z, idx)
        out += [now, d1, d2, ck]
    return out


def main():
    print("torch", torch.__version__, "triton", triton.__version__, torch.cuda.get_device_name())
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
    D, bad = 7, 0
    for flatten in (False, True):
        for N, T, U in ((129, 3, 2), (129, 4, 3), (256, 3, 2), (300, 5, 2), (64, 6, 3)):
            X, Y, Z = (torch.randint(-3, 4, (T * N,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int8) for _ in range(3))
            I = torch.randint(0, D, (T * N,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int32)
            Data = torch.randint(-3, 4, (N * D,), generator=g, dtype=torch.int8)
            C = torch.zeros(4 * N, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
            flow_nested[(triton.cdiv(N, 256),)](X.cuda(), Y.cuda(), Z.cuda(), I.cuda(), Data.cuda(), C, N, T, D, U, True,
                                                BLOCK=256, LOOP_STAGES=2, INNER_STAGES=3, FLATTEN=flatten,
                                                UNROLL=1, DISALLOW=False, num_warps=1, num_stages=2)
            want = reference(X.tolist(), Y.tolist(), Z.tolist(), I.tolist(), Data.tolist(), N, T, D, U)
            got = C.tolist()
            diff = [k for k in range(4 * N) if got[k] != want[k]]
            bad += bool(diff)
            first = f" first: element {diff[0]} (lane {diff[0] // 4}, output {diff[0] % 4}) got {got[diff[0]]} want {want[diff[0]]}" if diff else ""
            print(f"flatten={flatten} N={N} T={T} U={U}: {len(diff)} of {4 * N} wrong{first}")
    sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Expected: all ten cases report 0 wrong. Actual: the f

items.title: Autotuner memoizes incorrectly on mixed-architecture setups
items.author: turboderp
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

`Autotuner.cache` is keyed only on key-arg values and dtypes. So a process using one decorated kernel on two devices of different capability uses the config from whichever device ran first, even if the second device is incompatible. `_bench()` drops configs that raise `OutOfResources`, but only on the device that ran the benchmark.

Miminal example is one kernel with two configs, where one config needs >64 kB smem, run on an Ampere GPU and then on a Turing GPU; nothing causes the autotuner to treat the two GPUs differently, so the second launch fails if autotuning picked the >64 kB config.

As far as I can tell it's fixable in [`Autotuner.run()`](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/3078daa76bbd55c1c3509f7ee8e899b1ed6a127e/python/triton/runtime/autotuner.py#L238) by appending e.g. `driver.active.get_current_target()` to the key, mirroring what the JIT compile cache already does.

### Environment details

Triton: Latest
GPU: Mixed setups
