items.title: [Bug] KV event sync never matches engine-reported prefixes with the default block size
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
With `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_KV_EVENT_SYNC_ENABLED=true`, the prefixes the engines report through KV events never match a request, at least with the default settings.

The two sides cut prompts into blocks differently. The router turns the prompt into bytes, 4 per token, and splits them every `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE` bytes. A BlockStored event is hashed one engine block at a time, and an engine block is `block_size` tokens. So the hashes only line up when the env value happens to be 4 × the engine's block size. For vLLM's default 16-token blocks that's 64. The code default is 16, and the gateway manifests and release overlays set 128.

Here's what `SyncPrefixHashTable` on main returns for a prompt whose blocks a vLLM pod reported, with 16-token blocks:

| AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE | match |
|---|---|
| 16 | 0% |
| 64 | 100% |
| 128 | 0% |

Nothing logs an error. Routing still matches the hashes the router records for its own picks, so KV sync quietly behaves like the standard mode, and since those hashes never match an engine block, BlockRemoved events can't clean them up either. Setting the env to 64 doesn't really fix it. Block size depends on the model and attention backend, and one env value covers every model the gateway serves.

The events already carry the engine's block size, so the index can learn it per model and split requests to match. I have a PR ready.

items.title: GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule: much higher incomplete-generation rate on Hopper (SM90) vs Blackwell (SM120), same model/LoRA/config
items.author: anhngml
items.body_excerpt:
## GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule on Hopper (SM90): significantly higher rate of premature/incomplete generation vs Blackwell (SM100/SM120), same model/weights/config — suspect numerical difference, not a config issue

**flashinfer version**: `0.6.16.post3`
**Model**: `numind/NuExtract3` (Qwen3.5-family, hybrid Mamba/GDN attention) + a LoRA adapter, served via `vllm/vllm-openai:latest` (vLLM 0.28.0)
**GPUs compared**: NVIDIA H100 NVL (Hopper, SM90) vs NVIDIA RTX 5090 (Blackwell, SM120)

### Summary

Running the exact same model + exact same LoRA adapter (verified byte-identical, SHA256 match) + exact same serving config against the exact same input documents, we see a **~20-45% rate of incomplete generation** (model emits a natural stop token, `finish_reason='stop'`, before finishing valid JSON — output is missing a closing bracket at the very end) on an H100 (SM90), but **0/10 on an RTX 5090 (SM120)** in a matched test. We've ruled out every config-level variable we could think of and are left suspecting something in the GDN chunk_gated_delta_rule computation itself behaves differently (numerically) between SM90 and SM100/SM120.

### What we're doing

Structured extraction: model is prompted (via `chat_template_kwargs.template`, the NuExtract-style type-marker DSL) to fill in a JSON template for a large, deeply-nested schema (~19 repeating array/table fields, up to 5 levels of nesting, template itself ~8.6KB as JSON). Generation is **free-text** (no `response_format`/grammar constraint) — nothing enforces the model to close every bracket before stopping. `temperature=0.0`.

### The failure signature (confirmed by directly capturing raw model output + `finish_reason`)

For the majority of failures on H100:
- `finish_reason == "stop"` (NOT `"length"` — not a token-budget truncation; `completion_tokens` typically 1500-3700, nowhere near any configured ceiling)
- The resulting text fails `json.loads()` with `Expecting ',' delimiter` at a position exactly equal to `len(content)` — i.e. the model produced a fully well-formed JSON body but is missing exactly the outermost closing `}` (verified by manual bracket-depth counting: final depth = 1 on one captured example)
- The **same physical input document** reproducibly fails on some runs and succeeds on others (not a per-document deterministic thing) — confirmed directly: one specific document failed in one sequential run and succeeded in a later sequential run, same everything.

### What we ruled out (each tested directly, not assumed)

- **Not batching/preemption/concurrency**: fully sequential (1 request in flight at a time, `vllm:num_preemptions_total` stayed at 0 throughout) still reproduces the failure at the same rate (20-44% across several N=8-18 runs) as under concurrent load.
- **Not KV-cache size**: A/B test going from a 20G fixed KV cache pool (with heavy preemption under load) to a ~43GB auto-sized pool (zero preemption) left the failure rate unchanged (27.5% → 25%).
- **Not `--max-model-len`/token budget**: raised 65536 → 131072; a separate, distinct failure mode (genuine context overflow, `finish_reason='length'`) went away, but this premature-stop mode is unaffected (still ~20% after the change).
- **Not the vLLM version**: tried `0.26.1rc1.dev1046+gba07e4a48` (pinned via `pip install --no-deps` over the same base image, same torch 2.13.0/CUDA 13.0 — confirmed compatible, no start-up errors) on the H100 — failure rate was *higher* (45%), not lower.
- **Not `--gdn-prefill-backend`**: tried `triton` explicitly — same failure rate (20% over N=15) and same failure signature.
- **Not the LoRA adapter**: `sha256sum` of `adapter_model.safetensors` is byte-identical between the H100 and RTX 5090 hosts.
- **Not the prompt/template construction**: the reverse-derived `chat_template_kwargs.template` DSL we send matches, byte-for-byte (diffed programmatically), the template used to fine-tune the LoRA adapter in the first place.
- **Not the pipeline config**: identical JSON config (temperature, `pages_per_call`, all flags) on both hosts.

### The one variable we couldn't equalize: GPU architecture

| | H100 NVL (SM90) | RTX 5090 (SM120) |
|---|---|---|
| Failure rate, same 10-15 sequential requests, same documents | 20-45% (multiple runs) | **0/10** |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend` | default (`flashinfer`) and `triton` both tested, same result | default |

We traced flashinfer's own dispatch (`gdn_prefill.py`) and confirmed that on SM90 the default (non-CP) path already calls `chunk_gated_delta_rule_sm90` — i.e. we are *not* stuck on some older code path; this is the current SM90 kernel. We also found and briefly tried forcing vLLM's `--gdn-prefill-backend cutedsl`, but stopped immediately once we realized that vLLM's in-tree `cutedsl` GDN kernel (`vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/ops/gdn_chunk_cutedsl/`) is a separate, SM100-specific implementation (`Sm100ChunkUWKernel`) — forcing it onto SM90 risks silently wrong results rather than a real fix, so we didn't pursue that path further or measure accuracy under it.

### Question

Is there a known numerical-precision or algorithmic difference between the SM90 and SM100/SM120 `chunk_gated_delta_rule` kernels that could plausibly manifest as occasional incorrect/divergent output for the *same* input at `temperature=0`? Or any pointers on how to get a tighter repro (we can build a minimal standalone script calling `flashinfer.gdn_prefill.chunk_gated_delta_rule` directly with saved intermediate tensors, if that would help — we currently only have this at the full vLLM-serving level; the exact input documents are real government records and can't be shared, but the schema shape and reproduction steps can be shared/generalized).

Happy to run any diagnostic you'd suggest — we have both a Hopper and a Blackwell machine available for A/B testing.
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性

items.title: [Bug]: KV cache estimation probe's V2 host tier is bounded by neither `kv_cache_config.host_cache_size` nor the cgroup limit (can be OOM-killed at startup under a 16 GiB cgroup limit)
items.author: Smallfu666
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- x86_64; 1× NVIDIA H200 (143771 MiB), driver 580.65.06
- Container `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29` (TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc29), `trtllm-serve`
- Slurm job, cgroup v2 `memory.max` = 16 GiB, `swap.max` = 0

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [ ] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

1.3.0rc29 container, `trtllm-serve` Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct bf16, TP=1, 1× H200, under a cgroup v2 memory limit of 16 GiB with no swap (Slurm `--mem=16G`). Six interleaved starts per arm. Not every default-arm start is OOM-killed; see the last paragraph of actual behavior.

`cfg.yaml`:

```yaml
kv_cache_config:
  host_cache_size: 1073741824
```

Default arm (estimation on):

```bash
trtllm-serve serve <path/to/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct> --host 127.0.0.1 --port <port> --log_level info --no-telemetry --config cfg.yaml
```

Skip-estimation arm: the same command with `TRTLLM_SKIP_KV_CACHE_ESTIMATION=1` set in the environment.

### Expected behavior

KV cache estimation should not cause a startup OOM when the configured `host_cache_size` fits within the cgroup limit, however much memory the rest of the node has free: here the same launch with estimation skipped came up 6/6 with a 1.00 GiB host tier. One option is to bound the probe's auto tier by `host_cache_size` when one is set; another is for the auto path to use the cgroup-aware `effective_available_host_memory()` in `_torch/models/checkpoints/hf/rank_striped_read_ahead.py:183`.

### actual behavior

With KVCacheManagerV2, an explicit `kv_cache_config.host_cache_size` does not bound host memory during KV cache estimation. The estimation pass deliberately leaves the budget unset for its probe managers (`_drop_explicit_offload_tier_budgets`, added in https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/17850 so that probes stop pinning the full configured host tier), so the probe falls back to the auto host tier, which it sizes and pins as min(probe device quota, `SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` × page size / local ranks / 2, memlock × 0.8) (`kv_cache_manager_v2.py:425-432`, `:1656`). Neither the configured budget nor the cgroup memory limit enters that bound. `SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` is node-wide free memory (it equalled `MemFree` on our nodes), so that term tracks what the whole node has free, not the cgroup's headroom.

In this run TRT-LLM logged 141.6–156.3 GiB of available host memory, so the device-quota term was the binding one (17.37 GiB; the `SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` term was 71–78 GiB):

| arm | probe host tier (log) | result |
|---|---|---|
| default (estimation on) | 17.37 GiB | 6/6 OOM-killed during `profiling_kv_cache_allocation` (cgroup `oom_kill` +1 each) |
| `TRTLLM_SKIP_KV_CACHE_ESTIMATION=1` | no probe; host tier 1.00 GiB | 6/6 ready in 72–74 s, no OOM |

In a separate run with `host_cache_size` = 8 GiB under `--mem=48G`, all six starts came up, but every probe tier exceeded the budget: 11.3–17.4 GiB, with the `SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` term binding in two of them (11.32 and 16.84 GiB).

The OOM does not always happen. In a later job with the same container, model, config and 16 GiB cgroup, a default-arm start logged 14.22 GiB of available host memory, sized the probe tier at 7.11 GiB, and became ready in 88.9 s with no OOM kill. A start is OOM-killed when the auto tier does not fit in the cgroup's remaining headroom. To test this, we overrode only the `SC_AVPHYS_PAGES` value in the tier sizing, alternating starts in a separate job on one node: starts with a 17.00 GiB probe tier were OOM-killed 3/3, and starts with a 4.00 GiB tier came up 3/3. Here the tier is half of that value (node `MemFree`, as above) until it reaches the device quota, so whether a start is OOM-killed depends on node free memory at probe time.

### additional notes

main `fced9ff98` has the same code (`_util.py:2829-2833`, `kv_cache_manager_v2.py:425-432`, `:1656`; line numbers in this issue are from that commit); the runs were on rc29. Open #19650 changes when host-tier pages are committed; I have not tested it.

items.title: [Performance]: KVCacheManagerV2 host-tier copies on NVLink-C2C use SM kernels and leave decode persistently slower
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On a system with a coherent (NVLink-C2C) CPU-GPU link, `BatchedPageCopier` (cpp/tensorrt_llm/batch_manager/kv_cache_manager_v2/batchedPageCopy.cu) always moves GPU<->host-tier pages with its SM copy kernel:

    bool const kernelViable = mTopology.coherentLink || HostMem::shouldUseChunkedRegistration();

We see that once these kernels have read/written registered host memory a few times (i.e. after the first few evictions to the host tier), every decode step of the serving process becomes slower by a fixed amount and never recovers. Switching the same binary to the existing copy-engine path (`launchCopyEngine`, `cuMemcpyBatchAsync`) removes the slowdown, with byte-identical outputs.

### Setup

- Kimi K3 (NVFP4) with a speculative drafter, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes (TP8 attention), SM107 with an NVLink-C2C CPU link, CUDA graphs, PyTorch backend.
- KVCacheManagerV2, C++ backend (default), block reuse on, host tier on.
- Single client, requests issued sequentially: short probe requests (2K prompt) interleaved with quality prompts; we track the median decode step time of each probe from the iteration stats.

### Observation

The step time is flat until the GPU pools fill and pages start to be offloaded to the host tier, then jumps after ~5 offloads and stays there for the rest of the process lifetime, independent of context length:

| build (same binary for the last two rows) | 2K-prompt probe decode step, after vs before offloads start | 32K-prompt probe at end vs start of run |
|---|---|---|
| main (SM copy kernel on C2C) | +1.22 ms (+7.0%) | +1.22 ms |
| copy engine on C2C | -0.04 ms (noise) | -0.08 ms (noise) |
| copy engine build, kernel forced back on | +1.17 ms (+6.7%) | +1.2 ms |

- Outputs of all 99 requests are token-identical across the three runs.
- The trigger is the offload itself: with `kv_cache_config.host_cache_size: 0` (pools still fill, pages are dropped instead of offloaded) there is no step. It does not matter whether the offloaded pages are recurrent-state (KDA) pages or MLA KV blocks.
- A long-context run (393K-token prompt, KV blocks offloaded to host) shows the same effect on decode: about 1.3 ms/step (~4%) slower with the SM copy kernel than with the copy engine.

### What the profile shows

nsys before/after the step (40-step windows): no compute kernel gets slower, and no new kernels or copies appear. What grows is the idle gap between consecutive kernels inside the CUDA graph replay on (at least) one rank: from ~406 us to ~1335 us per step, spread over almost every kernel boundary (~0.2 us each). The other ranks absorb it as allreduce wait. The cost therefore scales with the number of kernels per step: a configuration with more kernels per step (non-fused verify path) lost 3.35 ms/step (+13.5%) in the same way. We have not identified the underlying mechanism; the fix does not depend on it.

### Cost of the copy engine

The only regression we measured: reloading a fully host-resident 393K-token prefix (~6K blocks, ~13 GB per rank) takes ~0.19 s (~9%) longer TTFT with the copy engine than with the kernel. #20311 also measured that on an idle GPU the copy engines are at or slightly above the kernel's bandwidth on NVLink-C2C, and that under SM load the kernel's copy latency grows 1.2-4x while the copy engines are unaffected.

### Proposal

Make the copy engine the default on coherent links too, keep an opt-in environment variable for the kernel, and keep the kernel when host registration is chunked (the copy-engine descriptors cannot cross a registration boundary). PR to follow.

cc @lowsfer (author of #18541) @tzulingk (#20311 lists this as the follow-up)

items.title: How to make Tensor static and only call kernel by pointer?
items.author: peterbjorgensen
items.body_excerpt:
I am trying to turn Python cute dsl kernels into TensorRT QDP Plugins. It restricts the kind of parameters the PTX can have to (input_pointers..., scalar_arguments..., output_pointers...). I have it working for a simple "add_one_kernel" (see the program listing below if interested).

Instead of writing the kernel with pointer arguments, I would like to write it with some StaticTensorPointer class that automatically turns the layout etc. into compile-time variables and only the pointer ends up as a PTX parameter. I guess it's possible with a custom `DynamicExpression`, but I find the documentation a bit vague on this. Any ideas how to achieve this?

Another question: Is it possible to get the shared memory needed for a compiled kernel? I need it for the kernel launch parameters of the kernel in the plugin.

```
import tensorrt as trt
import numpy as np
from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map
import tensorrt.plugin as trtp
import torch
import torch_tensorrt
import cutlass.cute as cute

from quack.cute_dsl_utils import torch2cute_dtype_map

trt_logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.VERBOSE)

STATIC_SHAPE = (16, 16)
STATIC_STRIDE = (1, 16)

@cute.kernel
def add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    STATIC_LAYOUT = cute.make_layout(shape=STATIC_SHAPE, stride=STATIC_STRIDE)
    tensor_x = cute.make_tensor(x, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tensor_y = cute.make_tensor(y, STATIC_LAYOUT)
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    bidx, _, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()
    idx = bidx * cute.arch.block_dim()[0] + tidx
    if idx < cute.size(tensor_x):
        tensor_y[idx] = tensor_x[idx] + 1

@cute.jit
def apply_add_one_kernel(x: cute.Pointer, y: cute.Pointer):
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE

    add_one_kernel(x, y).launch(
        grid = [num_blocks, 1, 1],
        block = [BLOCK_SIZE, 1, 1],
    )


@torch.library.custom_op("my::add_one", mutates_args=())  # type: ignore[misc]
def add_one(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    assert x.is_cuda
    y = torch.empty_like(x)
    input_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[x.dtype]
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, y.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, x.data_ptr(), cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")
    compiled(x_ptr, y_ptr)

    return y


@torch.library.register_fake("my::add_one")
def _(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return X

@trtp.register("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_desc(X: trtp.TensorDesc) -> tuple[trtp.TensorDesc]:
    # Output has the same shape and dtype as the input.
    return X.like()


@trtp.aot_impl("my::add_one")
def add_plugin_aot_impl(
    X: trtp.TensorDesc, outputs: tuple[trtp.TensorDesc], tactic: int
) -> tuple[
    str | bytes, str | bytes, trtp.KernelLaunchParams, trtp.SymExprs
]:
    # Choose the pointer type based on the input dtype.
    if X.dtype == trt.float32:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float32]
    elif X.dtype == trt.float16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.float16]
    elif X.dtype == trt.bfloat16:
        x_dtype = torch2cute_dtype_map[torch.bfloat16]
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unexpected dtype")
    input_dtype = x_dtype
    y_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 32, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)
    x_ptr = cute.runtime.make_ptr(input_dtype, 64, cute.AddressSpace.gmem, assumed_align=32)

    compiled_kernel = cute.compile(apply_add_one_kernel, x_ptr, y_ptr, options="--keep-ptx")


    # Build symbolic launch parameters.
    BLOCK_SIZE = 256
    num_blocks = (np.prod(STATIC_SHAPE).item() + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE
    launch_params = trtp.KernelLaunchParams()
    launch_params.grid_x = num_blocks  # number of thread blocks
    launch_params.block_x = BLOCK_SIZE  # threads per block
    launch_params.shared_mem = 0  # bytes of shared mem (I have no idea how to get this)

    # ``extra_args`` are scalar arguments appended to the kernel's argument list at
    # launch. Here ``n_elements`` is passed as a 32-bit symbolic integer so TRT
    # evaluates it from the actual tensor size at runtime.
    extra_args = trtp.SymIntExprs(0)

    kernel_name_ptx = list(compiled_kernel.kernel_info.keys())[0]
    return (
        kernel_name_ptx,  # kernel function name in PTX
        compiled_kernel.artifacts.PTX,  # PTX source — embedded in TRT engine
        launch_params,
        extra_args,
    )


torch_tensorrt.dynamo.conversion.plugins.generate_plugin_converter(
    "my::add_one",
    supports_dynamic_shapes=False,
    requires_output_allocator=False,
    use_aot_if_available=True,
)


class MyModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        res = torch.ops.my.add_one.default(X)
        return res


if __name__ == "__main__":


    my_model = MyModel().to("cuda").eval()
    m = torch.full(STATIC_SHAPE, 2, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    assert my_model(m)[0][0] == 3.0
    assert my_model(m)[1][1] == 3.0

    with torch_tensorrt.logging.debug():
        trt_inputs = [m]
        model_trt = torch_tensorrt.compile(
            my_model,
            inputs=trt_inputs,
            min_block_size=1,
        )
        print("Model compiled successfully!")
        print("Running inference with compiled model...")
        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in range(10):
                res = model_trt(m)
                assert torch.allclose(res, my_model(m)), "Results do not match!"

        program = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.trace(
            my_model,
            arg_inputs=trt_inputs,
        )
        engine_bytes: bytes = torch_tensorrt.dynamo.convert_exported_program_to_seri

items.title: [ROCm] PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True causes INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED (!handles_.at(i)) in HIPCachingAllocator.cpp during large-model inference
items.author: Vinnieassaulter
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## 🐛 Bug description

On ROCm 7.2.4 (WSL2, RDNA3), setting `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`  
makes the HIP caching allocator raise an internal assert during inference on a large  
fp8 diffusion model:

```
RuntimeError: !handles_.at(i) INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at "/pytorch/c10/hip/HIPCachingAllocator.cpp":446, please report a bug to PyTorch.
```

The assert fires from `ExpandableSegment::map()` — in the v2.12.0 source this is  
`TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT(!handles_.at(i))` at `c10/cuda/CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:445`  
(the shipped ROCm wheel labels the file `/pytorch/c10/hip/HIPCachingAllocator.cpp:446`).  
The assert means the allocator attempted to map a virtual-address slot whose  
bookkeeping entry was already occupied, i.e. the expandable-segment map/unmap state  
machine desynchronized.

**The failure is deterministic** (same seed → same assert, reproduced 6 times) and is  
**not memory pressure**: it fires with ~4–5 GiB of the 15.8 GiB still free. Removing  
the env var makes every attention backend work; with the env var set, whether it  
crashes depends only on the allocation pattern of the workload.

## Environment

- PyTorch: **2.12.1+rocm7.2** (official wheel from `download.pytorch.org/whl/rocm7.2`), triton-rocm 3.7.1
- ROCm runtime: **7.2.4** (`/opt/rocm-7.2.4`), `librocdxg` 1.2.2 (WSL GPU-access library), `HSA_ENABLE_DXG_DETECTION=1`
- OS: Windows 11 + **WSL2**, Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.6.x)
- GPU: AMD Radeon RX 7800 XT (RDNA3 / Navi 32; `rocminfo` reports **gfx1101** under ROCm 7.2), 16 GB VRAM
- Workload: ComfyUI 0.39.0, Krea 2 Turbo fp8_scaled (12.24 GiB fp8_e4m3fn weights via  
  comfy-kitchen emulated fp8 ops), 1024×1024 txt2img, 8 steps, text encoder on CPU

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install torch 2.12.1+rocm7.2 in WSL2 as above.
2. Load any large (~12 GiB) model whose sampling loop does many large alloc/free  
   cycles (repro used ComfyUI + Krea 2 Turbo fp8; see notes below).
3. `export PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`
4. Run a generation. → KSampler raises the INTERNAL ASSERT above.
5. Unset the env var, restart, run the identical workflow with the same seed → succeeds.

### Evidence matrix (all runs on the same stack, same workflow, same seed)

| `expandable_segments:True` | attention backend             | result                                                              |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ✅ set                      | default (sub-quadratic)       | **INTERNAL ASSERT**                                                 |
| ✅ set                      | `--use-sage-attention`        | **INTERNAL ASSERT** (4 runs)                                        |
| ✅ set                      | `--use-split-cross-attention` | OK (71 s) — allocation pattern happens to avoid the corrupting path |
| ❌ unset                    | default (sub-quadratic)       | OK (209 s)                                                          |
| ❌ unset                    | `--use-sage-attention`        | OK (44 s)                                                           |
| ❌ unset                    | `--use-split-cross-attention` | OK (40 s)                                                           |

Also tested with `--lowvram` / `--disable-smart-memory` / `--cache-none` /  
`--disable-pinned-memory` / `--disable-async-offload` in all combinations: the assert  
fires regardless, confirming it is not an offloading/OOM interaction.

Side observation: in some earlier runs torch emitted  
`UserWarning: expandable_segments not supported on this platform` **while expandable  
segments were demonstrably active** (the assert itself fired inside  
`ExpandableSegment::map()`), so the ROCm support-detection around this feature looks  
inconsistent as well.

## Expected behavior

Either expandable segments work on ROCm/WSL, or the setting is rejected cleanly.  
It must never corrupt segment bookkeeping and surface as an internal assert  
mid-inference.

## Notes for maintainers

- The corrupting path needs a workload with many large (multi-GiB) alloc/free cycles;  
  small benchmarks won't hit it. I could not reduce it to a standalone snippet so far.  
  If it helps, I can (a) capture `CUDA_ALLOC_CONF` debug output, (b) run with  
  `TORCH_SHOW_CPP_STACKTRACES=1` for a C++ stack, or (c) test specific ROCm/WSL  
  combinations (`hipMemAddressReserve` / `hipMemCreate` / `hipMemMap` availability on  
  WSL via librocdxg may be relevant).
- On torch 2.9.1+rocm6.4 with the same env var, the same workload hit a clean  
  `torch.OutOfMemoryError` instead of the assert (the assert appears to be a  
  regression in the 2.12.1 ROCm build, though I cannot rule out the 6.4 build  
  silently falling back to the standard allocator).
- WSL2 ROCm uses `librocdxg` instead of the bare-metal KFD stack; VMM primitives  
  (`hipMemAddressReserve` etc.) may behave differently there — the  
  `ExpandableSegment` constructor does call `hipMemAddressReserve` under `USE_ROCM`.

### Versions

Is debug build: False
CUDA used to build PyTorch: N/A
ROCm SDK used to build PyTorch: 7.2.1

Something like a loop that allocates/frees large ROCm tensors of varying sizes (to mimic the sampling loop's alloc/free pattern) with `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True` set should be enough to trigger the same bookkeeping desync if the allocation pattern is the real trigger.

comments.author: davidk-croesus
comments.body:
Another data point, from **bare-metal Linux** (not WSL). Here `expandable_segments:True` never hit the assert; instead it caused **silent memory corruption and GPU page faults**.

- GPU: RX 7900 XT (gfx1100), Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0, torch 2.14.1+rocm7.2 (HIP 7.2.53211)
- Workload: ComfyUI 0.39/0.40, LTX-2.5 22B int8 image-to-video (~21 GB of weights streamed through 20 GB VRAM, 32 GB RAM), `--disable-pinned-memory --disable-async-offload --disable-dynamic-vram --cache-none`

With `PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`:
- **The same seed/inputs gave a different video every run** (PSNR between runs 16-23 dB).
- The first prompt after start came out washed-out/colour-shifted. Sometimes the audio was NaN, and the encoder rejected it.
- Repeatedly, `hipErrorIllegalAddress` at the start of the *next* prompt (`module.to()` moving VAE weights to the GPU). dmesg showed `amdgpu ... [gfxhub] page fault` at a 2 MiB-aligned address that was **no longer mapped in the process**. That looks like a stale/unmapped expandable-segment page.
- `AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL=3 AMD_SERIALIZE_COPY=3` did not help, so it's not a stream race.

Removing `expandable_segments` (the only change):
- 0 page faults.
- The same seed is now **bit-identical** across prompts and across process restarts (5/5 runs, framemd5 identical).
- Also slightly faster.

So on bare-metal gfx1100 the desync seems to surface as silent corruption rather than the assert. Happy to test #200774 if a wheel becomes available.

items.title: CuTeDSL: width-only f-string format spec emits a malformed device printf format (%8) and silently drops the value
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`FormattedValue.to_str` in `cutlass/base_dsl/ast_helpers.py` (~lines 731-737) converts a non-empty single-token `format_spec` into a printf conversion by emitting `"%{format_spec[0]}"`. That is only valid when the spec actually ends in a conversion character. A width-only spec such as `{x:8}` is legal Python but produces the literal format `%8`, which consumes no argument and prints garbage.

Unit-level repro (against `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.0`):

```python
from cutlass.base_dsl.ast_helpers import FormattedValue
import cutlass

fv = FormattedValue(value=cutlass.Int32(7), conversion=-1, format_spec=["8"])
print(fv.to_str()[0])    # prints: %8
fv = FormattedValue(value=cutlass.Int32(7), conversion=-1, format_spec=[".2f"])
print(fv.to_str()[0])    # prints: %.2f  (fine)
```

End-to-end, `cute.printf(f"[{x:8}]")` with a dynamic `x` makes the device print `[     8]`-style text where the value never appears: the kernel receives format string `[%8]` plus an unconsumed vararg. No diagnostic is raised.

### Suggested fix

Validate that the spec terminates in a known conversion character. Either raise `DiagId.UNSUP_FSTRING_FORMAT` for specs without one, or map a bare numeric spec to a sensible default conversion per the value's dtype (e.g. append `d` for integer types, `f`/`g` for float types) so `{x:8}` keeps its Python meaning.

items.title: CuTeDSL: print_warning_once re-warns when more than one distinct message is used (lru_cache maxsize=1)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`BaseDSL.print_warning_once` (`cutlass/base_dsl/dsl.py` ~line 813) caches on `(self, message)` with `@lru_cache(maxsize=1)`:

```python
@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def print_warning_once(self, message: str) -> None:
```

With more than one distinct message, every new message evicts the previous cache entry, so alternating messages re-warn forever instead of once each.

Repro against `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.7.0`:

```python
import warnings
from cutlass.base_dsl.dsl import BaseDSL

dsl = object.__new__(BaseDSL)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as rec:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    for msg in ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A"]:
        dsl.print_warning_once(msg)
print(len(rec))   # 5 warnings emitted; correct behavior is 2 (one per unique message)
```

Actual output: `5`.

### Suggested fix

Keep an instance-level `set` of already-emitted messages, or move the cache to a module-level function keyed on the message alone with unbounded size.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL: FloatNV8E5M3FNU.to(Float32) returns inf for the entire top exponent binade (codes 248-254)
items.author: tdophung
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
Converting a `FloatNV8E5M3FNU` (UE5M3) value to `Float32` returns `inf` for
every code in the top exponent field (`E=31`, codes `248`–`254`), instead of
the finite values `65536.0` … `114688.0`.

UE5M3 is a *finite-only* format: unsigned, 5-bit exponent (bias 15), 3-bit
mantissa, **no infinity encoding**, `0xFF` is the only NaN, and `0xFE` is the
maximum finite value `114688.0`. The decode appears to apply IEEE
`inf`/`NaN` semantics to the top exponent field, which is correct for
`Float8E5M2` but not for this format.

Two things narrow it down:

1. **Encoding is unaffected**, so the round trip is asymmetric —
   `114688.0` → code `254` (correct) → `inf` (wrong).
2. **`Float8E4M3FN` decodes correctly.** That format has the same shape of
   problem — finite-only, NaN living in the top exponent field — and all 256
   of its codes decode exactly. So this looks like an inconsistency in the
   UE5M3 path rather than a deliberate convention.

Sweeping all 256 codes of every 8-bit narrow float the DSL exposes:

| Type | Mismatching codes / 256 |
|---|---|
| **`FloatNV8E5M3FNU`** | **7** (codes 248–254) |
| `Float8E4M3FN` | 0 |
| `Float8E5M2` | 0 (`E=31` genuinely *is* inf/NaN there) |
| `Float8E8M0FNU` | 0 |

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
1. Save the script below.
2. Run `python repro.py` on any supported GPU.
3. Observe that codes 248–254 decode to `inf`, while the analogous
   `Float8E4M3FN` codes decode exactly.

```python
import torch
import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack


@cute.kernel
def decode_kernel(gCodes: cute.Tensor, gUE5M3: cute.Tensor, gE4M3: cute.Tensor):
    t, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    if t < 256:
        gUE5M3[t] = gCodes[t].bitcast(cutlass.FloatNV8E5M3FNU).to(cutlass.Float32)
        gE4M3[t] = gCodes[t].bitcast(cutlass.Float8E4M3FN).to(cutlass.Float32)


@cute.jit
def run(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, c: cute.Tensor):
    decode_kernel(a, b, c).launch(grid=[1, 1, 1], block=[256, 1, 1])


# UE5M3: bias 15, 3 mantissa bits, no inf, 0xFF is the only NaN
def expected(code):
    E, M = code >> 3, code & 7
    return 2.0**-14 * (M / 8) if E == 0 else 2.0 ** (E - 15) * (1 + M / 8)


codes = torch.arange(256, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
ue5m3 = torch.zeros(256, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
e4m3 = torch.zeros(256, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
run(from_dlpack(codes), from_dlpack(ue5m3), from_dlpack(e4m3))
torch.cuda.synchronize()

print(f"{'code':>6} {'expected':>12} {'got':>8}")
for c in range(248, 255):
    print(f"{c:>6} {expected(c):>12.1f} {float(ue5m3[c]):>8}")

print("\nnon-finite codes outside the NaN encoding:")
print("  FloatNV8E5M3FNU ->", [c for c in range(255) if not torch.isfinite(ue5m3[c])])
print("  Float8E4M3FN    ->",
      [c for c in range(256) if (c & 0x7F) != 0x7F and not torch.isfinite(e4m3[c])])
```

**Observed error:**

```
  code     expected      got
   248      65536.0      inf
   249      73728.0      inf
   250      81920.0      inf
   251      90112.0      inf
   252      98304.0      inf
   253     106496.0      inf
   254     114688.0      inf

non-finite codes outside the NaN encoding:
  FloatNV8E5M3FNU -> [248, 249, 250, 251, 252, 253, 254]
  Float8E4M3FN    -> []
```

**Expected behavior**
Codes 248–254 should decode to the finite values 65536.0, 73728.0, 81920.0,
90112.0, 98304.0, 106496.0 and 114688.0 respectively. Only `0xFF` should
produce NaN, and no UE5M3 code should ever produce an infinity.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
- GPU: Blackwell+, CUDA 13.4
- CUDA: 13.4 (V13.4.59)
- `nvidia-cutlass-dsl`: 4.8.0.dev0
- Python: 3.12.3
- PyTorch: 2.14.0a0
- OS: Linux 6.17.0 aarch64

**Additional context**
Workaround, in case it helps anyone else — decode by explicit bit
construction instead of `.to()`:

```python
def decode_ue5m3(code):          # code: Uint8
    c = code.to(cutlass.Uint32)
    E = c >> cutlass.Uint32(3)
    M = c & cutlass.Uint32(7)
    # normal: 2^(E-15) * (1 + M/8); fp32 exponent field is (E-15)+127
    bits = ((E + cutlass.Uint32(112)) << cutlass.Uint32(23)) | (M << cutlass.Uint32(20))
    normal = bits.bitcast(cutlass.Float32)
    sub = M.to(cutlass.Float32) * cutlass.Float32(2.0**-17)   # E == 0
    is_norm = (E != cutlass.Uint32(0)).to(cutlass.Float32)
    return normal * is_norm + sub * (cutlass.Float32(1.0) - is_norm)
```

We have not checked whether the 4-bit and 6-bit finite-only types
(`Float4E2M1FN`, `Float6E2M3FN`, `Float6E3M2FN`) have the same issue in their
top binade; they are harder to sweep because they cannot be bitcast from a
`Uint8` directly. Might be worth checking alongside a fix.

items.title: [BUG] `cute.ceil_div` throws internal error with int64 input
items.author: kainzhong
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
`cute.ceil_div` doesn't work with `cutlass.Int64`

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
```python
from cutlass import cute, Int32, Int64

def run(name, fn, a, b):
    try:
        cute.compile(fn, a, b)
        print(f"{name:45s} OK")
    except Exception as e:
        lines = [l for l in str(e).splitlines() if l.strip()]
        print(f"{name:45s} FAIL: " + next((l for l in lines if "mismatch" in l or "INTERNAL" in l), lines[0])[:110])

@cute.jit
def only_cdiv_64(a: Int64, b: Int64):
    cute.ceil_div(a, b)                      # result unused, nothing else in the function

@cute.jit
def only_cdiv_32(a: Int64, b: Int32):
    cute.ceil_div(a, b)

@cute.jit
def cdiv_then_add_64(a: Int64, b: Int64):
    q = cute.ceil_div(a, b)
    _ = q + Int64(1)                         # plain arithmetic on the result

run("ceil_div(Int64, Int64) only, unused", only_cdiv_64, Int64(100), Int64(7))
run("ceil_div(Int64, Int32) only, unused", only_cdiv_32, Int64(100), Int32(7))
run("ceil_div(Int64, Int64) + arithmetic", cdiv_then_add_64, Int64(100), Int64(7))
```

Gives:
```
ceil_div(Int64, Int64) only, unused           FAIL: error[INTERNAL]: The compiler could not build valid IR for this code.
ceil_div(Int64, Int32) only, unused           OK
ceil_div(Int64, Int64) + arithmetic           FAIL: error[INTERNAL]: The compiler could not build valid IR for this code.
```

**Expected behavior**
Either support int64 or give a better error message (I'm not sure if it's intended for cdiv to not support int64)

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
`nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.8.0`

items.title: Collective operations do not work with `torch.BoolTensor`s on `gloo` and raise `Invalid scalar type`
items.author: sadra-barikbin
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Hi, collective operations do not work with `torch.BoolTensor`s on backend `gloo`. Actually `GENERATE_ALL_TYPES` macro in `torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupGloo.cpp` seems to raise `RuntimeError: Invalid scalar type`.

To reproduce:
```python
import torch.distributed as dist

tensor = torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
    gather_list = [torch.empty((5,),dtype=torch.bool) for _ in range(dist.get_world_size())]
else:
    gather_list = None
dist.gather(tensor, gather_list)
```
This is also the case for `all_gather`, `reduce`, `all_reduce` and `broadcast`. Changing `dtype=torch.bool` to `dtype=torch.uint8` resolves the error, while `torch.bool == torch.uint8` evaluates to `True`.

items.title: [Core][LLM][Serve] Finalize Pydantic v2 migration by removing remaining v1 compatibility paths
items.author: Bye-legumes
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

## Summary

  We have already:
  - dropped support for `pydantic==1.*`
  - removed `python/ray/_common/pydantic_compat.py`
  - migrated the remaining core/dashboard/train callsites away from `dict()`, `json()`, and `parse_obj()`

  This follow-up tracks the remaining work needed to fully remove residual Pydantic v1 compatibility paths and finish migrating Ray to Pydantic v2-native
  APIs.

  ## Remaining work

  ### 1. Remove remaining v1 compatibility bridges

  We still keep a serializer bridge for `pydantic.v1.fields.ModelField` in:

  - `python/ray/util/serialization_addons.py`

  This should be evaluated and removed if FastAPI no longer requires it under Pydantic v2. If it must remain temporarily, it should be isolated as an explicit FastAPI compatibility bridge rather than general Pydantic compatibility support.

  ### 2. Migrate remaining v1-style validators/config patterns to v2-native APIs

  Replace:
  - `@root_validator(...)` -> `@model_validator(...)`
  - `class Config:` -> `model_config = ConfigDict(...)`

  Files currently in scope:
  - `python/ray/llm/_internal/batch/processor/base.py`
  - `python/ray/llm/_internal/batch/processor/sglang_engine_proc.py`
  - `python/ray/llm/_internal/batch/stages/base.py`
  - `python/ray/llm/_internal/batch/stages/sglang_engine_stage.py`
  - `python/ray/llm/_internal/batch/stages/vllm_engine_stage.py`

  ### 3. Remove remaining v1/v2 dual-path fallbacks

  Examples:
  - `__fields__` fallback logic in `python/ray/llm/_internal/serve/config_generator/utils/overrides.py`

  Any remaining v1/v2 branching or comments referring to dual support should be cleaned up as part of this work.

  ### 4. Clean up residual legacy test usage

  Migrate remaining test-only Pydantic v1-style APIs such as:
  - `parse_obj()`
  - `parse_raw()`
  - `dict()`
  - `json()`

  where appropriate.

  ## Goal

  After this issue is complete:
  - Ray should not rely on `pydantic.v1` except for any explicitly documented temporary upstream compatibility bridge
  - remaining code should use Pydantic v2-native APIs consistently
  - residual v1/v2 fallback logic should be removed

items.title: [Serve] Support passing an ordered list of model_ids to controllers
items.author: daturkel
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`RequestMetadata.multiplexed_model_id` (and the corresponding `DeploymentHandle.options(multiplexed_model_id=...)` ) only supports a single model ID per request. For use cases where several model IDs are acceptable for a given request — and the caller wants to route to whichever is already resident, rather than one fixed ID — there's currently no way to express that elegantly. (A workaround is a comma-separated "model_id" that a custom router parses internally.)

Proposal is something like:

```
handle.options(multiplexed_model_id=["model-v3", "model-v2", "model-v1"]).remote(...)
```

or a distinct field to avoid changing multiplexed_model_id's existing type/semantics:

```
handle.options(candidate_multiplexed_model_ids=["model-v3", "model-v2", "model-v1"]).remote(...)
```

Selection/ranking logic would remain entirely up to the custom RequestRouter.

### Use case

We have a Ray Serve app where each request is associated with a family of interchangeable models (e.g. different training-run versions of the same logical model, where any recent-enough version is acceptable to the caller). We'd like a custom RequestRouter to route to a replica that already has one of these acceptable models loaded — preferring, say, the newest resident one — rather than being forced to pick one exact model ID upfront and accept a cold load if that specific replica-model pairing isn't warm.

items.title: [Data] Split ORC DataSourceV2 read tasks by stripe
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

The ORC DataSourceV2 path proposed in [#66524](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66524) treats each ORC file as an indivisible read unit. A single large file containing multiple stripes therefore cannot be read by multiple Ray tasks. Add stripe-level read units so separate tasks can read disjoint stripes from the same file.

Use stripe metadata to identify read units without decoding their rows during planning, and read only the stripes assigned to each task. Keep the existing whole-file path when the optional metadata backend is unavailable. Preserve row values, schema alignment, projection, filters, limits, path and partition validation, pickled-object safety, retries, and the existing `preserve_order` behavior. Verify that multiple tasks read different stripes without missing or duplicating rows, and measure metadata cost and actual stripe reads.

Stripe sizes used for task grouping are encoded-byte weights, not estimates of peak decoded memory. Reading a stripe may materialize the whole stripe even when the output batch size is smaller. This issue provides the read-unit foundation needed for stripe-level pruning in [#66995](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/66995); statistics-based pruning remains a separate change.

### Use case

When an ORC dataset contains only a few large multi-stripe files, whole-file read units limit parallelism to the file count and can leave available Ray workers idle. Users want those files to be read by multiple tasks while retaining the same results and read semantics.

items.title: [Data] Generated checkpoint ID silently overwrites the synthesized path column on a name collision
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

On the Parquet DataSourceV2 path, `include_paths=True` and `CheckpointConfig(generated_id_column="path")` both request a synthesized column named `path`. When the input file contains only an `id` column, the read succeeds without rejecting the name collision, but the output `path` column contains generated row-ID structs instead of source file path strings.

**Actual behavior:** `path` has an Arrow struct type, and its Python row values are dictionaries containing `path_prefix`, `file_name`, `fragment`, `num_fragments`, `num_rows`, and `row_id`. This silently changes the documented meaning and type of the column produced by `include_paths=True`.

**Expected behavior:** Reject the conflicting configuration with a clear error before data execution rather than silently choosing one of the two synthesized columns. When the names differ, the source path and generated ID should remain separate columns.

Using `generated_id_column="generated_id"` is a working control: the output contains `path: string` and a separate `generated_id` struct column.

This reproduces on merged `master` code using the documented boolean `include_paths=True`; no custom path-column name or unmerged PR is needed. Generated-ID functionality was added in [#66732](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/66732). This concerns synthesized-column name collisions and is distinct from the expression-filtering problem in [#66916](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/66916).

The current [extra synthesized-column collision check](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/7e2ef925eb26c43eddec91bb52c6635566c244b7/python/ray/data/_internal/datasource_v2/formats/parquet/parquet_datasource_v2.py#L349) checks the file/partition schema before built-in synthesized columns are added. The [reader then replaces any previously produced same-named column](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/7e2ef925eb26c43eddec91bb52c6635566c244b7/python/ray/data/_internal/datasource_v2/common/file_reader.py#L287) while processing synthesized columns.

This report isolates read-time column synthesis. It does not claim a checkpoint-writing or recovery failure.

### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: `3.0.0.dev0`.
- Ray Data Python source: merged `master` commit [`7e2ef925eb26c43eddec91bb52c6635566c244b7`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/commit/7e2ef925eb26c43eddec91bb52c6635566c244b7), verified in the driver and actual read workers.
- Python: `3.13.7`.
- OS: macOS `27.0.1`, arm64.
- PyArrow: `25.0.1`; pandas: `3.0.6`; NumPy: `2.5.3`.

The native Ray wheel was reused and was not rebuilt from the source revision above. The reproduction used real local Parquet files and Ray workers, without mocking the reader or synthesized columns.

### Reproduction script

Run in a Ray environment containing the generated-ID functionality described above. The input has three rows, two row groups, and no physical `path` column.

```python
import os
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

os.environ["RAY_DATA_PARQUET_FOOTER_NUM_ACTORS"] = "1"

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from pyarrow.fs import LocalFileSystem
import ray
from ray.data import DataContext
from ray.data.checkpoint import CheckpointConfig

ray.init(address="local", num_cpus=2, include_dashboard=False)
ctx = DataContext.get_current()
previous_checkpoint = ctx.checkpoint_config
previous_v2 = ctx.use_datasource_v2
try:
    with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
        file = Path(directory) / "data.parquet"
        pq.write_table(pa.table({"id": [1, 2, 3]}), file, row_group_size=2)
        ctx.use_datasource_v2 = True
        ctx.checkpoint_config = CheckpointConfig(
            generated_id_column="path",
            checkpoint_path=str(Path(directory) / "checkpoint"),
            override_filesystem=LocalFileSystem(),
        )
        ds = ray.data.read_parquet(
            str(file), include_paths=True, partitioning=None,
            override_num_blocks=1,
        )
        rows = ds.take_all()
        print("path Arrow type:", ds.schema().base_schema.field("path").type)
        print("path Python type:", type(rows[0]["path"]).__name__)
        print("path value:", rows[0]["path"])
finally:
    ctx.checkpoint_config = previous_checkpoint
    ctx.use_datasource_v2 = previous_v2
    ray.shutdown()
```

The observed `path` Arrow type is a struct, and the Python type is `dict`. Changing only `generated_id_column="path"` to `generated_id_column="generated_id"` preserves the source path as a string and adds the generated ID separately.

items.title: [Code] Remove excessive logs when "model.aibrix.ai/port" is not available by default and improve efficiency
items.author: zhangjyr
items.body_excerpt:
Currently, the gateway outputs excessive warning logs when the "model.aibrix.ai/port" label is not available. The log is output by the following code in pkg/util/pod.go.

```
func GetModelPortForPod(requestID string, pod *v1.Pod) int64 {
	value, ok := pod.Labels[modelPortIdentifier]
	if !ok {
		klog.Warningf("requestID: %v, pod: %v is missing port identifier label: %v, hence default to port: %v",
			requestID, pod.Name, modelPortIdentifier, defaultPodMetricPort)
		return defaultPodMetricPort
	}

	modelPort, err := strconv.ParseInt(value, 10, 32)
	if err != nil {
		klog.Warningf("requestID: %v, pod: %v has incorrect value: %v for port identifier label: %v, hence default to port: %v",
			requestID, pod.Name, value, modelPortIdentifier, defaultPodMetricPort)
		modelPort = defaultPodMetricPort
	}
	return modelPort
}
```

This code leads to two problems:
1. Excessive warning logs if the label is missing.
2. Inefficiency if the label is available because the string will be parsed on a per-request basis.

items.title: [Bug] token_load charges multimodal requests by their encoded body size, not their prompt tokens
items.author: hengguangcui11-cyber
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`token_load` charges every request its estimated prompt length: the prefill charge (`chargeTokenLoad`) and the decode charge (`chargeDecodeTokenLoad`) in `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/router/router.go` both use

```go
func EstimatePromptTokens(reqBody []byte) int {
	return len(reqBody) / bytesPerTokenEstimate // 4
}
```

For a multimodal chat request that estimate has nothing to do with the prompt the engine sees:

- **Inline media** (`data:` URLs) are counted as base64 text, so the charge follows the image's file size.
- **Media referenced by URL** add only the URL's length, so the image's tokens are not charged at all.

The number of tokens an image takes depends on its resolution, not on how large its file is.

I measured it against vLLM v0.31.0 (CPU build) serving Qwen/Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct. Each request is a chat completion with one JPEG and one sentence of text and `max_tokens: 1`. The table compares the gateway's estimate with the engine's `usage.prompt_tokens`. "Flat" is a single-color image and "noise" a random one, so the two have the same resolution and very different file sizes. Real photos fall in between.

| image | sent as | body bytes | `EstimatePromptTokens` | vLLM `prompt_tokens` | estimate / actual |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (text only) | — | 156 | 39 | 26 | 1.5 |
| 448×448 flat | base64 | 5,272 | 1,318 | 284 | 4.6 |
| 448×448 noise | base64 | 241,056 | 60,264 | 284 | 212 |
| 896×896 flat | base64 | 17,816 | 4,454 | 1,052 | 4.2 |
| 896×896 noise | base64 | 961,404 | 240,351 | 1,052 | 228 |
| 1344×1344 flat | base64 | 38,724 | 9,681 | 2,332 | 4.2 |
| 1344×1344 noise | base64 | 2,160,756 | 540,189 | 2,332 | 232 |
| 896×896 (either) | URL | 271–272 | 67–68 | 1,052 | 0.06 |
| 1344×1344 (either) | URL | 273–274 | 68 | 2,332 | 0.03 |

The same image costs the same 1,052 tokens whether its file is 13 KB or 720 KB, while the charge ranges from 67 to 240,351.

What this does to routing:

- A request with an inline image is charged many times its real prompt on its prefill pod (the active charge until prefill returns, the resident-KV charge until the request completes) and on its decode pod (until the request completes). One request can make a decode pod look as full as hundreds of chat requests, so `token_load` steers traffic away from it for the request's whole lifetime.
- Requests with media URLs are charged almost nothing, so pods serving them look emptier than they are.
- With `AIBRIX_DECODE_TOKEN_LOAD_CAPACITY_AWARE` (#3027) the decode charge is compared with the pod's real KV capacity, so an overcharge can exceed the pod's whole capacity. In the table, 540,189 is about 66 times the 8,192-token context of the test server.

Multimodal requests are becoming a main path for PD routing with #2962 / #3069.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Serve a vision-language model with vLLM (I used `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct` v0.31.0).
2. Send a `/v1/chat/completions` request with an `image_url` content part, once as a `data:image/jpeg;base64,...` URL and once as an `http(s)` URL.
3. Compare `len(body) / 4` with `usage.prompt_tokens` in the response.

Through the gateway, the charges show up in the `pd_router token_load charge` / `pd_router token_load decode charge` V(4) logs and in the `token_load` scores.

### Expected behavior

A multimodal request is charged roughly its real prompt length on both pods. Two parts, either of which helps on its own:

1. **Estimate without the media payload.** Leave media content parts out of the byte count, and add a per-item estimate for each image, audio or video part instead (for example a configurable default).
2. **Correct the charges with the engine's count.** For vLLM's synchronous prefill the gateway already reads the prefill response for the KV transfer parameters, and that response carries `usage.prompt_tokens`, which includes the image tokens (as measured above). Replacing the charges that outlive the prefill call (the decode charge and the prefill pod's resident-KV charge) with that count makes them exact on that path. Engines and modes where the prefill response isn't available before decode keep the estimate from (1).

I'd like to work on this, starting with (2) and the media-aware estimate from (1).

### Environment

AIBrix main at 99325e77. vLLM v0.31.0 built for CPU on macOS (Apple Silicon), Qwen/Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, `--max-model-len 8192`, `--mm-processor-kwargs '{"max_pixels": 1806336}'` (1344×1344, so no test image was resized by the cap).

items.title: [Bug] Metrics from a vLLM data-parallel pod only reflect one engine
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
When a pod runs vLLM with `--data-parallel-size N` behind a single API server, `/metrics` reports each metric once per engine, with an `engine="<rank>"` label. AIBrix reads these as if the pod had one engine, and the two places that read them don't even pick the same one:

- The autoscaler (`FetchTypedMetric`) uses the first series, which is engine 0.
- The gateway cache (`FetchAllTypedMetrics`) keeps whichever gauge series comes last.

For a pod with four engines, main returns:

| Metric | Whole pod | Autoscaler | Gateway cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| `num_requests_waiting` | 20 | 5 | 5 |
| `num_requests_running` | 32 | 10 | 2 |
| `kv_cache_usage_perc` | 0.625 (mean) | 0.9 | 0.1 |

A KPA/APA scaling on waiting requests only sees a quarter of the queue, and the routers can send more traffic to a busy pod just because its last engine happens to be idle.

Merging the engine series right after `/metrics` is parsed would let both paths see the whole pod. I'll open a PR for it.

items.title: DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit
items.author: kahyunnam
items.body_excerpt:
# FlashInfer — DGX Spark (SM121) Current Support Audit

**Date:** 2026-04-24
**Scope:** Audit of SM121 (compute capability 12.1, DGX Spark) support across FlashInfer ops, APIs, backends, and testing.
**Goal:** Improve Spark usability on FlashInfer by identifying existing gaps.

**Note: skip to "15. Consolidated Action Items" for TLDR.**

---

## Architecture Context

| Gencode | Target | CUDA Requirement |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `compute_120a` / `sm_120a` | RTX 5090 (SM120) | CUDA 12.8 |
| `compute_120f` / `sm_120f` | SM12x family (120 + 121) | CUDA 12.9 |
| `compute_121a` / `sm_121a` | DGX Spark (SM121) | CUDA 12.9 |

### SM120 vs SM121: Implications for FlashInfer

Per the [CUDA 13.2 Programming Guide — Compute Capabilities](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html) (Tables 29–33), SM120 and SM121 share a single "12.x" spec column: identical shared memory (99 KB/block, 100 KB/SM), warps (48/SM), registers (64K/SM), tensor core data types (TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8), TMA, and cluster support. [Table 28](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.2.0/cuda-programming-guide/05-appendices/compute-capabilities.html#compute-capabilities-family-specific-compatibility) confirms `compute_120f` is compatible with **both** CC 12.0 and 12.1. The chip-level differences (SM121 = aarch64 host, unified LPDDR5x, 84 SMs vs SM120's x86_64, discrete GDDR7, up to 170 SMs) do not affect kernel correctness — only SM-count-based heuristics and host toolchain.

### `f` vs `a` compilation targets: performance implications

Per the [PTX ISA 9.3](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html) (§9.7.15.5.14 for dense `mma`, §9.7.15.6.3 for sparse `mma.sp`), `120f` (family) is a subset of `120a`/`121a` (arch-specific). Most SM12x features — including **dense** NVFP4/MXFP4 block-scaled MMA — are family-specific and available via `120f` from PTX ISA 8.8. The arch-specific restriction (requiring `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`) applies **only to sparse MMA** (`mma.sp`) with `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4`:

| PTX Feature | `compute_120` (baseline) | `compute_120f` (family) | `compute_120a` / `compute_121a` (arch) |
|-------------|--------------------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| FP4/FP6/FP8 conversions (`cvt`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| FP4/FP6 MMA, block-scaled MMA (`.kind::mxf8f6f4`) | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Dense** NVFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Dense** MXFP4 MMA (`.kind::mxf4`) | No | **Yes** (PTX ISA ≥ 8.8) | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** NVFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4nvf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Sparse** MXFP4 MMA (`mma.sp` `.kind::mxf4`) | No | **No** | **Yes** |

FlashInfer's b12x GEMM kernel (`dense_blockscaled_gemm_sm120_b12x.py`) uses `cute.nvgpu.warp.MmaMXF4NVF4Op` — a **dense** block-scaled MMA atom. This means `sm_120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 dense MMA instructions. Only **sparse** NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA (not currently used in FlashInfer) requires `sm_120a`/`sm_121a`.

> **Correction (2026-06-12):** An earlier version of this table stated that ALL `.kind::mxf4nvf4`/`.kind::mxf4` MMA was arch-specific-only. Per [Harry-Chen's feedback](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/3170#issuecomment-4677810517) and PTX ISA §9.7.15.5.14 vs §9.7.15.6.3, the restriction is limited to the sparse (`mma.sp`) variant.

### Wheel build arch targets

The release wheel CI (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the following SM12x targets:

| CUDA Version | SM12x target in `FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST` |
|---|---|
| < 12.9 | `12.0a` (SM120 arch-specific; no SM121 support) |
| >= 12.9, < 13.0 | `12.0f` (family; covers SM120 + SM121; includes dense NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA) |
| >= 13.0 | `12.0f` (same) |

**No `121a` target is included in any wheel build.** However, since FlashInfer's FP4 kernels use **dense** block-scaled MMA (`MmaMXF4NVF4Op`, not sparse), the `120f` wheels already emit native NVFP4/MXFP4 MMA instructions. The `121a` target would only be needed for future sparse MMA kernels. JIT compilation on SM121 still produces `121a` cubins for forward-compatibility.

### What this means for FlashInfer

- **Any kernel that runs on SM120 is architecturally compatible with SM121.** Hardcoded `sm_version == "sm_120"` or `minor == 0` checks in backend dispatch are over-restricting without justification.
- **Separate cubins matter for JIT but not for wheels.** `CompilationContext` correctly emits `sm_121a` for JIT on SM121. Since FlashInfer uses only dense block-scaled MMA (available on `120f`), the wheels do not lose FP4 GEMM performance. The `121a` JIT path provides forward-compatibility for future sparse MMA use.
- **SMEM capacity maps, tile configs, and MMA atoms are identical.** Code using `get_smem_capacity_in_bytes("sm_120")` returns the correct value for SM121 too — the only risk is `KeyError` if a map expects an `"sm_121"` key and doesn't have one.

### Key utility functions

| Function (`utils.py`) | Behavior for SM121 |
|------------------------|--------------------|
| `is_sm12x_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm121a_supported` | True (CUDA ≥ 12.9) |
| `is_sm120a_supported` | **False** (12.0 only) |
| `device_support_pdl` | True (`major >= 9`) |
| `determine_attention_backend` | Returns `fa2` (fa3 is SM90-only) |
| `determine_gemm_backend` | Returns `sm80` (no SM12x branch) |

---

## 1. Attention

### 1.1 Decode (batch paged KV)

| Backend | CC Gate | SM121 Status | Notes |
|---------|---------|--------------|-------|
| **fa2** | Generic | **Supported** | Default via `determine_attention_backend` for non-FP8 tensor-core decode |
| **fa3** | SM90 only | **Not available** | `determine_attention_backend` returns fa3 only on SM90 |
| **xqa** | `major in {9, 10, 12}` | **Supported** | `trtllm_batch_decode` auto → xqa when `major != 10` |
| **trtllm-gen** | `major == 10` only | **Not available** | Auto selects this

TL;DR of the cause: the reference and kernels are all fine. Most time is spent on cold kernel compilation. On a B200 I locally see ~800 cases that collapses to ~200 cute.compile calls based on the cache key logic.

For some kernels, B/tile_v/T/cache flags/pool-strides each key a new compile. Would be great if we can make the kernels batch and/or seqlen dynamic to systematically reduce unit testing time."

items.title: [Feature] GB300 (SM103): no shipped autotune configs, and tuning results are not reused across processes by default
items.author: nperrin-fr
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On GB300 (SM103), every process starts with no tuned tactics, and what it tunes is lost when it exits:

1. **No bundled configs for SM103 or for any GEMM.** With `FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNER_LOAD_FROM_FILE=1`, the loader imports `flashinfer.tuning_configs.v0_1_trtllm_fused_moe_NVIDIA_GB300`, which does not exist. The package ships only `v0_1_trtllm_fused_moe_NVIDIA_B200.py` and `v0_1_trtllm_fused_moe_NVIDIA_GB200.py`, and both cover only trtllm fused MoE; no bundled file covers a GEMM op on any GPU.
2. **flashinfer-jit-cache-sm103a ships no configs either.** It contains compiled modules only (950 `.so` files plus `manifest.json`).
3. **No persistence by default.** `autotune(True)` results stay in process memory. A fresh process re-tunes from scratch unless the caller passes `cache=` or uses the experimental `autotune_v2` (#3920).

## Environment

- flashinfer-python 0.7.1, flashinfer-cubin 0.7.1, flashinfer-jit-cache and flashinfer-jit-cache-sm103a 0.7.1+cu130
- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0, torch 2.14.0+cu130
- NVIDIA GB300 (SM103), aarch64

## Reproduce

Save the script below as `repro_autotune.py`, then run:

```bash
export FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE=$PWD/fi_ws && mkdir -p $FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE
python repro_autotune.py tune; python repro_autotune.py tune   # two fresh processes
FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNER_LOAD_FROM_FILE=1 python repro_autotune.py serve
```

<details><summary>repro_autotune.py</summary>

```python
"""On GB300 nothing tuned ships, and tuning results are not reused across processes by default.

    export FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE=$PWD/fi_ws
    python repro_autotune.py tune      # run twice: each fresh process re-tunes from scratch
    FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNER_LOAD_FROM_FILE=1 python repro_autotune.py serve
"""

import importlib
import importlib.metadata as md
import os
import pathlib
import sys
import time

import torch

import flashinfer
from flashinfer.autotuner import AutoTuner, autotune
from flashinfer.autotuner import autotuner as fi_autotuner

SHAPES = [(4096, 4096), (7168, 2048), (2048, 7168)]  # (n, k)


def timed(fn):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    start = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return time.perf_counter() - start


def run_all(m):
    for n, k in SHAPES:
        a = torch.randn(m, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        b = torch.randn(n, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16).t()  # (k, n), column-major
        flashinfer.mm_bf16(a, b, backend="auto")


print(f"flashinfer {flashinfer.__version__}, {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
mode = sys.argv[1]

if mode == "tune":
    with autotune(True):
        print(f"cold tuning of mm_bf16(backend='auto'), 3 shapes: {timed(lambda: run_all(16)):.1f} s")
    print(f"tuned entries held in memory: {len(AutoTuner.get().profiling_cache)}")
    root = pathlib.Path(os.environ["FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE"])
    print(f"json files under FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE: {sorted(str(p.relative_to(root)) for p in root.rglob('*.json'))}")

elif mode == "serve":
    # What ships for this GPU: the legacy bundled configs, and the jit-cache wheels.
    module = fi_autotuner.get_config_path(is_module=True)
    try:
        importlib.import_module(module)
        print(f"bundled config module {module}: found")
    except ImportError:
        print(f"bundled config module {module}: NOT FOUND")
    bundled = sorted(p.name for p in (pathlib.Path(flashinfer.__file__).parent / "tuning_configs").glob("*.py"))
    print(f"flashinfer/tuning_configs: {bundled}")
    for dist in md.distributions():
        name = dist.metadata["Name"] or ""
        if name.startswith("flashinfer-jit-cache") and dist.files and str(dist.locate_file("")).startswith(sys.prefix):
            other = [str(f) for f in dist.files if not str(f).endswith((".so", ".pyc")) and "dist-info" not in str(f)]
            print(f"{name} {dist.version}: {sum(str(f).endswith('.so') for f in dist.files)} .so, other files {other}")
    # Serving outside autotune(): every GEMM falls back to tactic -1.
    with autotune(False):
        run_all(16)
```

</details>

## Result

Each `tune` run is a fresh process with the same `FLASHINFER_WORKSPACE_BASE`.

| run | tuning time, 3 shapes | tuned entries in memory | tuning results on disk |
|---|---|---|---|
| tune, process 1 | 100.7 s | 15 | none |
| tune, process 2 | 18.7 s | 15 | none |

Process 2 repeats the full tuning pass. Process 1 is slower only because it also JIT-built `bf16_gemm_cutlass` and `tinygemm2`, which the sm103a jit-cache does not include; process 2 loaded those builds from `cached_ops/`.

`serve` with `FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNER_LOAD_FROM_FILE=1`:

```
bundled config module flashinfer.tuning_configs.v0_1_trtllm_fused_moe_NVIDIA_GB300: NOT FOUND
flashinfer/tuning_configs: ['v0_1_trtllm_fused_moe_NVIDIA_B200.py', 'v0_1_trtllm_fused_moe_NVIDIA_GB200.py']
flashinfer-jit-cache-sm103a 0.7.1+cu130: 950 .so, other files ['.../providers/sm103a/__init__.py', '.../_build_meta.py', '.../manifest.json']
[Autotuner]: Loading configs for ('bf16_gemm', 'CudnnBf16GemmRunner', ...) from file failed; Using default configs instead.
(the same line for CublasltBf16GemmRunner, CutlassBf16GemmRunner, TGVRunner and TinyGemmBf16GemmRunner, for every shape)
```

At model scale, a full startup tuning pass of a large NVFP4 MoE model at TP4 on GB300 took 1612 s cold, versus 26-31 s when the framework persisted the results itself.

## Request

Ship tuned configs for SM103, including the GEMM ops, for example next to the per-arch jit-cache wheels. Or make persisted tuning the default by graduating `autotune_v2`. Today every deployment on GB300 pays the full tuning cost on every start unless the framework builds its own persistence.

items.title: feat: Add AIBrix Chat - a frontend demo portal for LLM inference
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

AIBrix provides powerful infrastructure for LLM inference, but we lack a user-facing demo to showcase its capabilities. Currently, users need to interact with AIBrix through API calls, or third-party clients, which creates friction when:

- Live demos — Presenting AIBrix at conferences, meetups, or internal reviews requires a polished UI
- End-to-end validation — Testing the full stack (gateway routing, model serving, load balancing) benefits from a real frontend client
- Onboarding — A working chat UI makes it easier for new contributors to understand the user-facing value of the infrastructure

### Use Case

Add a lightweight chat portal under apps/chat/web/ that serves as both a demo and a functional frontend for AIBrix-managed LLM endpoints.

What it includes:
- Chat interface with conversation management (create, search, delete, move)
- Project organization for grouping related conversations
- Model selector supporting multiple backends
- Sidebar navigation with chat history
- Dark-themed, responsive UI built with React + Vite + Tailwind CSS


Architecture:
```
  apps/
  ├── chat/
   │   ├── web/          # React frontend
   │   └── api/          # Backend proxy for LLM endpoints (planned)
```

### Proposed Solution

Why in-repo (not a separate project)?

1. Dogfooding — The chat portal consumes AIBrix gateway APIs directly, validating routing algorithms, model selection, and streaming behavior from a real client
2. Faster iteration — Co-locating with infrastructure code means API and frontend changes can land together
3. Visibility — Contributors are more likely to maintain something that lives alongside the core project
4. Demo-ready — A single repo clone gives users everything needed for a complete demo

### Task break down

#### Models and vLLM adaptatio

> Note: we do not necessarily need to host every model, each model endpoint should be fully replaced by cloud api. that means if we find some model are not supported in vllm-omni, we just use openai endpoint as replacement.

- [x] Test some ASR models (e.g.Qwen3-ASR) and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [x] Test some TTS models and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [x] Test Image Edit or Image Generation model  and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [x] Test Video Generation model  (e.g. WAN-2.1) and make sure vLLM or vLLM-omni support it.
- [ ] Enable tool search/web search for LLM models.

#### Platform
- [x] Build lightweight frontend framework (nodejs)
- [x] Build python backend skeleton (python)
- [x] Make sure endpoint is compatible with OpenAI API
- [ ] Make sure endpoint is compatible with self-hosted models (via vllm directly).
- [ ] Make sure endpoint is compatible with self-hosted models (via aibrix directly - test with standalone, faster).
- [ ] Build applications -> CI, Docker, Deployment
- [ ] Prepare AIBrix deployment yaml for all the demo @Jeffwan 

#### Features
- [ ] Support reasoning model, UI shows thinking etc.
- [ ] Make sure streaming, reasoning are working well with the web UI.
- [ ] Enable user Login using github or simple login
- [ ] Enable user - level token based rate limiting
- [ ] P2: Finish Job Queue for near real time submission
- [ ] P2: Support object storage uploads if user configure the backend storage
- [ ] P2: Introduce SQLite to persist the conversation dat
- [ ] P2: Add intent router or intent classification component
- [ ] P2: Add Prompt Enhancer module

items.title: [Bug]: Qwen3-VL: rewriting video_metadata.total_num_frames without rescaling fps makes default HF frame sampling keep only min_frames and produces wrong `<t seconds>` timestamps
items.author: john-liu-dev
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM 1.3.0rc25 (`785c948`); transformers 5.5.4 (the version pinned in `requirements.txt`, also on `main`).
- Re-checked on `main` at `760a584` (2026-10-12): `_decide_do_sample_frames` and `Qwen3VLInputProcessorBase._preprocess` are identical to rc25 (main L169-221 and L349-425).
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct` (the 8B model goes through the same code path).
- Seen end-to-end through the NVIDIA Dynamo TensorRT-LLM backend (`7e8b9fc2`) in aggregated multimodal mode; the reproduction below is CPU-only and needs only the HF processor.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [x] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`Qwen3VLInputProcessorBase._preprocess` (`tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/modeling_qwen3vl.py`, L400-412 in rc25, L402-414 on `main`) forwards `VideoData.metadata` to the HF processor with `total_num_frames` rewritten to `len(vd.frames)`, so that HF's `sample_frames` (`np.linspace(0, total_num_frames - 1, num_frames)`) stays in range. The metadata `fps` (source video fps) and `frames_indices` are left untouched. When the IO layer has already subsampled the clip (e.g. 40 frames out of a 10 s / 24 fps / 240-frame video), HF's `Qwen3VLVideoProcessor` therefore believes the video is 40/24 = 1.67 s long and, with its class defaults (`fps=2`, `min_frames=4`), samples `int(40/24*2) = 3 -> 4` frames. This is the default path: when the caller passes no `do_sample_frames` / `num_frames` / `fps`, `_decide_do_sample_frames` (L167-219 in rc25, L169-221 on `main`) turns sampling on to match HF's class default. Two consequences:

1. Only 4 of the 40 decoded frames reach the ViT (1760 visual tokens instead of 11880). Any caller that does not pass `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` (or an exact `num_frames`) silently gets a 4-frame summary of the video, regardless of clip length (a 30 s clip decoded to 40 frames gives the identical 4-frame result).
2. The `<t seconds>` timestamp tokens inserted by the processor are computed from the resampled indices over the rewritten `total_num_frames` divided by the *source* fps, so they are compressed by (decoded frames / source frames): for the 10 s clip the model sees `<0.3 seconds>` and `<1.4 seconds>` for frames that are actually at about 0 s, 3.3 s, 6.7 s and 10 s.

With `do_sample_frames=False` the processor uses `frames_indices / fps`, and both the frame count and the timestamps are correct, which shows the frame list itself is fine; only the sampling-path metadata is inconsistent. For comparison, HF sampling the 240-frame source itself at the default fps=2 would keep `int(240/24*2) = 20` frames with timestamps in source seconds, so the rewrite also makes the default path diverge from stock HF, which `_decide_do_sample_frames` intends to match.

Reproduction (CPU only, HF processor only):

- Decode a 10 s, 24 fps, 1280x720 H.264 clip into 40 uniformly spaced RGB float32 `(C, H, W)` tensors in [0, 1], metadata = `{"fps": 24.0, "total_num_frames": 240, "duration": 10.0, "frames_indices": linspace(0, 239, 40)}`.
- Apply the same rewrite as `_preprocess` (`total_num_frames := 40`) and call `AutoProcessor.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct")(text=[chat_template_text], videos=[frames], video_metadata=[meta], do_sample_frames=True, do_rescale=False, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")`.
- Observe `video_grid_thw == [2, 44, 80]`, 1760 `<|video_pad|>` tokens, timestamps `<0.3 seconds>`, `<1.4 seconds>`.
- Same call with `do_sample_frames=False`: `video_grid_thw == [20, 36, 66]`, 11880 tokens, timestamps `<0.1 seconds>`, `<0.6 seconds>`, `<1.1 seconds>`, `<1.6 seconds>`, ... (one per 0.5 s across the clip).
- Without the rewrite (original `total_num_frames=240`) HF raises `IndexError: index 50 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 40`, which confirms why the rewrite exists.
- End-to-end: the Dynamo TensorRT-LLM worker's `/metrics` reports `trtllm_prompt_tokens_total = 1789` (= 1760 visual + 4 vision markers + 12 timestamp tokens + 13 text) for this request.

### Expected behavior

Either (a) when rewriting `total_num_frames` to the decoded count, also rescale `fps` to `len(frames) / duration` and reset `frames_indices` to `range(len(frames))`, so HF's duration and timestamps stay consistent with the frames it receives, or (b) default `do_sample_frames` to False whenever the caller passes an already-subsampled frame list with `frames_indices` (the IO layer has done the sampling), and only sample when the caller explicitly asks for `num_frames` / `fps`.

### actual behavior

With default `mm_processor_kwargs`, 4 of 40 decoded frames reach the ViT and the timestamps are compressed by 40/240 (details under Reproduction).

### additional notes

**Impact.** Silent quality loss for every video request that relies on defaults (temporal reasoning over a ~2 s window of a longer clip, wrong timestamps), plus misleading throughput numbers (the prompt is ~7x shorter than intended).

**Workaround.** Pass `mm_processor_kwargs={"do_sample_frames": False}` per request (the frame count is then whatever the IO layer decoded, e.g. `DYN_MM_VIDEO_NUM_FRAMES` in Dynamo).

The metadata rewrite and `_decide_do_sample_frames` were introduced in #15598.

**Related:** #20138 (Qwen3-VL video over the E/PD handoff; its reproduction passes `do_sample_frames=False` to get all decoded frames into the ViT, i.e. the workaround above).

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.
